chunks.text:
Legal is a two-horse capital race. Harvey served more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations in over 60 countries as of March 2026 — its own disclosure . Sacra's user count is materially higher, carries no source, and post-dates Harvey's own by two months, so the site uses the company's. Harvey raised at $11bn in March 2026 on an estimated $300m ARR ; Legora raised $550m at $5.55bn . Harvey's last well-sourced revenue figure is the $100m it reached in August 2025, three years after founding .

Support agents are the richest-priced. Sierra raised $950m at a $15.8bn post-money valuation in May 2026 . There are two revenue denominators available and they disagree: Sacra estimates $200m , while Sierra itself said it had passed $150m in February 2026, with coverage of the May round still reporting ARR above $150m . This page uses the company's figure, which is the lower revenue and therefore the less flattering multiple. Either way the growth is steep: an estimated $26m at the end of 2024 . Decagon raised $250m at $4.5bn in January 2026 against an estimated $35m annualized in October 2025 .

Enterprise search and GTM. Glean went from $100m ARR at fiscal year end January 2025 to $300m in May 2026 . Clay reached an estimated $150m ; Perplexity an estimated $500m in April 2026 , where the reported ~335% growth rate and the separate full-year-2025 figure on the same page are two different comparisons and must not be welded together.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
applications — Concentration & chokepoints. The obvious chokepoint is the model bill. OpenAI's inference costs reached an estimated $8.4bn in 2025 , and the lineage matters: the figure originates with Ed Zitron's leaked-document reporting and Sacra is plausibly downstream of it. That is one original plus one relay, not two measurements.

Forecast, per Sacra: OpenAI inference costs projected at $14.1bn for 2026, against $8.4bn in 2025 . Independent reporting corroborates only the direction — that the day-to-day expense of running models quadrupled in 2025.

The less obvious chokepoint is measurement, and it is the reason for this page's verdict. One research shop supplies the denominator for most of the layer's valuation arithmetic: Claude Code's $2.5bn , Abridge's $100m , Sierra's $26m and $200m , Decagon's $35m , Replit's $525m and its margin range , Harvey's $300m are all single-source, and several carry an explicit corpus flag that they may not anchor a verdict alone. There is no equivalent of a 10-Q anywhere in this layer.

Customer concentration runs the other way from the layers below: it is diffuse at the bottom and concentrating at the top. Anthropic reported more than 300,000 business customers as of October 2025 — the count is Sacra-lineage, though the accompanying claim that business customers are ~80% of revenue is independently corroborated — and more than 1,000 customers spending over $1m a year by April 2026 . Enterprise passed 40% of OpenAI revenue in 2026 on Sacra's estimate , which is the mix shift that makes this layer look like software rather than like a consumer subscription business.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
applications — Lead times & capacity. There is no permit queue here and no lead time on physical supply. The two real constraints are how fast a product gets inside a regulated profession, and what a token costs when it gets there.

The first constraint is slower than the funding rounds imply. Harvey took three years from founding to $100m ARR . Glean took roughly sixteen months to triple from $100m to $300m . Cursor is the outlier that everyone extrapolates from, tripling from $1bn to $3bn in six months.

The second constraint does not reliably move in the vendor's favour. Inference prices for fixed benchmark performance fell at a median 50× per year in Epoch AI's regression , which is the tailwind every app-layer business plan assumes. But Anthropic has scheduled Claude Sonnet 5's output price to rise from $10 to $15 per million tokens on 1 September 2026 . Per-capability deflation and per-product price increases are both true, and an application with fixed $0.99 outcome pricing eats the difference.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
applications — 2019 → today. 2019. This layer does not exist. AI is a feature inside software priced per seat, and no company buys a model.

2022–23. ChatGPT arrives and the horizontal assistant becomes a category. Pricing is a monthly consumer subscription bolted onto a research preview.

2025. Revenue at scale, and the shape becomes visible: coding first, then legal, then support. Cursor crosses $1bn annualized in November ; Harvey crosses $100m in August ; Glean crosses $100m at its January fiscal year end .

2026. Three things land at once. Outcome pricing appears as a published list price . Valuations detach from measurable revenue — $15.8bn for Sierra , $11bn for Harvey . And the layer produces a real exit at $60bn in stock , which is the first hard number in the layer's short history.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
applications — Commoditization pressure. The clearest commoditization evidence in the layer is a vendor cutting prices and growing anyway. Clay cut many native enrichment prices by 50 to 90% in March 2026 while restructuring to a dual-meter pricing system , and reached an estimated $150m ARR in May . Two qualifiers travel with that: the dual-meter restructuring is confirmed on Clay's own live pricing page, but the 50–90% cut is Sacra-only, and 90 is the top of a range rather than a point. Sacra's quoted tier price also does not match what Clay's live page shows, which is a small discrepancy pointing at a stale reading.

What resists commoditization is not the model and not the interface. It is the depth of the workflow and the switching cost inside a regulated profession — Harvey's 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations are a distribution position, not a technology one. The uncomfortable corollary is that the moat being purchased in legal AI is capital: $11bn behind Harvey and $5.55bn behind Legora is a two-horse race financed to exhaust a market, which is a distribution strategy rather than a product one.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
applications — Failure modes. Margin inversion. Replit's 2025 range from +36% to −14% is the mechanism: an agent that runs longer costs more, and a flat-priced product cannot pass that through. OpenAI's 33% shows the same pressure at the top of the layer. Blast radius: every outcome-priced product, and every seat-priced product whose usage is unbounded.

A multiple built on an estimate. Decagon's $4.5bn against $35m annualized is roughly 128 times — arithmetic over the two facts cited in this sentence, and the denominator is an estimate. Sierra's $15.8bn is roughly 105 times the company's own ">$150m" , and roughly 79 times Sacra's higher estimate . A site whose whole claim is citation discipline should not quietly pick the denominator that makes the multiple look better, so this page prints the company's. Harvey's $11bn against an estimated $300m is roughly 37 times forward , on the same kind of unverified denominator.

Absorption by the model provider. Claude Code at a reported $2.5bn annualized means Anthropic sells both the coding product and the tokens powering its largest competitor in that category. The application layer's suppliers are also its rivals, and they see its usage data.

Measurement failure. Abridge is the warning case: the widely repeated $316m Series E extension in April 2026 is not company-confirmed and comes from secondary-market data providers , and its last solid revenue figure is the estimated $100m from May 2025 . A layer whose numbers arrive through this pipe will reprice suddenly when a real filing appears.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: applications — Open questions. - What is the real gross margin of an agentic application? One company's range, from one unsourced sentence, is the entire public evidence base . Every valuation in the layer implies an answer nobody has published. - Does outcome pricing survive a cost spike? Fin's $0.99 is a fixed price against a variable cost. Anthropic's scheduled September 2026 increase is the first live test. - Do the vertical apps hold their seats once the labs ship the same workflow? Harvey's 100,000 lawyers are the strongest evidence for yes; Claude Code's growth inside coding is the evidence for no. - Is the $60bn Cursor mark a price or an artefact of stock? It was all-stock , paid in the equity of a private buyer, and the corpus has no data on the exchange terms. - Where does enterprise revenue actually settle relative to consumer? OpenAI passing 40% enterprise against 900 million weekly consumers describes two businesses with different margins, and only the estimate exists for the split.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the capital-policy layer: overbuilt. The commitments that set the narrative are intents — a letter of intent, an attributed total, a tender not yet issued. The obligations that are contractual sit in bankruptcy-remote subsidiaries.

The counter, per The Federal Reserve's Financial Stability Report: AI debt is being layered onto an under-levered corporate sector: total US private nonfinancial credit was $42.2tn in Q2 2025, with the debt-to-GDP ratio at its lowest level in two decades.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
capital-policy — Introduction. Two documents decide whether the other fifteen layers get built. A term sheet, and an export licence.

This is the layer where the discourse is loudest and the underlying paper is softest. The two most-quoted numbers in the entire AI buildout — NVIDIA's "$100bn into OpenAI" and OpenAI's "$1.4 trillion of commitments" — are, respectively, a letter of intent that had not closed as of NVIDIA's own annual filing, and a figure Sam Altman attributed in November 2025 covering roughly eight years. Meanwhile the paper that is binding — an $8.5bn term loan secured on substantially all the assets of a bankruptcy-remote CoreWeave subsidiary and a pledge of its equity — gets almost no coverage at all. This page is organised around that inversion.

August 2026 supplied a third, larger example. NVIDIA signed memorandums of understanding with Apollo Global, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to mobilise more than $500bn of third-party capital for the build-out . Read the instrument, not the headline: memorandums of understanding, and NVIDIA's own language is that the deal is subject to final agreement. It belongs in the same column as the letter of intent and the attributed total — a number that shapes expectations without yet obliging anyone to pay.

The market said as much on the day. NVIDIA fell about 1.1% on the report and closed 2.9% lower, erasing close to $60bn of market capitalisation . A half-trillion-dollar funding partnership announced by a supplier read to investors as evidence of circularity rather than of demand, which is the cleanest market verdict on this layer's structure anyone has yet delivered.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
The market said as much on the day. NVIDIA fell about 1.1% on the report and closed 2.9% lower, erasing close to $60bn of market capitalisation . A half-trillion-dollar funding partnership announced by a supplier read to investors as evidence of circularity rather than of demand, which is the cleanest market verdict on this layer's structure anyone has yet delivered.

Two more figures arrived with it, and both are forecasts rather than measurements: Morgan Stanley's projection that hyperscalers spend $3.5tn between 2026 and 2028 , and Apollo president Jim Zelter's estimate of more than $8tn of eventual investment — the latter from an executive whose firm earns fees financing it. The same reporting carries one item that is not a number at all: NVIDIA in talks to guarantee a 10 GW data centre in Ohio leased to OpenAI, sourced to one person familiar with the matter, with no amount and no conclusion . Recorded here at low confidence precisely because it is the shape of claim this layer keeps mistaking for a commitment.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
capital-policy — What this layer is. Money that must be repaid on a schedule, and permission that can be withdrawn by rule.

The capital half has three tiers. Investment-grade bonds issued on a hyperscaler's own credit. Private credit and asset-backed structures, where the collateral is a rack of GPUs or a lease on a building. Vendor equity, where the supplier of the chips is also an investor in the buyer of the chips.

The policy half is one agency's rulebook. The Bureau of Industry and Security decides which accelerators may leave the United States, for whom, and on what conditions — and its rulebook has been written, rescinded, and in one central case left unreplaced.

The physical anchor: a signature page, and a certification form. Neither appears in any of the fifteen layers below, and both can stop all of them.

chunks.heading: Unit economics — the price of AI money
chunks.text:
capital-policy — Unit economics — the price of AI money. The price of AI money is set by where the asset sits, not by what the asset is — and CoreWeave's $8.5bn delayed-draw term loan, closed 30 March 2026, is the cleanest demonstration. It runs through a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary, is secured by substantially all of that subsidiary's assets plus a pledge of its equity, and funds GPU capital expenditure for an unnamed customer contract . That structure is the correction that matters: the corpus previously recorded the collateral as having shifted from GPUs to customer contracts — lending against counterparty credit rather than asset value. The filed structure is the opposite. The GPUs are the lien. The customer contract sits in the covenant package, not in the security.

The terms are the part worth memorising, because they are the only actual price of AI credit in this corpus rather than a headline about one. The facility priced at SOFR plus 225 basis points, with a 50 basis point fee on the undrawn commitment, a 1.15 times debt-service-coverage covenant, and a maturity of 31 March 2032 . Read those four numbers together and the structure explains itself: a spread that prices this as leveraged credit rather than infrastructure, a fee that makes idle capacity expensive, a coverage test that binds on cash flow rather than on asset value, and a six-year tenor set against GPUs whose useful life the operators one layer down cannot agree on.

chunks.heading: Unit economics — the price of AI money
chunks.text:
The terms are the part worth memorising, because they are the only actual price of AI credit in this corpus rather than a headline about one. The facility priced at SOFR plus 225 basis points, with a 50 basis point fee on the undrawn commitment, a 1.15 times debt-service-coverage covenant, and a maturity of 31 March 2032 . Read those four numbers together and the structure explains itself: a spread that prices this as leveraged credit rather than infrastructure, a fee that makes idle capacity expensive, a coverage test that binds on cash flow rather than on asset value, and a six-year tenor set against GPUs whose useful life the operators one layer down cannot agree on.

At the other end of the spectrum, the same class of asset gets financed at investment grade by moving it off the sponsor's balance sheet entirely. Meta and Blue Owl issued approximately $27bn of A+ rated bonds plus about $2.5bn of equity through a joint-venture SPV arranged by Morgan Stanley in October 2025, anchored by PIMCO . Same electrons, same silicon, a rating gap of many notches — and the gap is structural rather than operational. Compare the unsecured route on a hyperscaler's own credit: Meta's $30bn October 2025 bond drew an order book of about $125bn , roughly four times the deal, and Oracle raised $18bn in September 2025 largely to serve one customer contract .

The asset class did not exist three years ago. CoreWeave's $2.3bn facility of August 2023, led by Magnetar and Blackstone and collateralized by H100s , was the first at-scale GPU-backed loan; the $7.5bn delayed-draw facility followed in May 2024 .

Forecast, per Morgan Stanley Research: Approximately $2.9tn of global data-center capital expenditure from 2025 through 2028 , of which about $1.5tn requires debt financing, roughly $800bn of it from private credit . Note that a financing need is a different concept from debt outstanding.

chunks.heading: The loop
chunks.text:
capital-policy — The loop. In a normal capital structure the supplier, the customer and the investor are three parties. Here they are frequently one or two, and NVIDIA is the clearest case.

NVIDIA announced a letter of intent in September 2025 to invest up to $100bn in OpenAI, released progressively as each gigawatt of at least 10 GW of NVIDIA systems is deployed . Three qualifiers travel with that number and the site will not print it without them. "Letter of intent" is NVIDIA's own word in its own newsroom release, not a paraphrase — an earlier correction wrongly recast it as a memorandum of understanding on a Wikipedia citation, inverting the source hierarchy. NVIDIA's own forward-looking-statements section flags the $100bn as forward-looking, and the release closes by looking forward to "finalizing the details in the coming weeks." And NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K, filed months later, confirms no transaction had completed.

The same pattern repeats across the layer, each instance individually defensible: $5bn into Intel ; a pre-funded warrant for 21,065,936 Nebius shares raising about $2bn ; a $2bn private placement of CoreWeave Class A shares at $87.20 ; an agreement to purchase CoreWeave's residual unsold capacity valued at $6.3bn through 2032 ; and, with Microsoft, up to $15bn combined into Anthropic in the same month Anthropic committed to purchase $30bn of Azure capacity running on NVIDIA systems .

AMD's version is the most explicit price ever put on demand. It issued OpenAI a warrant on 5 October 2025 for up to 160 million shares at $0.01 each, vesting in tranches tied to Instinct deployments with the final tranche gated on a $600 share price . The load-bearing term is not the share count: full vesting is contingent on 6 GW of deployment . The "about 10% of the company" line in circulation appears nowhere in the 8-K — it is press arithmetic on the share count.

chunks.heading: The loop
chunks.text:
AMD's version is the most explicit price ever put on demand. It issued OpenAI a warrant on 5 October 2025 for up to 160 million shares at $0.01 each, vesting in tranches tied to Instinct deployments with the final tranche gated on a $600 share price . The load-bearing term is not the share count: full vesting is contingent on 6 GW of deployment . The "about 10% of the company" line in circulation appears nowhere in the 8-K — it is press arithmetic on the share count.

Microsoft holds both sides at once: an investment in OpenAI Group PBC valued at approximately $135bn, about 27% on an as-converted diluted basis after the October 2025 recapitalization , while OpenAI simultaneously contracted to buy an incremental $250bn of Azure services . Oracle's $300bn five-year, 4.5 GW contract with OpenAI is the reason its remaining performance obligations reached $455bn in Q1 FY2026, up 359% year over year . AWS added $38bn , and CoreWeave's combined OpenAI contracts reached about $22.4bn .

The one genuinely new thing in the loop is a buyer from outside it: Jane Street signed a $6bn AI cloud agreement with CoreWeave and made a $1bn equity investment . A gigawatt-scale compute buyer that is neither a hyperscaler nor a lab is the only datapoint here that widens the counterparty base rather than tightening it.

chunks.heading: How to read $1.4 trillion
chunks.text:
capital-policy — How to read $1.4 trillion. This is the most abused number in the AI discourse, and getting it right is the single most useful thing this page does.

Sam Altman said in November 2025 that OpenAI had about $1.4tn of data-center commitments, covering roughly 30 GW over about eight years . Four things follow.

It is an attributed figure, not a sum. The corpus previously recorded it as an aggregation of the Oracle, Microsoft, AWS and chip deals. That method was defective three ways: the cited contracts total $588bn, not $1,400bn, so roughly $800bn was unverifiable under the site's own rules; it counted NVIDIA's up-to-$100bn investment into OpenAI as an outbound purchase; and Oracle's $300bn is largely delivered through Stargate sites carrying their own $500bn headline, so the sum double-counted. Any chart presenting this as a stacked bar of the named deals is wrong. The site's own cited contracts account for $588bn of it ; the balance is not publicly itemised.

The denominator has to be named. OpenAI's annualized revenue run rate exceeded $20bn exiting 2025, against full-year 2025 revenue of approximately $13bn . The comparison in circulation uses the $13bn, which is a full-year figure and roughly 35% low against the metric the sentence claims to be measuring. Use the run rate.

The horizon has to be stated. Commitments spanning about eight years set against a single year of revenue compare unlike things. The valid observation is narrower and still striking: a company whose equity was marked at $500bn in an October 2025 secondary sale, up from $157bn a year earlier , has signed forward compute obligations that are a large multiple of any revenue it has yet earned.

chunks.heading: How to read $1.4 trillion
chunks.text:
The horizon has to be stated. Commitments spanning about eight years set against a single year of revenue compare unlike things. The valid observation is narrower and still striking: a company whose equity was marked at $500bn in an October 2025 secondary sale, up from $157bn a year earlier , has signed forward compute obligations that are a large multiple of any revenue it has yet earned.

Stargate's own headline is a plan, not a contract. It was announced in January 2025 with a stated intent to spend up to $500bn on US AI infrastructure by 2029 — logged as a company claim. The reported equity structure was never confirmed by the parties and does not internally reconcile: SoftBank and OpenAI at $19bn each for 40%, with Oracle and MGX at about $7bn each — components that do not reconcile with other researchers' descriptions of founding-partner equity in the same vehicle.

chunks.heading: Where the leverage actually sits
chunks.text:
capital-policy — Where the leverage actually sits. The vehicle is the point. Private capital groups including Apollo and Blackstone have built multibillion-dollar, investment-grade-rated financings for companies such as Meta and Intel that sit off those companies' corporate balance sheets . Capital is raised into a separately rated entity, so the obligation never appears as corporate debt and never shows up in the leverage ratios anyone screens on. That is the same architecture as the bankruptcy-remote subsidiary below, sold to a different buyer — and it is why a sector that looks under-levered at the parent can be carrying a great deal of contracted obligation one entity down.

Not on OpenAI's balance sheet. This is the correction that matters most in the layer, because the entire circular-capital argument is about whose credit carries the risk.

A JPMorgan-led lender group provided a $7.1bn construction loan in May 2025 — and the borrower is the Crusoe–Blue Owl joint venture developing Abilene Phase 2, which Oracle leases, not OpenAI . The corpus previously named OpenAI as borrower and conflated this facility with a smaller Phase 1 loan from late 2024. SoftBank's $15bn one-year bridge, signed 10 April 2025 across 21 banks, is real and closed .

chunks.heading: Where the leverage actually sits
chunks.text:
A JPMorgan-led lender group provided a $7.1bn construction loan in May 2025 — and the borrower is the Crusoe–Blue Owl joint venture developing Abilene Phase 2, which Oracle leases, not OpenAI . The corpus previously named OpenAI as borrower and conflated this facility with a smaller Phase 1 loan from late 2024. SoftBank's $15bn one-year bridge, signed 10 April 2025 across 21 banks, is real and closed .

The template is documented in Meta's own filings, and it is worth reading carefully because it will be copied. Meta and Blue Owl formed a joint venture in October 2025 to develop the Richland Parish campus, committing to fund pro rata shares of approximately $27bn in total estimated development costs — that is a cost estimate funded over time, not the JV's size. Now put the headline next to what was actually capitalised. At formation Meta contributed $4.3bn and Blue Owl $7.0bn in cash — $11.3bn in total — and Meta immediately took a one-time distribution of $2.6bn while holding a 20% interest . So the venture that carries a $27bn number opened with $11.3bn of equity, of which Meta's net cash outlay was $1.7bn . That gap is not an accounting curiosity — it is the structure. Meta then leases the campus back, with operating leases commencing at the end of the decade, renewal options extending for decades after that, and a residual value guarantee covering the venture's early years. The Venture is an unconsolidated variable interest entity accounted for under the equity method — which is the whole point of the structure.

The number that actually measures the exposure is not the $27bn headline. Meta disclosed maximum exposure to loss of $45.95bn against an equity carrying value of $1.83bn as of 31 December 2025 . Twenty-five times the carried equity, on one venture, disclosed by the sponsor, with no residual-value-guarantee liability recorded.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
capital-policy — 2019 → today. 2019. AI capex comes out of operating cash flow. Export controls are entity-specific and rare. There is no such thing as a GPU-backed loan.

2023–24. The asset class is invented, and it is invented by one company: a $2.3bn GPU-collateralized facility then a $7.5bn delayed-draw term loan . Nobody had previously lent billions against depreciating silicon.

2025–26. Structure replaces balance sheet, and the regulator notices. $27bn of A+ JV bonds , an $8.5bn bankruptcy-remote facility , and concentration to match: the Magnificent 7 went from about 20% to nearly 35% of S&P 500 market capitalization between November 2022 and late 2025 . 30% of the Federal Reserve's market-outreach contacts named AI among salient financial-stability risks in Fall 2025, up from 9% in Spring .

Michael Burry's claim that hyperscalers will understate depreciation by about $176bn across 2026–28 by extending server useful lives belongs in this timeline as what it is: the opinion of a named short-seller with positions, arguing about the layer above.

chunks.heading: What the export rules actually say
chunks.text:
capital-policy — What the export rules actually say. Read the rule text, not the preamble. The January 2026 BIS rule permits case-by-case licensing to China and Macau only for commodities certified below 21,000 total processing performance , with a companion cap on total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s ; the rule names the H200 and MI325X as the reference class. Everything above the thresholds keeps a presumption of denial. The loosening covers a sub-frontier tier only.

Two details are routinely reported wrong. First, the volume cap is not a unit ratio. The rule caps licensed China and Macau exports at 50% of the aggregate total processing performance cumulatively shipped to US end users for the same commodity , measured from first commercial US shipment through to the licence application date. The preamble states it loosely in product-volume terms; the operative section binds on cumulative aggregate TPP, which is materially stricter — a vendor cannot backload China volume, and the ratio is scored against lifetime US performance shipped. Any chart showing this as a unit ratio is mislabelled.

Second, there are nine certification conditions, not five : US volumes and specs, US supply sufficiency and no foundry diversion, the aggregate-TPP cap, no military or WMD end use, consignee KYC against remote access, a list of IaaS remote end users in named restricted destinations, a commitment not to transfer model weights or grant remote access to restricted parties, a physical-security demonstration, and third-party lab review of every shipment before export. The earlier count of five came from merging preamble bullets and dropping four conditions.

chunks.heading: What the export rules actually say
chunks.text:
Second, there are nine certification conditions, not five : US volumes and specs, US supply sufficiency and no foundry diversion, the aggregate-TPP cap, no military or WMD end use, consignee KYC against remote access, a list of IaaS remote end users in named restricted destinations, a commitment not to transfer model weights or grant remote access to restricted parties, a physical-security demonstration, and third-party lab review of every shipment before export. The earlier count of five came from merging preamble bullets and dropping four conditions.

The Gulf side of the same policy is narrower than its headline too. BIS moved the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 to A:5 effective 10 July 2026, granting licence-free access to advanced computing items — but the named approved entities in Supplement 8 are two: G42, including G42 Cloud Technology LLC, and Core42. MGX is not one of them; BIS says only that it intends to review MGX applications favourably, and licences are still required. And the authorisation for G42 and Core42 automatically expires on 6 April 2027 absent further notice. Supplement 8 separately lists eight US-headquartered AI companies and their subsidiaries, which makes the rule a US-cloud-in-the-Gulf authorisation as much as a UAE one. The frequently drawn contrast — the UAE gets no cap while China gets 50% — survives only with that sunset attached.

Two things the rulebook does not contain are as important as what it does. The GAIN AI Act passed the Senate inside the FY2026 NDAA on 9 October 2025 and was stripped before the Act was signed on 18 December , leaving export-control authority over AI chips discretionary and unlegislated. And the AI Diffusion rule — the first US control on model weights — was rescinded, with NVIDIA reporting in May 2026 that the scope, timing and requirements of any replacement remained uncertain 12 months later . A Federal Register search returns neither a rescission rule nor a replacement.

chunks.heading: What the export rules actually say
chunks.text:
Two things the rulebook does not contain are as important as what it does. The GAIN AI Act passed the Senate inside the FY2026 NDAA on 9 October 2025 and was stripped before the Act was signed on 18 December , leaving export-control authority over AI chips discretionary and unlegislated. And the AI Diffusion rule — the first US control on model weights — was rescinded, with NVIDIA reporting in May 2026 that the scope, timing and requirements of any replacement remained uncertain 12 months later . A Federal Register search returns neither a rescission rule nor a replacement.

Then there is the arrangement that exists only verbally. US officials expressed an expectation of receiving 15% or more of revenue from licensed NVIDIA sales to China — and NVIDIA's own 10-Q states that the government "did not publish a regulation codifying such requirement" . A sovereign revenue share operating on expectation, absent from the January 2026 rule text.

chunks.heading: The enforcement gap
chunks.text:
capital-policy — The enforcement gap. Rules tightened on paper while the machinery that enforces them slowed down. Between 2018 and 2024, BIS added entities to the Entity List every 35 days on average . As of 26 June 2026, eight months had passed with no additions at all — the longest gap since 2008 . The September 2025 affiliates rule, which extended controls to any entity at least half-owned by a listed party and covered an estimated 20,000 companies in China , was suspended for 12 months and is reimposed effective 10 November 2026 .

Scale the enforcer against the problem. Gregory Allen reported BIS operating on a budget just under $200m with fewer than 600 employees — a 2024 figure, with no newer public equivalent. Against that: a March 2026 indictment alleges a Southeast Asian intermediary purchased approximately $2.5bn of servers from a US manufacturer for unlicensed diversion to China , including at least about $510m in the three weeks between late April and mid-May 2025 alone . The concealment method is the detail worth keeping: thousands of non-working physical replica servers staged to defeat the manufacturer's own compliance audits. That is the strongest available evidence that OEM end-use verification fails at scale. These are allegations, not adjudicated facts.

One case is adjudicated. Prosecutors stated that a Texas network exported or attempted to export at least $160m of controlled H100 and H200 GPUs between October 2024 and May 2025 — and the principal pleaded guilty, which makes this the layer's one conviction rather than an allegation. A separate November 2025 indictment charges four defendants with routing NVIDIA GPUs to China through Malaysia and Thailand using a Florida realty company that had never conducted a real estate transaction , naming the transshipment corridor.

chunks.heading: The other side of the wall
chunks.text:
capital-policy — The other side of the wall. The most counter-intuitive finding in this layer: NVIDIA's China data-center collapse was caused by Beijing, not Washington. Chinese guidance in November 2025 requires state-funded data-centre projects to use only domestically made AI chips, with projects less than 30% complete ordered to remove installed foreign chips . Two readings differ on whether the rule bans acquiring or also mandates removal, and NVIDIA's own filing does not describe it — its adjacent language is that the Chinese government "has encouraged customers to purchase from our China-based competitors," which is circumstantial support only. The result is not ambiguous: NVIDIA shipped no Data Center Hopper products to China in the quarter ended 26 April 2026, against $4.6bn a year earlier , and Jensen Huang said in April 2026 that NVIDIA's share of China's AI accelerator market had fallen to zero . A country that believed itself choked would not ban the chips it can still get.

Forecast, per Bloomberg Intelligence: The four largest US hyperscalers spend more than $400bn on AI capital expenditure in 2026, while five named Chinese cloud providers stay flat from a 2025 base below $40bn . The Chinese side of that ratio counts five listed commercial cloud providers, not state-directed programmes, so read it as a comparison of corporate buildouts rather than of countries.

China's leverage is downstream instead. The IEA estimates full implementation of its expanded rare-earth export controls would put about $6.5tn a year of downstream production outside China at risk . ASML records that China suspended those restrictions for 12 months until 10 November 2026 — the same date the US affiliates rule comes back into force . Two truces, negotiated separately, lapsing on one day. That is the calendar risk on this page.

chunks.heading: The other side of the wall
chunks.text:
China's leverage is downstream instead. The IEA estimates full implementation of its expanded rare-earth export controls would put about $6.5tn a year of downstream production outside China at risk . ASML records that China suspended those restrictions for 12 months until 10 November 2026 — the same date the US affiliates rule comes back into force . Two truces, negotiated separately, lapsing on one day. That is the calendar risk on this page.

The tail risk is Taiwan, and the honest position is that nobody has modelled it for the AI era. Rhodium Group estimated that a Chinese blockade halting all Taiwan trade would put well over $2tn of global economic activity at risk , and Rhodium itself calls that "a conservative and partial estimate," excluding second-order effects, escalation and sanctions. Bloomberg Economics' widely quoted alternative measures a different thing — first-year GDP loss, not activity at risk — so the two must not be averaged. Neither uses 2025 AI-era trade weights. That is a genuine gap, not a disagreement.

chunks.heading: Sovereign AI: announced is not committed
chunks.text:
capital-policy — Sovereign AI: announced is not committed. The single most repeated error in this layer is treating an announcement as an appropriation. The corpus now separates them, and the results are unflattering.

The EU. The Commission has announced that €20bn will be mobilised for AI gigafactories through the InvestAI Facility, with the formal tender due summer 2026 and first construction in 2027 . It was announced on 9 February 2025. Eighteen months later the tender has not issued, no site is funded, and nothing is under construction — which is why "mobilised" and not "committed" is the correct verb. The much larger figure widely attached to this programme is an EU-wide mobilisation target and does not appear on the Commission's own gigafactory page at all.

Japan. METI and NEDO awarded the five-year FRONTia foundation-model project, running fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2030, to Noetra Corp. and AIST on 30 June 2026 — and contracted only fiscal 2026 and 2027, with an annual stage-gate review deciding continuation thereafter . There is no government-published total. The trillion-yen five-year figure and the first-year tranche that circulate with this programme both trace to a single news outlet; neither appears in any METI or NEDO document, and NEDO's own public call leaves the five-year total for the applicant to propose. This site therefore prints no Japanese sovereign AI number at all, which is itself the finding: the most-quoted sovereign AI commitment in Asia has no primary source behind its headline.

chunks.text:
Japan. METI and NEDO awarded the five-year FRONTia foundation-model project, running fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2030, to Noetra Corp. and AIST on 30 June 2026 — and contracted only fiscal 2026 and 2027, with an annual stage-gate review deciding continuation thereafter . There is no government-published total. The trillion-yen five-year figure and the first-year tranche that circulate with this programme both trace to a single news outlet; neither appears in any METI or NEDO document, and NEDO's own public call leaves the five-year total for the applicant to propose. This site therefore prints no Japanese sovereign AI number at all, which is itself the finding: the most-quoted sovereign AI commitment in Asia has no primary source behind its headline.

India. India's IndiaAI Mission was sanctioned in March 2024 at Rs 10,371.92 crore over five years, of which Rs 4,563.36 crore is the compute pillar . Sanctioned is the operative word. Per the government's own parliamentary reply, roughly Rs 401 crore — about 3.9% of the sanctioned outlay — had actually reached the mission in its first two years , against successively larger revised estimates each year. No official US dollar equivalent exists for any of these figures, so the site does not print one.

South Korea. South Korea allocated KRW 10.1tn, about $7.25bn, to AI in its 2026 budget, more than tripling the KRW 3.3tn allocated for 2025 . Proposed in August 2025 and cleared by the National Assembly, this is the one genuinely appropriated sovereign AI figure in the corpus, as distinct from announced, mobilised or sanctioned.

Set any of them against the private sector: Bridgewater expects about $650bn from four US companies in 2026 alone . Sovereign AI, as currently funded, is an access-subsidy programme with a national-champion label. It is not a counterweight.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
capital-policy — Failure modes. An intent that does not convert. NVIDIA's $100bn is staged per gigawatt and had not closed as of its own 10-K ; AMD's warrant only fully vests at 6 GW and a $600 share price . If deployment slips, the equity that made the demand look funded never arrives, and the purchase commitments remain.

The structure that hides the exposure. $45.95bn of disclosed maximum loss against $1.83bn of carried equity is one venture at one sponsor. Morgan Stanley's $800bn private-credit share of the financing need is the part of this market with the least public disclosure, and therefore where a shock would be hardest to see.

A covenant, not a default. CoreWeave's $8.5bn facility lives inside a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary with a parent guarantee limited to specified bad acts , and the binding test is a 1.15 times debt-service-coverage covenant — a ratio, not a payment. The first failure in this layer will look like a covenant breach at a subsidiary nobody has heard of, not a missed coupon at a parent everybody has.

Two truces lapsing together. 10 November 2026 . Rare-earth restrictions return and the affiliates rule returns on the same day, in a market where enforcement staffing is a fraction of the flows it polices .

Policy by discretion. With the GAIN AI Act stripped , no replacement for the AI Diffusion rule , and a 15% revenue expectation that was never codified , the rules governing the industry's most valuable export can change without legislation. That is a risk to capital formation regardless of which direction they move.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: capital-policy — Open questions. - What is the other $800bn? Altman's $1.4tn exceeds the site's cited contracts by roughly that much, and the balance is not publicly itemised. Until it is, no honest chart of OpenAI's commitments can be a stacked sum. - Does the NVIDIA–OpenAI letter of intent convert? NVIDIA's own filing says there is no assurance . First phase was targeted at H2 2026 on Vera Rubin, which makes this falsifiable within months. - Who holds the residual on the leaseback? Meta discloses an exposure ceiling and a residual value guarantee on the leased campus , but ceilings are not probabilities and no liability had been recorded at year end . - Is the Entity List freeze policy or capacity? Eight months without an addition against a 35-day historical cadence is consistent with a negotiated pause and equally consistent with an under-resourced agency. The corpus cannot distinguish them. - Does the under-levered-corporate steelman hold? Total US private nonfinancial credit was $42,235bn in Q2 2025 with debt-to-GDP at a two-decade low . That is an aggregate. It says nothing about the leverage concentrated in the specific SPVs financing this buildout.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the cloud layer: overbuilt. Capex is running near three times depreciation on assets whose useful lives the operators themselves cannot agree on. The demand is real; the accounting is a bet.

The counter, per The filings themselves, plus Amy Hood's 'demand continues to exceed supply': Backlog is contracted, not hoped for: Alphabet's RPO went from $108bn to $520bn in a year, and Microsoft's stands at $633bn. You do not sign that and then not need the machines.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
cloud — Introduction. Every argument about whether AI is a bubble eventually lands here. Not on the chips, and not on the models — on the depreciation schedule of the machines in between.

This is the layer where the money becomes an asset, and where an assumption about how long that asset lasts decides whether the industry is profitable. Change the number from five years to six and roughly seven billion dollars of operating income appears . Nobody has to lie for this to go wrong. They only have to be optimistic about how long a GPU stays useful.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
cloud — What this layer is. Two businesses wearing one name.

The hyperscalers — Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta — own the land, the power contracts, the buildings and the machines, and rent compute as one line in a much larger software business. The neoclouds — CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda and several hundred smaller entrants — do only this. They buy GPUs with borrowed money and rent them out, which means they have no other revenue to hide a bad year in.

The physical anchor: a rack of eight-GPU servers, drawing more power than a suburban street, sitting in a shell that took three years to permit and energise. The hyperscaler treats it as a depreciating asset on a balance sheet full of other things. The neocloud treats it as collateral.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
cloud — Unit economics. Calendar 2025 combined capital expenditure across the big four was $376.1bn in cash, or $406.4bn including finance leases . Q1 2026 alone was $129.8bn, up 80% year over year .

The ratio that matters: over the trailing four quarters to March 2026, that capex ran at approximately 2.9 times the $149.2bn of depreciation and finance-lease amortization behind it . Two qualifiers travel with that number and the site will not print it without them. The denominator excludes intangible amortization — include it and the ratio is 2.78. And Amazon is 47% of the denominator on a caption that bundles roughly $16–19bn a year of capitalised video content; strip the non-PP&E items and the ratio goes above three. The strongest version of the depreciation argument is the one its proponents have not been making.

Cash conversion is where it bites. Amazon's trailing-twelve-month capex equalled 102% of operating cash flow . The business is now spending slightly more on machines than it generates from operations.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
cloud — The players. The hyperscalers guided roughly $650–725bn for 2026 — Meta at $125–145bn , Alphabet $175–185bn and rising , Amazon around $200bn , Microsoft tracking near $190bn . Treat the aggregate as a spread, not a number: it comes from three different forecasters, none of it is guidance in the strict sense , and Q1 actuals annualise to about $519bn, so every version of it requires a steep intra-year ramp.

CoreWeave is the layer's stress test, because it runs the same business without the cover. Q1 2026 revenue $2.078bn, up 112% . Adjusted EBITDA $1.157bn at a 56% margin — and a GAAP net loss of $740m in the same quarter . Both numbers are true at once, and the bridge between them is $536m of quarterly net interest against $24.9bn of debt on $4.8bn of equity . Backlog is $99.4bn ; capex is outrunning operating cash flow roughly five-to-two .

Nebius is the same shape earlier: $399m of quarterly revenue, up 684% , against contracts of $17.4bn with Microsoft and about $27bn with Meta , and 2026 capex guidance of $20–25bn on $3.0–3.4bn of revenue .

Oracle has quietly become a neocloud with an enterprise software business attached: $55.7bn of FY2026 capex against guidance of about $50bn , and RPO of $523bn .

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
cloud — Concentration & chokepoints. The chokepoint here is not technical. It is counterparty concentration, and it points at one customer.

OpenAI has contracted roughly $300bn with Oracle , an incremental $250bn with Azure , and up to $11.9bn with CoreWeave — against a company whose annualized revenue run rate exited 2025 above $20bn . Sam Altman has put total commitments at about $1.4 trillion across roughly 30 GW and eight years .

Two honesty notes on that comparison, because it is the most-abused number in the discourse. The $1.4tn is Altman's own attributed figure, not a sum of the contracts above — those account for $588bn of it , and the remainder is not publicly itemised. And it spans about eight years, so setting it against a single year of revenue compares unlike things. The real observation is narrower and still striking: the layer's growth is underwritten by forward commitments from a small number of counterparties, at least one of which is spending far ahead of its income.

CoreWeave's own concentration was 62% Microsoft as recently as 2024 ; the Meta agreement at $21bn diversifies the name at the top of the list without changing the shape of the risk.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
cloud — Lead times & capacity. Demand is not the constraint and has not been for two years. Microsoft reported $633bn of remaining performance obligations, up from $398bn six months earlier, while stating plainly that demand continues to exceed supply . Alphabet's total RPO reached $519.5bn as of June 2026, against $108.2bn a year earlier — it roughly doubled in a single quarter .

Supply is the constraint, and it is upstream of this layer: power, shells, and volume GPU lead times reported at 36–52 weeks . If demand doubled tomorrow the answer would be set by the grid queue and the turbine order book, not by anything a cloud provider controls.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
cloud — 2019 → today. 2019. Cloud is a software-margin business. Capex tracks revenue. Servers depreciate over three or four years and nobody outside accounting cares.

2022–23. The useful-life extensions arrive, and they arrive everywhere. Microsoft goes from four years to six . Alphabet goes to six, worth about $3.4bn of depreciation . Amazon follows to six, worth about $3.2bn . Each is defensible alone. Together they lengthen the industry's assumed asset life just as the assets start changing faster.

2025–26. The consensus breaks in public. In January 2025 Meta extends to 5.5 years — and Amazon shortens a subset of servers from six years back to five, taking $889m of extra depreciation and $677m off net income in nine months . Two companies with the same machines, the same customers and the same quarter, moving in opposite directions.

Meta's own numbers show what the extension is fighting: depreciation on property and equipment still rose from about $11.0bn in 2023 to $18.0bn in 2025, despite the longer life .

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
cloud — Commoditization pressure. Renting a GPU is commoditizing. Renting a platform is not, and the price data separates them cleanly.

H100 on-demand pricing fell 64–75% from its 2024 peak, to $1.80–3.50 an hour , having once exceeded $12 at list . But one-year reserved contract pricing bottomed at $1.70 in October 2025 and rebounded about 38% to $2.35 by March 2026 — providers sold out, and little Hopper capacity came off contract. And hyperscaler on-demand pricing still runs three-to-five times marketplace rates .

So the deflation is real, generation-tiered, and not monotonic. The useful evidence against "GPUs are a commodity that depreciates to zero in three years" is Azure retiring V100s roughly 7.5 years after launch . Newer silicon is not following the same curve — B200 rentals were $4.50–7.00 an hour in Q2 2026 with marketplace rates rising month over month .

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
cloud — Failure modes. The depreciation reset. If useful lives compress back toward four years, the added depreciation lands directly on operating income at roughly $7bn per year per year of change . Amazon has already moved one subset in that direction. Blast radius: earnings across the big four, and every valuation resting on them.

The leveraged neocloud. CoreWeave shows the mechanism — 56% EBITDA margins and a GAAP loss, separated by interest on $24.9bn of debt. A refinancing window that closes, or a large counterparty that renegotiates, converts a growth story into a solvency one. The financing structure is now explicit about this: the $8.5bn facility closed in March 2026 sits in a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary, secured on substantially all of that subsidiary's assets . The GPUs are the lien.

Off-balance-sheet contagion. Meta and Blue Owl's Richland Parish venture commits the parties to pro-rata shares of roughly $27bn in development costs , structured so most of it does not consolidate. Morgan Stanley projects about $1.5tn of data-center debt financing need through 2028, roughly $800bn from private credit . That is where a shock would be hardest to see.

Counterparty failure. One customer's inability to pay its compute bill would reprice the backlog of everyone who sold to it.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: cloud — Open questions. - Which useful life is right? Nobody knows, including the operators — that is what January 2025 demonstrated. The V100 lasting 7.5 years and a B200 rental market that is still tightening both argue for longer lives; the pace of architectural change argues for shorter. - Does the 2026 ramp happen? Q1 actuals annualise to ~$519bn against the $650–725bn forecast range . The gap resolves by December, one way or the other, and it is the cleanest falsifiable test on this page. - Is contracted backlog the same as revenue? Alphabet's RPO quadrupled in a year. RPO measures obligations, not cash, and the site has no data on cancellation or renegotiation terms. - Who holds the residual risk in the SPVs? The disclosures give exposure ceilings, not probabilities. Meta's own filing puts maximum exposure to loss at $45.95bn against $1.83bn of carried equity in one venture . - What happens to the neoclouds if hyperscaler capex flattens? They are the marginal buyer of GPUs and the marginal seller of capacity. A pause upstream reaches them first.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the compute-silicon layer: fairly-priced. A 74.9% gross margin held through a product transition is scarcity rent set by packaging supply, not pricing power over customers. The risk here is not the economics — it is who is paying.

The counter, per the deal documents — Broadcom/Apollo/Blackstone, June 2026, and Anthropic's own April 2026 announcement: The buyers are a handful of labs funding purchases with credit, not cash flow: Apollo led a $35bn first tranche for over 20 GW, and Anthropic has committed more than $100bn to AWS over ten years.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — Introduction. The interesting question about this layer stopped being "can anyone catch NVIDIA" about a year ago. Custom silicon caught it, in the sense that matters — Broadcom's AI business is now guided at $16.0 billion a quarter — and NVIDIA accelerated anyway.

That is the fact this page has to explain. Two things are both true: custom ASICs are taking real volume, and NVIDIA's data center line grew 92% year over year to $75.2 billion in a single quarter . The resolution is upstream. Nobody in this layer is winning sockets off anybody else while advanced packaging is sold out.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — What this layer is. The layer designs the thing that turns electricity into linear algebra, and increasingly does not sell it as a chip.

Merchant silicon is NVIDIA and AMD: a part with a price list, sold to anyone. Custom silicon is Broadcom and Marvell doing design and packaging for a buyer who owns the product — Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium, Meta's and OpenAI's accelerators. Challengers are architecture bets: Groq's inference LPU, Cerebras's wafer-scale part.

The physical anchor: a die the size of a drink coaster, flanked by stacks of memory millimeters away, bolted onto a board, seventy-two of which now behave as one machine. NVLink 6 carries 260 TB/s of all-to-all fabric bandwidth inside a single Vera Rubin NVL72 rack . Google's equivalent is a pod: 9,216 Ironwood TPUs delivering 42.5 exaflops , each chip at 4,614 TFLOPs peak . The unit of sale is drifting from the chip to the rack, and that drift is the layer's actual strategy.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — Unit economics. For scale on what that margin has bought: NVIDIA's market capitalisation reached $5.26tn in August 2026, fifteen times its level at the end of 2022 .

NVIDIA's total revenue was $81.6bn in Q1 FY2027, the quarter ended April 2026, up 85% , of which data center was $75.2bn, up 92% . Data center is therefore about ninety-two percent of the company . GAAP gross margin was 74.9% , held near that level straight through the Blackwell-to-Rubin transition — the moment when a hardware company's margin usually dips.

The comparison that sizes the gap: AMD's Q1 2026 revenue was $10.253bn , its data center segment $5.775bn, up 57% , at a 55% non-GAAP gross margin — 53% GAAP . A roughly twenty-point structural margin gap has now persisted through the entire AI cycle. And NVIDIA's networking line alone, at $14.8bn for the quarter, up 199% , is larger than AMD's whole data center segment .

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — The players. NVIDIA. Full fiscal 2026 revenue $215.9bn, up 65% , with data center at $193.7bn, up 68% .

AMD is the credible second merchant supplier and prices like one. Its route to differentiation is increasingly partnership rather than part — AMD and Cerebras announced a disaggregated inference system in July 2026 claiming up to 5x higher tokens per second per watt , which is a vendor claim on a vendor configuration and is logged as one.

Broadcom is the layer's real structural change. Q2 FY2026 total revenue $22.187bn, up 48% , following $19.311bn in Q1 . AI semiconductor revenue inside that was $10.8bn, up 143% . This is the best single datapoint anywhere on custom-ASIC share gains.

Forecast, per company guidance — NVIDIA (May 2026), AMD (May 2026), Broadcom (June 2026): NVIDIA guided Q2 FY2027 revenue to $91.0bn plus or minus 2% . AMD guided Q2 2026 to approximately $11.2bn plus or minus $300m . Broadcom guided Q3 FY2026 AI semiconductor revenue to $16.0bn, up 200% year over year . Guidance is a forecast even when the forecaster is the company being forecast, and the three are what the whole additive-versus-substitutive argument below is tested against.

The captive designers. Google's Ironwood carries 192 GB of HBM per chip at 7.37 TB/s . Anthropic announced access to up to 1,000,000 Google Cloud TPUs in October 2025, worth tens of billions of dollars , and separately stated in April 2026 that it already uses more than 1,000,000 AWS Trainium2 chips to train and serve Claude . Note the difference between those two: one is a commitment, one is chips in production. The corpus keeps them apart and so should any chart.

The challengers thinned out. Groq raised $750m in September 2025 and $650m in June 2026 for its inference cloud — and in between signed away the architecture bet, which section 7 takes up. Cerebras announced plans for 200 MW of AI compute capacity in Europe by end-2027 .

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — Concentration & chokepoints. The chokepoint for this layer is not in this layer. It is the packaging line one level down.

Morgan Stanley projected NVIDIA's 2026 CoWoS allocation at roughly 595,000 wafers, about 60% of total capacity , against 2026 global CoWoS demand near 1.0 million wafers versus about 670,000 in 2025 . Lead times were 52–78 weeks with capacity fully booked through end-2026 . Whoever holds packaging slots ships accelerators; whoever does not, does not, however good the architecture.

The second chokepoint is regulatory, and it is memory bandwidth rather than compute. The BIS rule effective 15 January 2026 caps licensable China and Macau exports at total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s , alongside a total-processing-performance ceiling of 21,000 . The second gate, not the first, is what separates an H200-class part from a Blackwell-class one.

And the third is demand concentration. Anthropic committed in April 2026 to spend more than $100bn on AWS technologies over ten years , under an agreement covering up to 5 GW of new AWS capacity with about 1 GW of Trainium2 and Trainium3 online by end-2026 . A layer whose growth is underwritten by a small number of labs inherits their financing risk.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — Lead times & capacity. Here is the argument the numbers actually support: custom ASIC gains are additive, not substitutive — and the reason is that supply lags demand, so an ASIC wafer is a new wafer rather than a wafer taken from NVIDIA.

Test it against the two growth rates. NVIDIA's data center revenue grew 92% to $75.2bn in the April 2026 quarter , which means it added roughly $36bn of quarterly data center revenue year over year . Broadcom's entire AI semiconductor line, at the guided $16.0bn , is under half of that single increment. If ASICs were displacing merchant GPUs, NVIDIA's growth would be decelerating as Broadcom's accelerated. Instead NVIDIA guided the following quarter up to $91.0bn .

The mechanism sits in packaging. CoWoS demand is rising from about 670,000 wafers to about 1.0 million against capacity that went from roughly 35,000 wafers a month at end-2024 to 72,500–80,000 at end-2025 , with everything booked through end-2026 . In a rationed market, a Google TPU order does not cancel an NVIDIA order — it consumes capacity that did not exist a year ago. The substitution question only becomes answerable when the queue clears.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — 2019 → today. FY2019. NVIDIA's full-year revenue was $11.72bn . It is a graphics company with a promising accelerator business.

FY2022. Revenue $26.91bn , of which data center $10.61bn — roughly two-fifths of the company . Gaming still matters.

FY2026 and after. Revenue $215.9bn , data center $193.7bn , and a single quarter now larger than the whole of FY2022 . Meanwhile the China business went from material to zero: revenue from customers headquartered in China including Hong Kong fell to $4,550m in the April 2026 quarter, from $9,659m a year earlier — and that measure is booked by customer headquarters, not shipping destination, so it is not a China-destination number.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — Commoditization pressure. A 74.9% gross margin held through an architecture transition is the single strongest piece of evidence against commoditization at the top of this layer. The pressure is real but it is arriving as vertical integration — buyers designing their own parts — rather than as price competition on merchant parts. Vertical integration compresses a supplier's volume, eventually. It does not compress its price while the queue is full.

What did commoditize is the challenger tier, and it consolidated rather than competed. Groq signed a non-exclusive licensing agreement with NVIDIA on 24 December 2025 worth $17bn in cash across three installments by end-2026 , with CEO Jonathan Ross and president Sunny Madra moving to NVIDIA and the CFO becoming CEO. The structure is independently corroborated, which matters — this was a single-source claim until it was not. Press reporting put the total value at about $20bn, of which $17bn was the cash ; the two numbers are different things and should never be used interchangeably. Read plainly, it is a soft exit of the independent-LPU thesis: the most credible architectural challenge to the GPU was resolved by a payment rather than by a benchmark.

Speaking of benchmarks, treat vendor throughput claims as claims. NVIDIA and CoreWeave stated in July 2026 that Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers 10x more throughput per megawatt than Grace Blackwell NVL72 — one benchmark, one workload, both parties interested.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
compute-silicon — Failure modes. Policy, in one line item. NVIDIA took a $4.5bn charge in the April 2025 quarter for excess H20 inventory and purchase obligations after the US required licences for that class of chip . That is the cost of a single export-control reclassification to a single vendor. It has since gone further: no data center Hopper products shipped to China in the April 2026 quarter, against $4.6bn a year earlier , and zero revenue had been generated under the February 2026 H200 licensing programme as of the May 2026 filing . Supply was legalised in Washington while demand stayed banned in Beijing. Jensen Huang, an interested party, says NVIDIA's China accelerator share has fallen to zero .

Credit-financed demand. Silicon demand is now partly a private-credit product. If that channel reprices, the order book upstream reprices with it.

Forecast, per Broadcom, Apollo and Blackstone, June 2026: The platform announced in June 2026 targets more than 20 GW of global AI deployments through 2028 , on an initial tranche of $35bn led by Apollo . The gigawatts are an announced plan, not deployed capacity; the tranche is committed capital. The two must not be added together or drawn as one bar.

Buyer concentration among labs. More than $100bn committed to AWS by one lab , up to a million TPUs from another vendor , multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU capacity with Google and Broadcom from 2027 . The customers are few, large, and mostly pre-revenue relative to what they have signed.

The queue clearing. The additive-not-substitutive argument in section 5 is conditional on scarcity. When packaging capacity catches demand, the same ASIC volumes stop being incremental and start being displacement. That is the mechanism by which this layer's margin, not its revenue, breaks first.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: compute-silicon — Open questions. - What is NVIDIA's actual unit share, and of what? The corpus has revenue and margin, not share. Broadcom at $16.0bn guided against NVIDIA at $75.2bn of quarterly data center revenue is a revenue ratio, not a socket ratio, and the two differ because ASICs are cheaper per unit. - Does the additive story survive the packaging queue clearing? The falsifiable test is NVIDIA's data center growth rate in the quarter after CoWoS lead times fall below a year . - What are the captive parts actually costing their owners? Google and Amazon disclose specs, not cost per delivered FLOP. Without that, "TPUs are cheaper" is an assertion. - Does AMD ever close the margin gap? Twenty points of structural difference has not narrowed in the strongest demand environment either company will ever see. - Was Groq the last independent architecture bet? If a $17bn licensing cheque is the exit path, the next challenger's investors already know their base case.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the data-supply layer: fairly-priced. Real revenue at real margins, and the only layer in the stack where the labour got a raise. But the equity is priced on gross billings that the vendors mostly pass straight through.

The counter, per CNBC's reporting on Google's plan to split from Scale: One $14.3bn cheque cost Scale its largest customer. A franchise that a single investor can damage by buying into it is thinner than any revenue multiple implies.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
data-supply — Introduction. Every other layer in this stack buys something built on purpose. This one buys other people's work: text written for human readers, judgment sitting inside someone's head, and the labour of pointing at what is correct.

Both ends of that supply repriced at once, in about eighteen months. The free end is being fenced off — 45 percent of the C4 web corpus is now restricted once terms of service are counted . The paid end stopped being piecework and became credentialled experts billing above $85 an hour .

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
data-supply — What this layer is. Three inputs, one destination. Scraped corpora — the web, crawled. Human-generated data — labels, preference rankings, demonstrations, graded answers, and the reinforcement-learning environments that produce them. Synthetic data — tokens a model writes for another model to learn from.

The physical anchor is two objects that have nothing in common. One is a plain text file on a web server that tells a crawler no. The other is a physician at a kitchen table, paid by the hour, marking which of two model answers would have hurt the patient.

That second object is new. The labelling industry was built on the first kind of worker — high volume, low skill, priced per task. The reinforcement-learning era buys the second kind, and the price per hour is not in the same universe.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
data-supply — Unit economics. The unit used to be the task. It is now the hour, and the hour is expensive. Mercor reached $2bn of annualized gross revenue in June 2026, up from a $760m run-rate at end-2025 . Contractors keep 60 to 70 percent of that top line at average rates above $85 an hour, with over $2m of payouts a day .

Net that out and the business is roughly $600–800m annualized — but read the qualifier before using the number. The 60–70 percent share and the $85 rate are Sacra estimates with no independent corroborator; TechCrunch independently confirms only the scale of the payouts, not the split. Every netting exercise on this layer, including that one, rests on a single uncorroborated ratio.

The older economics ran the other way. Scale AI reported $870m of 2024 revenue against a $1.5bn annualized run-rate at end-2024 and an estimated $2bn in 2025 , priced per completed task at a markup. The corpus holds those per-task price points in a source note rather than as citable facts, so this page will not print them; the direction is what matters, and the direction is from cents to dollars-per-minute-of-expert-attention.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
data-supply — The players. Scale AI is the wounded incumbent. Meta invested $14.3bn for a 49 percent non-voting stake at a $29bn valuation in June 2025 , which is the single most consequential event in this layer's history and not for the reason the headline implies.

Surge AI is the quiet one, and the least verifiable. Sacra estimates $1.2bn of annualized revenue in 2024, bootstrapped and profitable since its 2021 launch . No independent source for that figure exists — Surge is private and discloses nothing, and every restatement traces back to Sacra. In July 2025 it was reported in talks for its first outside capital, up to $1bn, at valuations reported between $15bn and $25bn . Twelve months on, no close has been reported. Surge is not a $25bn company; it is a company that was reported to be in talks.

Mercor is the RL-era entrant. It raised a $350m Series C at a $10bn valuation in October 2025 and quadrupled gross revenue in the eight months after. Sacra describes it as free-cash-flow profitable in early 2026, and names OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta as customers — which is also the problem.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
data-supply — Concentration & chokepoints. The buyer side is three or four companies. Every vendor in this layer sells the same product to the same frontier labs, and the labs are the only entities that need data at this scale. There is no long tail to fall back on.

The chokepoint, though, is not scale or skill. It is neutrality, and June 2025 demonstrated what happens when it breaks. Google — which spent about $150m with Scale in 2024 and had planned $200m for 2025 — moved to split from Scale after the Meta investment .

Now the correction, because this claim is widely told wrong and the corpus told it wrong too. "OpenAI departed Scale" is false, and was contradicted by the very CNBC report the claim was sourced to: OpenAI's CFO said the company would keep working with Scale as one of several data vendors. Google's move is reported intent, not a completed exit. Microsoft was reported to be pulling back; xAI was described as looking to leave. The dollar figures here are corroborated. The completeness of the exodus is not, and any page that lists four departures is inventing three of them.

What survives is the mechanism, and one hard number carries it. In July 2025 — one month after the Meta stake — Scale laid off 200 full-time employees, about 14 percent of staff, and ended roughly 500 contractor relationships . That is the evidence for "neutrality was the moat," and it is better evidence than the departure list, because it is a measured consequence rather than a reported intention. A labelling vendor's asset is that it is not aligned with any lab; an investor can damage that asset simply by buying in, and the damage shows up in the payroll within a quarter.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
data-supply — Lead times & capacity. There is no turbine queue here. The two constraints are permitted text and credentialled humans.

Text is running out by enclosure, not exhaustion. Between April 2023 and April 2024, 5 percent or more of all C4 tokens and 28 percent or more of tokens from its most actively maintained critical sources became robots.txt-restricted, rising to 45 percent of C4 once terms of service are included — a multi-thousand-domain audit across three major corpora, and the cleanest measurement of the enclosure that exists. Then Cloudflare, which says it serves about 20 percent of the web, made AI-crawler blocking the default for new domains on 1 July 2025 . That is a company claim about its own footprint, and it is the first time the default flipped from open to closed.

The escape valve is synthetic. DeepSeek-R1's reinforcement-learning phase generated approximately 2 trillion tokens on its own , against the 14.8 trillion tokens of scraped text used to pretrain V3 — one RL run self-generating a mid-teens percentage of an entire pretraining corpus .

Forecast, per Epoch AI: The indexed web holds roughly 500 trillion text tokens, and at 4x annual compute growth the text-only data constraint binds about five years from 2024 . Multimodal and synthetic sources are the named escape valves; neither has a measured quality ceiling in this corpus.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
data-supply — 2019 → today. 2019. Bounding boxes for autonomous vehicles. Data is free to take, labour is piecework, and the winning vendor is whoever manages the largest low-cost workforce.

2022–23. RLHF makes human preference the product. Human judgment, not human labelling, becomes the input frontier labs cannot synthesise, and the labelling vendors become strategic suppliers.

2025–26. Three things break at once. Consent closes — 45 percent of C4 restricted , crawler blocking on by default. Labour repriced upward to expert hours above $85 . And neutrality stops being free: $14.3bn buys 49 percent of the incumbent , and a month later that incumbent cuts 200 staff and around 500 contractors .

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
data-supply — Commoditization pressure. The bottom of this layer already commoditized. Per-task annotation is a managed-labour business with no defensible position, which is why the incumbent's growth slowed while the market it serves grew.

The top is moving the other way. Expert hours are getting more expensive, not less, because the supply of physicians and quantitative analysts willing to grade model outputs is genuinely finite. That is the rarest thing in this stack: a price going up.

The real pressure is not competition, it is disintermediation. Two forces route around the vendors entirely — synthetic data, which substitutes generated tokens for purchased ones at the margin, and in-housing, of which Meta's 49 percent stake is the most expensive example anyone has attempted. Neither has produced a measured quality limit in this corpus, which is precisely why the layer's medium-term shape is unresolved.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
data-supply — Failure modes. The neutrality break. Demonstrated, once, at a cost of one large customer. Blast radius: the vendor, not the stack. Any lab can switch suppliers in a quarter.

Buyer concentration. Three or four buyers, each large enough to be a majority of a vendor's revenue and each capable of building the capability internally. A single in-housing decision removes a vendor's growth story.

Gross-versus-net. Marketplace revenue at 60–70 percent pass-through is not software revenue, and valuations struck on the gross line assume a take rate the corpus cannot verify.

Consent and licensing. The corpus has no data-licensing deal figures at all — not one publisher contract, not one dollar amount. Enclosure is measured; the price of the permission that replaces it is not. That is a real hole in this page, and it is where a cost shock would appear first.

Contamination. If synthetic data degrades models trained on it, the escape valve closes. There is no measurement of this in the corpus either way.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: data-supply — Open questions. - What is Surge actually worth? Reported talks at $15–25bn in July 2025 , no reported close twelve months later. Either the round was repriced or it was never as firm as reported; the corpus cannot say which. - Does the expert-hour price hold? $85+ an hour could be a durable skill premium or a shortage premium that collapses as more credentialled people discover the work exists. - How much of Mercor's $2bn gross run-rate does Mercor keep? The netting rests entirely on one Sacra-only ratio. A disclosed take rate would settle the layer's most important number. - Did the labs actually leave Scale? One intent, one continuing relationship, two reported pullbacks. The corpus cannot close this and the version circulating publicly is wrong — what it can show is the July 2025 cut of 200 staff and ~500 contractors , which is the consequence regardless of who stayed. - Is synthetic data a substitute or a supplement? 2 trillion tokens from one RL run shows the volume is achievable. Nothing here shows what it costs in model quality.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the datacenter layer: underbuilt. Digital Realty banks land for 6,560 MW it cannot energise while re-pricing renewals up 25.4%. The scarce input here is not space or steel — it is a megawatt with a connection date.

The counter, per Uptime Institute's Jacqueline Davis, and Equinix's own growth rate: Equinix's retail colocation grew 10% while Digital Realty grew 29% — half of this layer has no supply problem at all — and Uptime's Jacqueline Davis argues liquid cooling stays niche for three years.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
datacenter — Introduction. The scarcity on this layer is borrowed. Land is abundant, concrete is available, and the cost of building a shell is rising more slowly than it was two years ago. What is missing arrives from the two layers below: a connection date.

The clearest single number in the corpus makes the point. Of the more than 280 data center industry experts surveyed, 48% named power availability as the most prominent obstacle to delivering projects on schedule . Not labour, not equipment, not capital.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
datacenter — What this layer is. A grey box, a substation, a chiller plant, and a lease.

Microsoft's Fairwater site in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin is the physical anchor: three buildings, 1.2 million square feet under roof on a 315-acre site, built with 46.6 miles of foundation piles and 26.5 million pounds of structural steel . Those are company figures, and the performance claims attached to them are marketing. But the mass is real, and it is the least interesting part of the project — the hard part was the megawatts.

The layer splits in two commercially. Wholesale and hyperscale landlords sell megawatts on long leases. Retail colocation sells racks and cross-connects. The AI cycle accrues almost entirely to the first.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
