datacenter — Unit economics. Construction is priced per watt, not per square foot, which tells you what is being sold. Tokyo was the most expensive market in 2025 at $15.2 per watt, followed by Singapore at $14.5 and Zurich at $14.2 . Cost per watt for a traditional air-cooled build rose 5.5% in 2025 — against 9.0% the prior year . Construction inflation is decelerating. That is not what a supply-constrained input looks like.

Nor is the cooling transition expensive in the way the discourse implies. US liquid-cooled AI facilities cost 7 to 10% more to build than air-cooled facilities of equivalent IT capacity — a consultancy midpoint on an unpublished method, and a single-digit premium either way.

The returns tell the real story. Digital Realty had 1,402 MW under construction at 100% share as of June 2026, 54% pre-leased, with $20.2bn of expected total investment at an 11.5% average expected stabilized yield . Renewal leases signed in Q2 2026 re-priced 25.4% higher on a cash basis . You do not get double-digit development yields and double-digit renewal spreads in the same quarter in a market with spare capacity.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
datacenter — The players. Digital Realty is the megawatt seller. Q2 2026 revenue of $1.9bn, up 29% year over year — a figure flattered by net promote income from a development joint venture and an insurance settlement, both of which the company discloses separately. Its backlog of signed-but-not-commenced leases reached a record $1.9bn of annualized GAAP base rent , and in July 2026 it signed two hyperscale leases alone worth $410m of annualized base rent — more than its entire Q2 bookings .

Equinix is the control group, and it is the strongest counterargument on this page. Q1 2026 revenue of $2.444bn grew 10%, with full-year guidance of $10.144–10.244bn and 2026 capex guided to about $4.1bn . Ten percent against Digital Realty's twenty-nine. Equinix says roughly 60% of its largest Q1 2026 deals were AI-related — its own characterisation, with "largest deals" and "AI-related" undefined, so treat it as a claim rather than a measurement.

Vertiv is where the layer's demand shows up first, because power and cooling equipment is ordered before the shell is finished. FY2025 net sales of $10.2bn against $8.01bn in 2024 , and a backlog that went from $7.2bn to $15.0bn in twelve months — roughly one and a half times annual revenue, with its own 10-K stating that orders are being placed in advance of its ability to fulfil them. Q1 2026 net sales were $2,650m, up 30%, at a 20.8% adjusted operating margin — margin expanding inclusive of tariff impacts, which is pricing power in plain sight.

Forecast, per Vertiv (company guidance, raised at Q1 2026): Full-year 2026 net sales of $13,500–14,000m with organic growth of 29 to 31% .

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
datacenter — Concentration & chokepoints. The chokepoint is not land. Digital Realty alone held land supporting 6,560 MW plus shells supporting 550 MW of future development capacity at 100% share , against 3.1 GW of operating IT capacity and about 8.5 GW buildable . One landlord is sitting on more than twice its operating fleet in undeveloped potential.

The chokepoint is the interconnection date behind each of those megawatts — the layer below — and, increasingly, permission. Data Center Watch counted 75 US projects worth about $130bn blocked or delayed in Q1 2026, which it describes as the largest single-quarter concentration in its own dataset . That is an advocacy-adjacent tracker counting with an unpublished method, and the superlative is its own — but the direction is corroborated by the count of active opposition groups, which more than doubled in the same window.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
datacenter — Lead times & capacity. The equipment order book is the leading indicator, and it is already showing what happens when demand doubles: Vertiv's backlog doubled in a year and its 10-K says customers are ordering ahead of what it can build. A shell can be poured in eighteen months. A transformer, a switchgear set and a chiller plant cannot be conjured, and a substation energisation date is not for sale.

Density is the other capacity question, and here the roadmap and the observation must be kept apart.

Forecast, per Uptime Institute: AI hardware roadmaps point to rack power soon surpassing 200 kW, with GPUs above 2 kW per module and CPUs approaching 1 kW per socket . This is a projection about what manufacturers are planning, not an observation of racks in service — the corpus previously recorded it as present tense and the fact-check retyped it.

Forecast, per NVIDIA: An 800 V DC power distribution architecture entering production in 2027 alongside Kyber rack systems, supporting rack densities from 100 kW to more than 1 MW . The announcement is fact; the claimed efficiency and copper savings are NVIDIA's own. Its engineering analysis puts a 1 MW rack on legacy 54 V distribution at up to 200 kg of copper busbar — a vendor estimate, and the reason the re-architecture exists.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
datacenter — 2019 → today. 2019. The unit of sale is the square foot and the kilowatt is an afterthought. Cooling is air. Power usage effectiveness is the efficiency metric anyone cares about, and Google is already winning it.

2022–24. AI racks arrive but are still air-cooled, rated at about 41 kW — Uptime Institute research whose exact article the corpus has not pinned down, so treat it as the best available anchor rather than a hard one. Build cost inflation runs at 9.0% a year . Immersion cooling looks like the future.

2026. Rack power draw during AI training swings by more than 100% within milliseconds, with GB200 NVL72 racks observed climbing from roughly 60–70 kW to more than 150 kW against a 132 kW specification . The spikes recur every second or two. The honest before-and-after is 41 kW to 150 kW — roughly a factor of four in two hardware generations, not the ninefold jump the corpus briefly recorded by mistaking a fluctuation for a level. Google reports a fleet-wide PUE of 1.09 against a surveyed industry average of 1.54 — company-reported, and the industry comparison is a survey Google cites rather than an independent audit.

And immersion cooling lost. LiquidStack, the immersion pioneer, announced a 300 MW direct-to-chip CDU order in January 2026 — a company claim with the customer undisclosed — and Trane Technologies completed its acquisition of the company two months later. The technology pivot and the exit happened in the same quarter.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
datacenter — Commoditization pressure. Shells are commoditizing. Megawatts are not.

The evidence for the first half is the cost curve: escalation halving from 9.0% to 5.5% , a liquid-cooling premium in single digits , and land banks measured in gigawatts . The evidence for the second is the rent: 25.4% renewal spreads and 11.5% stabilized development yields .

The historical analogue is warehousing after e-commerce. The building became a commodity; the location with a highway interchange did not. Here the interchange is a substation.

The strongest attributed argument that the density transition is slower than it looks: Uptime Institute's Jacqueline Davis argued in April 2026 that direct liquid cooling will remain confined to high-density AI and HPC applications and will not reach mainstream mission-critical adoption within three years , citing redundant CDU and manifold engineering, reduced ride-through time for generator start, and unresolved ownership of DLC components between facilities and IT teams.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
datacenter — Failure modes. Power quality, not power quantity. Racks that swing more than 100% within milliseconds and overshoot their specification are a facility engineering problem before they are a grid problem — and they are already a grid problem one layer down. Blast radius: the electrical design of every facility built to a pre-2025 spec.

Permission. $130bn of projects blocked or delayed in a single quarter is the failure mode that no amount of capital fixes, and it lands on the layer that has to site the building.

Shells without demand. The counter-example exists, offshore: data centre utilisation in China's subsidised western AI hubs was reported at 20 to 30%, in regions offering power-bill cuts of up to 50% . That figure has no published counting method anywhere in its source chain — no definition of utilisation, no sample, no facility count — so it is a caveat, not a finding, and this page will not build an argument on it.

Stranded density. If Davis is right and liquid cooling stays niche , the retrofit market that the equipment backlogs assume does not arrive on schedule.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: datacenter — Open questions. - Why is Equinix growing at 10% and Digital Realty at 29%? If the answer is purely product mix, this layer is only short of hyperscale megawatts. If retail colocation is also being crowded out of power, the shortage is wider than the rent data shows. - How firm is the 41 kW baseline? It now anchors every before/after density comparison on this site , and it rests on Uptime Institute research whose exact article the corpus has not located. The figure is almost certainly right; the citation is not yet publication-grade. - Does 200 kW happen, and when? It is a roadmap projection and NVIDIA's 800 V answer does not ship until 2027 . Everything built before then is built to a lower ceiling. - How much of the pre-leasing is the same demand counted twice? Digital Realty's 54% pre-leased construction and Vertiv's $15.0bn backlog may describe the same buildings from two sides. The corpus cannot net them. - Is the opposition count a trend or a spike? One quarter of an advocacy tracker's own data is not a series.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the distribution layer: fairly-priced. The platform tax is already near zero: 1.5% on large private offers, 0.5% on services. What moves an enterprise purchase is committed-spend drawdown, not the rake. Priced fairly, measured badly.

The counter, per Microsoft's own FY2026 disclosures: Bundling compounds faster than any fee schedule. Microsoft's AI run rate reached $37bn, up 123%, on commercial remaining performance obligations of $625bn, up 110%. Distribution power is being repriced upward.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
distribution — Introduction. The rake is not the moat. The accounting is.

AWS charges 1.5% on private offers of $10m or more and on every renewal , and in June 2026 it cut the fee on professional services private offers to 0.5% . Meanwhile 100% of the pretax amount of an eligible partner purchase made through Microsoft Marketplace decrements the customer's Azure consumption commitment . Only one of those changes a procurement decision, and it is not the one with the fee schedule.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
distribution — What this layer is. Four rails carrying AI software to a buyer. Hyperscaler marketplaces move the transaction and, more importantly, the procurement paperwork. The system integrators sell the implementation labour. Incumbent bundling attaches AI to a renewal the customer was signing anyway — Copilot, Agentforce, Now Assist. And a fourth exists on paper only: agent commerce, two protocols with no disclosed volume.

The anchor to picture is not a product. It is a line item on a cloud bill the enterprise has already committed to spend.

Say the gap out loud, because it is large: this layer has no reseller economics. Microsoft states plainly that its Marketplace cannot specify or pay reseller margin, so partner margins are arranged outside Microsoft's systems, while its Cloud Solution Provider network runs to tens of thousands of organizations . There is no rate to publish because Microsoft pays none through that rail. Google Cloud Marketplace's take rate could not be verified from a primary page at all, and this page does not assume parity .

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
distribution — Unit economics. AWS charges 3% on public software-as-a-service offers and 20% on public server offers including machine images and containers . That near-sevenfold spread means a vendor's packaging decision — hosted service or customer-run container — changes its platform tax more than any negotiation could. Then the rake regresses toward zero exactly where the money is: private offers fall from 3% below $1m of total contract value to 2% between $1m and $10m and 1.5% at or above $10m, with all renewals at 1.5% . Professional services private offers went from 2.5% to 0.5% in June 2026 — an 80% cut on new offers, readable as a bid to pull integrator implementation work onto the AWS transaction rail. Microsoft charges a 3% standard store service fee with no listing fee, on an agency model across 141 locations and 17 transaction currencies .

A marketplace taking 1.5% of a large contract is not exercising App Store pricing power. It is running a payments-and-procurement rail near cost and buying something else with the forgone margin.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
distribution — The players. Accenture is this layer's cautionary tale about metrics, not about demand. It recorded $5.9bn of generative-AI new bookings in fiscal 2025 , roughly 7.3% of $80.62bn of total new bookings in a year when total bookings fell 1% . Read that as a terminal value, not a point in a series: Accenture disclosed no generative-AI bookings or revenue figure in any of its three fiscal-2026 quarterly releases, the terms appearing zero times in each , and third-quarter bookings were $19.32bn, down 2% . The bear reading is that a company retires a growth metric when it stops flattering. The steelman is Accenture's own: generative AI stops being separable once AI sits inside most transformation programmes, and the mega-deal counts that replaced it may proxy the same demand better. Either way, nothing on this site may present the $5.9bn as current.

Capgemini is the only major integrator still publishing an AI share — more than 8% of group bookings in 2025 and more than 10% in the fourth quarter, on €24,356m of bookings , stated as a floor and above Accenture's terminal figure. Everyone else publishes positioning. Infosys reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $20,158m, up 3.1% in constant currency, with $14.9bn of large-deal contract value, and no AI-specific revenue, bookings or contract-value figure anywhere in the release — while describing itself as an AI-first consulting firm. Cognizant reported trailing-twelve-month bookings of $29.6bn, up 11%, and headcount of 357,600, up 21,300, with no AI figure either .

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
Capgemini is the only major integrator still publishing an AI share — more than 8% of group bookings in 2025 and more than 10% in the fourth quarter, on €24,356m of bookings , stated as a floor and above Accenture's terminal figure. Everyone else publishes positioning. Infosys reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $20,158m, up 3.1% in constant currency, with $14.9bn of large-deal contract value, and no AI-specific revenue, bookings or contract-value figure anywhere in the release — while describing itself as an AI-first consulting firm. Cognizant reported trailing-twelve-month bookings of $29.6bn, up 11%, and headcount of 357,600, up 21,300, with no AI figure either .

The incumbents disclose more, in units of their own choosing. Microsoft said its AI business surpassed a $37bn annual revenue run rate, up 123%, in the quarter ended March 2026 — a run rate whose composition is not broken out and whose product definition Microsoft has never published — against commercial remaining performance obligations of $625bn, up 110% , and Microsoft Cloud revenue of $51.5bn in the December quarter . The loudest Copilot number is the least formal: Satya Nadella said Microsoft 365 Copilot had more than 20 million paid enterprise seats, up from 15 million a quarter earlier — on the earnings call, absent from the press release, which is why the corpus holds it at medium confidence. Seats sold, not seats used.

At the $30 per user per month list price those seats imply roughly $7.2bn of annualised list value, about 19% of the disclosed $37bn . That is this site's derivation and a ceiling, not a measurement: volume agreements are discounted, bundling shifts attribution between SKUs, and Microsoft has never confirmed Copilot sits inside the run rate as defined. It bounds the distance between the loud number and the quiet one.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
At the $30 per user per month list price those seats imply roughly $7.2bn of annualised list value, about 19% of the disclosed $37bn . That is this site's derivation and a ceiling, not a measurement: volume agreements are discounted, bundling shifts attribution between SKUs, and Microsoft has never confirmed Copilot sits inside the run rate as defined. It bounds the distance between the loud number and the quiet one.

Salesforce reported $1.2bn of Agentforce annual recurring revenue, up 205%, inside a combined Agentforce and Data 360 figure of nearly $3.4bn that includes $1.1bn of acquired Informatica Cloud ARR — read the composition, not the headline. ServiceNow disclosed no absolute Now Assist contract value at all, reporting subscription revenue of $3,877m instead . Adobe said AI-first ARR tripled and passed $500m against $6.62bn of quarterly revenue — the smallest disclosed AI share of the three and the fastest-growing.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
distribution — Concentration & chokepoints. The chokepoint is eligibility, and the platform writes the rules. Microsoft's benefit is genuinely powerful: 100% of the pretax purchase amount of an Azure-benefit-eligible partner offer bought through Marketplace decrements the customer's Azure Consumption Commitment . For a CIO already carrying that commitment, buying through the marketplace is a zero-marginal-cash decision and buying direct is a budget request.

The conditions are the moat and they travel with the mechanism. The purchase must go through Marketplace inside the Azure portal on a subscription tied to the agreement, so credit-card purchases on the public marketplace do not count; Azure prepayment is ineligible; the licence must be used exclusively in Azure, so hybrid or on-premises deployment breaks eligibility; professional services are ineligible; reseller-routed deals close outside Marketplace and do not decrement the commitment at all; and to qualify in the first place an offer must attain Azure IP co-sell status . The vendor's incentive is to become co-sell eligible; the platform's is to keep that tied to Azure-exclusive deployment. Note the two hyperscalers moving opposite ways on services: AWS cut its services fee to 0.5% to pull implementation work onto its rail , while Microsoft excludes services from drawdown entirely .

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
distribution — Lead times & capacity. The queue in this layer is procurement, and it is pre-paid: Microsoft's $625bn of commercial remaining performance obligations, up 110% , is the size of the committed pool drawdown mechanics act on.

The bypass is bottom-up adoption. Menlo Ventures found 27% of enterprise AI application spend arriving through product-led growth motions in 2025 against 7% in traditional software , and startups capturing 63% of enterprise AI application spend, up from 36% a year earlier . Both come from one proprietary survey of 495 buyers, unreplicated, published by an investor with an incentive to emphasise exactly that shift. Flagged rather than discounted — it is the only measurement of the bypass the corpus has.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
distribution — 2019 → today. There is no pre-2024 anchor in the corpus for this layer, so the honest version is two snapshots and a warning.

2024. Marketplace software sales are a $30bn base and AWS's simplified schedule takes effect in January at 3% for SaaS, 20% for server offers . 2025. The AI metrics arrive: Accenture books $5.9bn , Capgemini passes 8% of bookings , two agent-payment protocols launch thirteen days apart in September .

2026. They start disappearing. Accenture drops the disclosure for three straight quarters , ServiceNow reports a 2030 target instead of a current figure , and AWS cuts its services fee by 80% . The channel got cheaper and less legible in the same year.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
distribution — Commoditization pressure. The rake is already commoditized. At 1.5% on the deals that matter and 0.5% on services , marketplaces are procurement rails priced near cost, and the growth they expect is in volume rather than in take.

Forecast, per Omdia, October 2025: Omdia forecasts enterprise software sales through hyperscaler cloud marketplaces rising from $30bn in 2024 to $163bn by 2030, a 29.1% compound annual growth rate over 2025–2030 . A named research shop's projection, not a measurement — and the corpus has no primary figure for current marketplace volume at all, because every available estimate traces to marketplace-tooling vendors' own content marketing.

The services half is where compression is live rather than forecast, and the executives are the ones saying so.

Forecast, per C. Vijayakumar, chief executive, HCLTech, April 2026: HCLTech's chief executive said AI deflation would reduce revenue by three to five percent in the coming year, in the same reporting round in which Tata Consultancy Services reported a 0.5% annual revenue decline . Note what the claim is about: price, not volume.

The counterweight is headcount. Capgemini employed 423,400 people at the end of 2025, up 82,300 or 24%, in the year generative AI passed 8% of its bookings — the WNS acquisition is part of that, so it is not a clean organic signal — and Cognizant added 21,300 . Whatever AI is doing to this channel, it is not yet collapsing the labour model.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
distribution — Failure modes. Measurement failure, already happening. When the layer's flagship metric is withdrawn and the second-largest US-listed integrator never published one , AI demand through the services channel becomes unauditable from outside. The blast radius is analytical and it lands on everyone downstream of the number.

Eligibility risk. A vendor whose pipeline depends on committed-spend drawdown is exposed to conditions it does not control — co-sell status, Azure-exclusive deployment, the exclusion of services and of reseller-routed deals . A rules change is a go-to-market change. And because reseller-routed and drawdown-eligible deals are mutually exclusive for the same contract while Microsoft publishes no marketplace reseller margin at all , vendors are choosing between two channels with published economics for one.

Agent commerce with no denominator. Stripe and OpenAI launched the Agentic Commerce Protocol in September 2025 with Etsy as first merchant, disclosing no transaction volume, no fee schedule and no governance body ; Google announced the Agent Payments Protocol thirteen days earlier with more than 60 partner organizations and no volume either . Ten months on, no agent-commerce volume figure exists in any primary source. Against that silence the routing is already measurable: Adobe Analytics reported AI-referred traffic to US retail sites up 138% year over year in May 2026, converting 54% better than non-AI traffic — Adobe's proprietary panel, and Adobe sells AI marketing tooling, so the incentive is real.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: distribution — Open questions. - What share of marketplace volume is drawdown-driven? The mechanism is documented in full and its usage is disclosed nowhere, so the Omdia trajectory cannot be attributed to a cause. Google Cloud Marketplace's own take rate is also unverifiable from any primary page, and the site will not assume it matches the 3% AWS and Microsoft both publish . - Is Accenture's silence a measurement problem or a demand problem? Bookings fell 2% in the quarter AI consulting was supposedly compounding , which is suggestive and not decisive. - Do Copilot seats convert to revenue? 20 million paid seats against a derived $7.2bn list-value ceiling is the widest gap between a loud number and a quiet one in this layer. - Did agent commerce actually ship? Two protocols, more than 60 named partners, zero disclosed volume . Reporting that one was already retired in favour of dedicated retailer apps came only from inadmissible sources, so the site records the question and no answer.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the end-customer layer: overbuilt. Enterprise genAI spend tripled to $37bn and moved into core IT budgets. It is still a tenth of one year of big-four capex, and the median employee's AI bill is under eleven dollars a month.

The counter, per a16z's 2025 enterprise survey — 100 CIOs, from a firm with portfolio exposure to the answer: The share of enterprise LLM spend funded from innovation budgets fell from 25% to 7% in one year. The money left the experiment column and entered recurring IT. That is not the shape of a pilot bubble.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
end-customer — Introduction. Every number in the fifteen layers below this one is a bet on this one. And this is the layer with the worst evidence in the stack.

There are no filings here. Enterprise AI demand is measured by surveys — run, in the two most-cited cases, by venture firms with positions in the answer — and by one payments processor's transaction data. The layer's headline finding and its headline counter-finding disagree by roughly a factor of nine on what looks like the same metric. That disagreement is the most useful thing on this page.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
end-customer — What this layer is. The buyer. A CIO with a budget line, a procurement process, and a security review.

The physical anchor is a purchase order and a renewal date. Enterprises spent $37bn on generative AI in 2025, up from $11.5bn in 2024 — Menlo Ventures' market model plus a survey of 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers fielded in November 2025. It is verbatim-confirmed on Menlo's own page and has never been independently replicated, so it does not get upgraded past a medium-confidence estimate, and Menlo's investor incentive travels with it.

Set that against the layer directly upstream: combined 2025 capital expenditure across Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta was $376.1bn in cash . The terminal customer's entire generative-AI spend is roughly a tenth of one year of the machines being built to serve it. Some of that gap is legitimate — capex is a multi-year asset, and consumer subscriptions and API developers sit outside the enterprise survey. None of the available data closes it.

chunks.heading: What they actually buy
chunks.text:
end-customer — What they actually buy. Three findings are strong enough to build on, and all three point the same way: the enterprise has stopped experimenting and started purchasing.

They buy rather than build. 76% of enterprise AI use cases were purchased rather than built internally in 2025, against 53% purchased in 2024 — a one-year reversal. MIT's independent survey agrees on the direction and the mechanism: purchased tools and vendor partnerships succeeded about 67% of the time, roughly three times the rate of internal builds .

The money is no longer discretionary. The share of enterprise LLM spending funded from innovation budgets fell from 25% in 2024 to 7% in 2025 . This is the single strongest rebuttal to the pilot-stall thesis, and the sample is 100 CIOs across 15 industries — small for the weight it carries, from a venture firm with the same incentive the site flags on Menlo.

Adoption is broad and shallow. 55.0% of businesses on Ramp's platform had paid AI adoption in June 2026 , up from its own January 2026 estimate. That is primary transaction data across tens of thousands of businesses, which makes it the best-evidenced number on this page — and Ramp's own census-comparable estimate is far lower, because its customer base skews young and technology-forward. Use it as a leading indicator, not a national rate. Meanwhile the median AI spend per employee was $10.59 in the June 2026 index period , on a distribution the source describes as extremely skewed.

Forecast, per a16z (survey of 100+ CIOs, 2025): Enterprise buyers expected average LLM spend to grow roughly 75% over the following year . This is a stated expectation, not realized spend.

chunks.heading: The contradiction: 5% or 47%
chunks.text:
end-customer — The contradiction: 5% or 47%. Menlo reports that 47% of enterprise AI deals reached production in 2025, against 25% for traditional SaaS . MIT NANDA reports that about 5% of custom enterprise generative AI tool efforts were successfully implemented .

The corpus previously defused this by saying MIT measured P&L outcome while Menlo measured deployment. That explanation does not survive the primary source. MIT's own section is titled "the pilot-to-production chasm" and its sentence is that 5% of custom enterprise AI tools reach production. Nominally, these are the same metric, nine times apart. Three real axes separate them, and none is a rounding difference:

- Population. MIT counts custom internal builds. Menlo counts purchased deals. Both studies independently find purchased tools succeed several times more often than internal ones , so the two numbers are partly measuring the two ends of that same spread. - Success bar. Menlo never defines "go to production" anywhere in its report. MIT defines success as a tool causing "a marked and sustained productivity and/or P&L impact" — a much higher bar, and one that would fail plenty of shipped software. - Incentive. Menlo is a venture firm and an Anthropic investor. MIT NANDA's report is dated July 2025, self-labelled Preliminary Findings, and self-limits to being "directionally accurate based on individual interviews rather than official company reporting."

MIT's methodology also deserves stating accurately, because it has been inflated in circulation: per the report itself, a review of over 300 publicly disclosed AI initiatives, structured interviews with representatives of 52 organizations, and survey responses from 153 senior leaders collected at four industry conferences. Not 150 interviews and a 350-person employee survey, which is what the corpus previously recorded. And the phrase "rapid revenue acceleration" attached to the 5% figure in most coverage is Fortune's, not MIT's.

chunks.heading: The contradiction: 5% or 47%
chunks.text:
MIT's methodology also deserves stating accurately, because it has been inflated in circulation: per the report itself, a review of over 300 publicly disclosed AI initiatives, structured interviews with representatives of 52 organizations, and survey responses from 153 senior leaders collected at four industry conferences. Not 150 interviews and a 350-person employee survey, which is what the corpus previously recorded. And the phrase "rapid revenue acceleration" attached to the 5% figure in most coverage is Fortune's, not MIT's.

The honest synthesis: neither number is a measurement of enterprise AI success. One is a purchased-deal deployment rate with an undefined bar, the other is a custom-build P&L rate from a preliminary conference survey. They are consistent with a world where buying works, building mostly does not, and nobody has yet measured the return on either.

chunks.heading: Where adoption is genuinely deep
chunks.text:
end-customer — Where adoption is genuinely deep. One use case is not in dispute. 50% of developers used AI coding tools daily in 2025 , and coding is where the application layer's revenue is concentrated. Everything else is thinner than the discourse suggests: only 16% of enterprise AI deployments qualified as true agents in Menlo's 2025 survey , with prompt design still the dominant customization technique. Agentic architectures are a minority of production deployments.

Vendor share is the one place where survey and transaction data can be checked against each other, and they agree. Menlo puts Anthropic at 40% of enterprise LLM spend against 27% for OpenAI and 21% for Google — from an Anthropic investor, so flagged. Ramp's independent card data puts 42.4% of AI-spending businesses paying Anthropic against 39.5% paying OpenAI . These measure different things — spend share versus a headcount of paying businesses — and the vendor gap is far narrower in Ramp's data than in Menlo's. But the ordering survives an independent test, which almost nothing else on this page does.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
end-customer — Failure modes. The bar gets defined. Menlo's 47% rests on an undefined "production". The first credible, defined measurement of enterprise AI ROI is the single event most likely to reprice this layer, in either direction.

Shallow spend does not deepen. $10.59 of median AI spend per employee per month is a rounding error in an IT budget. Broad adoption at that depth supports a large number of small vendors, not $376.1bn of annual capex .

Buy-versus-build reverses again. The 53%-to-76% swing toward purchasing is one year old and moved fast in one direction. It can move back if model capability makes internal builds cheap, and the application layer's revenue is the collateral.

The measurement apparatus is the risk. Two venture surveys and one payments processor set the consensus for a layer that justifies trillions of forward commitments. Ramp's own selection bias, disclosed by Ramp , is the most honest caveat in the corpus and it applies to the most-cited adoption number in the market.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: end-customer — Open questions. - Has anyone measured the return? No. Both flagship studies measure deployment or self-reported impact . There is no audited enterprise AI ROI figure in the corpus, from any source, at any date. - Does the 75% expected spend growth materialize? It is a buyer expectation from a 2025 survey , and the cleanest falsifiable test on this page: Menlo's 2026 model will either show it or it will not. - Is Ramp's 55% a leading indicator or a ceiling? The gap between it and Ramp's own census-comparable estimate is the whole question, and Ramp is the only party who can close it. - Where does the money actually create value? MIT's finding that over half of genAI budgets go to sales and marketing while measured returns concentrate in back-office automation implies a large misallocation, on a preliminary report's evidence. - What is the churn rate? Nowhere in this corpus. Adoption counts are published; renewals are not. For a layer whose entire thesis is recurring budget, that is the gap that matters most.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the fab-tooling layer: underbuilt. Revenue is growing twice as fast as wafers shipped, and every physical queue — EUV tools, CoWoS slots, ABF substrate — is oversubscribed. That is scarcity rent, not overcapacity.

The counter, per the companies' own schedules — ASML's 2027 capacity plan, TSMC's US announcements, Intel's Q2 2026 commitment: The relief is already scheduled and it lands together: ASML plans +30% capacity for 2027, TSMC has announced $265bn of US fabs, Intel ramps 14A in 2028. Nobody has contracted the demand that far out.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — Introduction. The narrowest pipe in the AI stack is not a chip. It is a machine, and there are about sixty-five of the good ones made per year .

Everything in the layers above is a claim on capacity that was allocated eighteen months ago. This is the layer where the queue actually lives — and over the last two years the queue has walked up-stack twice, from wafers to advanced packaging, and from packaging to the resin film the package is built on. The film is made by a company better known for seasoning.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — What this layer is. Three businesses that the word "fab" hides.

The toolmakers sell the machines: ASML for lithography, Applied Materials and its peers for deposition, etch and metrology. The foundries — TSMC, Intel, Samsung, SMIC — buy those machines and sell wafer starts at a named process node. The packagers take finished dies and bond them, with memory, onto an organic substrate: TSMC's CoWoS line, plus the substrate and build-up film suppliers underneath it.

The physical anchor: a polished silicon disc the width of a dinner plate goes into a fab and comes out months later carrying a few dozen dies the size of a drink coaster. Each disc passes a lithography tool dozens of times. A single High-NA lithography tool costs roughly $380 million , and fewer than a dozen exist anywhere. The coaster is then glued to a slab of resin-coated laminate — the cheapest input in the chain and, right now, the one with the longest queue.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — Unit economics. What is bought here is a wafer start at a node, and separately a slot on a packaging line. The unit is a 12-inch wafer. The price is not published.

TSMC's Q2 2026 revenue was $40.20bn, up 36.0% year over year , on 4.336 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers, up 16.6% . Read those two numbers together and the layer's economics fall out: growth is carried by price, not volume. Gross margin was 67.7% , against 59.9% for full-year 2025, itself up from 56.1% in 2024 and 54.4% in 2023 . Net profit was NT$706.56bn, up 77.4% .

Where the price goes: N2 wafers are expected to run above $30,000 each, against roughly $20,000 at N3 . That is an estimate and must stay one — TSMC does not disclose wafer prices, and the figure has no primary behind it.

Where the cost goes: building a fab in the United States runs four to five times the Taiwan baseline. The figure is CFO Wendell Huang's, given to CNBC in July 2026, and the value here is the midpoint of his range .

And the margin that best explains where the chokepoint sits now is not a chipmaker's at all. Ajinomoto's Functional Materials segment, which makes the ABF build-up film every advanced package needs, reported a business profit margin above 50% for the fiscal year ended March 2026 . One qualifier travels with it permanently: that is a segment margin, and the segment is "Electronic Materials and Others" — not an isolated margin on the film itself. Put the supply response next to it, because that is the whole argument: Ajinomoto's third ABF plant, in Kani City, Gifu, is planned to begin operations in 2032, with construction starting in 2028 . A margin above 50% is not remarkable on its own. A margin above 50% with the next plant six years out is a chokepoint.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — The players. TSMC is the layer, and its mix shows why. Nodes at 7nm and below were 77% of wafer revenue in Q2 2026 , with N3 at 30%, up from 25% the prior quarter , and N2 making its first-ever revenue contribution at 3% . HPC reached 66% of revenue, from 61% in Q1, while smartphone fell to 22% . The AI transition is visible in the platform mix quarter by quarter.

ASML is the hard ceiling. Q2 2026 net sales were €9.3bn at a 54.0% gross margin , of which EUV systems were €3.8bn of €6.6bn in net system sales, including one High-NA machine . Full-year guidance was raised in July to €43–45bn, from €36–40bn after Q1 . China fell to 29.1% of 2025 net sales, from 36.1% in 2024 .

Applied Materials is the read on tool demand outside lithography: fiscal Q2 2026 revenue $7.91bn .

Intel is less dead than consensus, and the corpus is specific about how much less. Q2 2026 revenue was $16.1bn, up 25%, which Intel called its strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years . Its first 18A products entered high-volume production at the start of 2026 — the start, not the back half of 2025, which is the date that circulated. Intel also produced the first commercial logic product made with High-NA EUV, announced in Q2 2026, a milestone TSMC has deliberately not chased, holding Low-NA for N2 and A16 . But Intel Foundry revenue was $5.77bn in the quarter against TSMC's $40.20bn , and only $293m of that $5,765m came from external customers — roughly 95% is Intel selling to Intel. That single ratio decides whether Intel Foundry is a merchant foundry yet, and the answer is not yet.

Samsung is reported to target foundry profitability by 2027 alongside a 20% share by revenue . That is an aspiration relayed from unnamed industry sources, not a Samsung announcement, and the base matters: share by revenue, not by capacity.

SMIC is the trailing-edge counterweight — 2025 revenue of $9,327m at a 21.0% gross margin , running at 93.5% utilisation on more than a million 8-inch-equivalent wafers a month . It sells everything it can make, at a margin thirty-nine points below TSMC's.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — Concentration & chokepoints. Three concentrations stack on top of each other here, and only one of them is the famous one.

Geographic. Taiwan held 66% of global advanced-process foundry capacity — 16/14nm and below — against Korea at 11%, the US at 10% and China at 9% . That is a 2024 measurement printed on a 2026 page, and it should be read as a baseline that US buildouts are actively eroding. Further up the node stack, Rhodium Group put Taiwan's share of logic below 10nm at 92% — a 2022 estimate, and the direction has not changed, because every TSMC fab at 5nm and below except Arizona is still on the island.

Customer. TSMC's ten largest customers were approximately 78% of 2025 net revenue, the largest at 19% and the second at 17% . The second-largest customer jumped from 12% while the largest fell from 22%. TSMC names neither.

Packaging. CoWoS capacity went from roughly 35,000 wafers per month at end-2024 to 72,500–80,000 at end-2025 , with a target of 120,000–130,000 by end-2026 . Against that, Morgan Stanley put 2026 global CoWoS demand near 1.0 million wafers, versus about 670,000 in 2025 and 370,000 in 2024 , and projected NVIDIA's 2026 allocation at roughly 595,000 wafers, about 60% of capacity .

One number that belongs in this section and cannot be used in it: the widely circulated claim that the top three CoWoS customers hold more than 85% of 2026 capacity . Traced back, it is an unattributed industry estimate — the arithmetic of the author of a WeChat post republished in English, credited to no analyst, and no admissible corroborator exists. It is printed here so a reader knows the site looked. Nothing on this page rests on it.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
One number that belongs in this section and cannot be used in it: the widely circulated claim that the top three CoWoS customers hold more than 85% of 2026 capacity . Traced back, it is an unattributed industry estimate — the arithmetic of the author of a WeChat post republished in English, credited to no analyst, and no admissible corroborator exists. It is printed here so a reader knows the site looked. Nothing on this page rests on it.

Substrate. The tightest queue is the least glamorous input. Four Taiwanese and two Japanese substrate suppliers were seeking upfront customer commitments to secure capacity for Intel's EMIB packaging as of May 2026 , on the record from Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan at a J.P. Morgan conference. The direction of the squeeze is worth stating precisely, because it is easy to invert: the suppliers want commitments from Intel, and Intel in turn asks its own packaging customers to help fund the substrate prepayment. When a supplier can demand cash before capacity, the supplier is the chokepoint.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — Lead times & capacity. If demand doubled tomorrow, the answer would be set in Veldhoven and in one packaging fab in Taiwan.

ASML plans to ship approximately 65 Low-NA EUV systems in 2026, with EUV net system sales growing above 45% year over year — the figure is CFO Roger Dassen's . That is the true width of the pipe at the top of the stack.

Forecast, per ASML CFO Roger Dassen, July 2026: ASML plans a 30% capacity increase for both Low-NA EUV and immersion systems in 2027, and is only investigating a further 30% increase for 2028 . The distinction is the whole forecast: 2027 is planned, 2028 is under investigation, and the metric is capacity — what ASML could build — not output. Any 2028 supply floor built on this is a floor built on an intention.

Packaging is the other queue, and it is already sold. CoWoS lead times ran 52–78 weeks as of Q1 2026, with capacity fully booked through end-2026 .

Forecast, per TrendForce, relaying unnamed institutional investors via Taiwan's Economic Daily News: CoWoS capacity is reported to reach 120,000–140,000 wafers per month by end-2026, with the supply-demand gap narrowing from about 20% to about 10% . Note the provenance: third-hand and unnamed, not TSMC, which discloses no CoWoS capacity at all. If it is right, packaging is still rationed at the end of the forecast period.

The money going into the queue is being raised as fast as the queue lengthens. TSMC guided 2026 capex to $52–56bn in April, after $40.9bn in 2025 , then raised it in July to $60–64bn . Total announced US investment reached $265bn in July 2026 after a further $100bn Arizona commitment . Annual capacity passed 17 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers in 2025, on shipments of 15.0 million .

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
The money going into the queue is being raised as fast as the queue lengthens. TSMC guided 2026 capex to $52–56bn in April, after $40.9bn in 2025 , then raised it in July to $60–64bn . Total announced US investment reached $265bn in July 2026 after a further $100bn Arizona commitment . Annual capacity passed 17 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers in 2025, on shipments of 15.0 million .

Forecast, per Applied Materials — CEO Gary Dickerson and CFO Brice Hill, May 2026: Applied projects over 30% growth in its semiconductor equipment business in calendar 2026, raised from over 20% guided in February , and over 50% growth in packaging revenues in calendar 2026 . Dickerson said "packaging revenues" — not packaging equipment revenue, which is a narrower line, and the distinction is the company's, not ours.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — 2019 → today. The corpus's earliest hard anchor in this layer is 2022, so the first snapshot is thinner than the others, and the page will not fill the gap with atmosphere.

2022–23. Taiwan makes 92% of logic below 10nm . Advanced nodes at 7nm and below are 58% of TSMC wafer revenue in 2023 , at a 54.4% gross margin . Advanced packaging is a line item, not a constraint.

2024. Advanced nodes reach 69% of wafer revenue at a 56.1% gross margin . CoWoS is around 35,000 wafers per month . Taiwan holds 66% of advanced capacity , and China is 36.1% of ASML's sales .

2025–26. Advanced nodes are 74% of wafer revenue for 2025 , gross margin 59.9% for the year and 67.7% in Q2 2026 . CoWoS roughly doubles again to 72,500–80,000 wafers per month . ASML's China share falls to 29.1% as export controls bite from both directions. N2 books its first revenue . And the binding constraint is now a resin film with a segment margin above 50% .

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — Commoditization pressure. The leading edge is moving away from commodity, not toward it, and the evidence is in the price. Revenue up 36% on units up 16.6% , gross margin up more than seven points in a year , and a new node priced fifty percent above the last . A commodity does not do that. TSMC guided Q3 2026 revenue to $44.6–45.8bn .

The commoditization is happening one or two nodes back, and in China specifically. SMIC's 21.0% gross margin on 93.5% utilisation is what a sold-out commodity fab looks like: full, and barely funding the next node. Chinese-made equipment rose from 25% to 35% of China's domestic tool market between 2024 and 2025, from a pre-controls base of 10–15% . Yet domestically produced chips were only about 30% of Chinese chip consumption in 2025, against a policy target of 70% — massive over-delivery on tools and mature nodes, large under-delivery on the headline goal. At the advanced end, SemiAnalysis conservatively estimated SMIC's advanced-node capacity at 45,000 wafers per month by end-2025, of which at most 20,000 was needed for Huawei Ascend production — one analyst's estimate, uncorroborated, and running DUV multi-patterning without EUV means yield rather than capacity is the binding term.

The analogue is the layer's own history: mature nodes commoditized once anyone could buy the tool. The leading edge has not, because one company sells the tool.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
fab-tooling — Failure modes. One island. 66% of advanced capacity and 92% of sub-10nm logic in one earthquake zone, feeding customers who are themselves concentrated — approximately 78% of TSMC revenue in ten names . Blast radius: everything above this layer, immediately.

The substrate. The cheapest input has the longest lead and the highest margin: suppliers demanding prepayment for capacity against a film business earning a segment margin above 50% whose own next plant does not begin operations until 2032 . A package that cannot be built stops a die that is already printed, and this is the one queue in the layer that no amount of 2027 capex shortens.

Tool politics. Export enforcement now reaches the tools directly. Applied Materials agreed in February 2026 to pay BIS $253 million to resolve an inquiry into China shipments , a settlement carrying a suspended denial order — breach would bar certain US exports outright. BIS separately revoked Validated End-User authorisations for three foreign-owned fabs in China, effective 31 December 2025 , removing blanket tool-import rights from the largest non-Chinese fabs inside the country.

Intel commits, customers do not. Intel committed in Q2 2026 to a 2028 high-volume ramp for 14A, with risk production in the second half of 2027 . That is Intel committing to Intel. The only report of a named first external 14A customer is a Reuters wire citing Elon Musk, for chips destined for Tesla's Austin Terafab complex — sourced to comments rather than to an announcement or a filing by either company, with every other outlet syndicating the same wire. Three months on, Intel's filings still describe external 14A demand as uncommitted. The caveat is the more important half: a second leading-edge supplier only relieves the chokepoint if someone signs.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: fab-tooling — Open questions. - Does the 2028 EUV capacity arrive? ASML plans 30% for 2027 and is investigating 30% for 2028 . Everyone modelling 2028 accelerator supply is implicitly answering this, mostly without saying so. - Who covers substrate between now and 2032? Ajinomoto's third plant starts operations in 2032 , which is after every accelerator roadmap the site has recorded. Either the incumbent lines debottleneck, a second film supplier qualifies, or packaging stays rationed for the rest of the decade — and the corpus has no capacity data on the alternatives. - Whose wafers fill the US fabs? $265bn announced at four to five times Taiwan construction cost . The site has no data on who has committed to those wafers at what price. - Is Taiwan still at 66%? The share is a 2024 measurement and the buildouts since are exactly the variable. A 2026 number would change several arguments on this page. - Does Intel land external 14A demand before the 2028 ramp? It is the cleanest falsifiable test of whether the leading edge stays a monopoly.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the foundation-models layer: overbuilt. Revenue compounds faster than anything in software history and gross margin still fell from 40 percent to 33, against a 46 percent internal target. The leaders differ 4x on the frontier's cost.

The counter, per Anthropic's own Series H disclosure and the enterprise contracts behind it: Anthropic went from a $30bn run-rate in April 2026 to $47bn in May, with more than 500 companies each paying over $1m a year. Demand that steep pays for a great deal of capex.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
foundation-models — Introduction. Two lines define this layer, and they run in opposite directions.

The cost of a frontier training run grew 2.4x per year from 2016 through 2024 . The price of a fixed level of capability fell about 10x per year from 2021 through 2024 . Everything else on this page — the valuations, the burn schedules, the open-weight price shocks, one lab renting GPUs from a rival's parent company — follows from those two lines. You must spend more each year to stay at the frontier, and what you sell gets cheaper while you do it.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
foundation-models — What this layer is. A foundation model is a file. The layer is the industrial process that produces one.

The physical anchor: DeepSeek-V3's full training run consumed 2.788 million H800 GPU-hours across 14.8 trillion tokens . That is a warehouse of accelerators running for weeks to produce a single artifact of a few hundred gigabytes, which is then copied for free.

Where the money goes inside that run is not where most people assume. For the GPT-4 and Gemini Ultra generation, frontier development cost split 47–67 percent hardware, 29–49 percent R&D staff, and only 2–6 percent energy . Compute and payroll are the business. Electricity, at this layer, is a rounding error — the power problem lives three layers down and arrives here as a capacity constraint, not a cost line.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
foundation-models — Unit economics. The overtake is real. The margin is not what circulated. Anthropic's run-rate revenue crossed $47bn in May 2026 . Sacra estimates OpenAI at approximately $33bn in the same month . That is roughly 1.4x, not the 1.9x that comes from setting May against OpenAI's $25bn February figure . And one carve-out travels with every OpenAI number here: Sacra states these annualized figures exclude Microsoft licensing revenue and large one-time deals, focusing on the core subscription and API business. Anthropic's $47bn carries no such exclusion. The two are not like-for-like, and the honest statement of the lead is "ahead on comparable-date estimates, by less than half again, on definitions that do not match."

Two more qualifiers on the $47bn itself. It is company-stated and unaudited. And it is a run-rate — Anthropic announced $30bn in April 2026 and $47bn seven weeks later, which annualizes a short window in which one large enterprise contract distorts the snapshot.

Margins are going the wrong way. OpenAI's gross margin was approximately 33 percent for FY2025 — down from 40 percent the prior year, against an internal target of 46 percent . The direction and the miss are the story, not the level: a company that planned for 46 and delivered 33 is losing the margin race against its own forecast, while growing revenue as fast as anyone ever has. The cost driver is inference: $8.4bn in 2025 , a figure that originates in leaked-document reporting and reaches the corpus through a single relay, not two independent measurements.

Forecast, per OpenAI internal projections, via The Information and Sacra: Inference cost is projected at $14.1bn for 2026 . Cash burn is projected at approximately $27bn in 2026 and $63bn in 2027, with cash-flow positive not expected until 2030 . The forecast was revised sharply upward in a single pass — the revision is a better fragility signal than any single year in the series.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
foundation-models — The players. Anthropic. $47bn run-rate , a $65bn Series H at a $965bn post-money valuation in May 2026 , and more than 500 companies each spending over $1m a year . Revenue mix is the distinguishing feature: Sacra estimates 70–75 percent of it comes from pay-per-token API calls . Never restate this as "80 percent from API" — the ~80 percent figure belongs to a different cut, revenue from more than 300,000 business customers , and the circulating claim looks like a corruption of it.

OpenAI. A $122bn round at an $852bn post-money valuation in March 2026 , corroborated by four independent organisations plus OpenAI itself. The fragility is inside the round rather than beside it. Amazon committed $50bn of it, of which $35bn is contingent on an initial public offering or on reaching artificial general intelligence . Read that twice. Roughly a third of the largest private round ever raised is conditional on an event that has no agreed definition, no test, and no date — which means the headline valuation and the money actually available are two different numbers. Distribution is the asset — ChatGPT exceeded 1 billion monthly active app users in May 2026 and OpenAI reported more than 9 million paying business users in February 2026 . The first of those is a Sensor Tower third-party estimate relayed by Reuters and CNBC, not an OpenAI disclosure; the second is best read as paying business seats.

xAI, now inside SpaceX. Revenue of $107m with a $1.46bn net loss for the quarter ended 30 September 2025 — Bloomberg's read of investor documents, and every subsequent outlet traces to that one origin. A $20bn Series E at a $230bn valuation followed in January 2026 , then SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock deal on 2 February 2026 at a $250bn xAI standalone valuation . Put the quarter and the valuation on the same line and the multiple speaks for itself.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
xAI, now inside SpaceX. Revenue of $107m with a $1.46bn net loss for the quarter ended 30 September 2025 — Bloomberg's read of investor documents, and every subsequent outlet traces to that one origin. A $20bn Series E at a $230bn valuation followed in January 2026 , then SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock deal on 2 February 2026 at a $250bn xAI standalone valuation . Put the quarter and the valuation on the same line and the multiple speaks for itself.

DeepSeek and the open-weight frontier. V4 shipped on 24 April 2026 with V4-Pro output at $0.87 per million tokens . Its V3.2 paper discloses no absolute training compute, no GPU count and no dollar cost — every widely repeated DeepSeek training-cost figure comes from somewhere other than DeepSeek. Alibaba's Qwen anchors the largest model ecosystem on Hugging Face, with over 100,000 derivatives , carrying the source's own warning that trackers counting finetunes as distinct models inflate such totals.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
foundation-models — Concentration & chokepoints. The chokepoint is compute access, and in 2026 it started crossing competitive lines.

Anthropic contracted with SpaceX — not xAI — for access to 220,000 GPUs and more than 300 MW of compute across Colossus 1 and 2, as of May 2026 . Both corrections matter: the lessor is the acquiring parent, and the lease covers both facilities.

The mechanism is the interesting part, and it is a utilization number. The agreement was reported at $1.25bn per month through 2029, struck after Colossus 1 fell to about 11 percent GPU utilization when xAI moved training onto Colossus 2 . Treat those terms as reported rather than filed — press attributes them to SpaceX's IPO filing, and the corpus types them as an estimate pending a check against the filing itself. But the shape is clear: an almost-idle cluster is worth more rented to a direct competitor than held empty. Rival-to-rival compute leasing is new, and it says something specific about this layer — at a certain scale, stranded accelerators are a worse problem than a strengthened rival.

Anthropic also disclosed agreements for up to 5 GW of new Amazon capacity plus 5 GW of next-generation TPU capacity with Google and Broadcom . Read the "up to." That is a company claim about future capacity, not energized load, and the queue that decides whether it arrives is in the grid layer, not this one.

The concentration that follows is unusual: three or four entities can plausibly assemble ten-gigawatt compute programmes, and they are the same entities buying data, renting clouds, and designing accelerators. The chokepoint is not a component. It is balance-sheet access.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
foundation-models — Lead times & capacity. Training runs are getting longer and more expensive on a schedule.

Forecast, per Epoch AI: The largest training runs are projected to cost more than $1bn by 2027 on an amortized hardware-and-energy basis. Runs of 2e29 FLOP are likely feasible by 2030, with power as the first binding constraint — orders of magnitude above the GPT-4 generation, and beyond what a single campus can energize, which is why the largest projected runs assume distribution across sites.

Two other queues are shortening. Reasoning is the new place compute goes: OpenAI scaled reasoning training compute 10x from o1 to o3 in four months , and Epoch expects reasoning training to reach the total-compute frontier not long after. And data binds eventually — roughly 500 trillion text tokens on the indexed web, with the text-only constraint arriving about five years from 2024 at 4x compute growth .

Meanwhile the cheap end proves how little compute a capability can need once the recipe is known. DeepSeek-R1's reinforcement-learning phase cost approximately $1m in hardware time, about 20 percent of its base model's pretraining cost . That is the number that should worry anyone underwriting a $121bn compute programme .

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
foundation-models — 2019 → today. 2019. Training a language model is a research expense. The largest runs cost single-digit millions, data is free to scrape, and no one outside a lab has an opinion about GPU-hours.

2022–23. GPT-4 arrives and the layer becomes an industry. Hyperscaler capex quadrupled between GPT-4's March 2023 release and late 2025 , and leading labs began showing more revenue per employee than major public tech companies.

2025–26. Three regime changes at once. Reasoning becomes the compute sink, at 10x per model generation . Open weights become a pricing force — DeepSeek-R1 launched at $2.20 per million output tokens against $60 for OpenAI o1 , the canonical margin-compression event. And revenue arrives in quantities nobody modelled: $47bn and ~$33bn run-rates at two companies that had almost no revenue three years earlier.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
foundation-models — Commoditization pressure. Capability commoditizes; the frontier does not. The mechanism is a ladder, not a price cut.

Per-capability deflation runs at roughly 10x a year , measured by tracking the cheapest model that still clears a fixed benchmark. But the premium tier barely moved. o1 sold output at $60 per million tokens in January 2025 ; today's flagships sit at $25 and $30 per million output tokens, with a new and more expensive tier stacked above them. Labs are not defending a price point. They are adding rungs at the top and letting the old ones collapse.

The open-weight gap is the number to watch, because it sets how fast the collapse propagates. The best open-weights model scored 51 against 61 for the leading closed model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index in July 2026 , on an index where the majority of evaluated models are now open weights. Chinese models trail leading US releases by 7 months on average since 2023, with a range of 4 to 14 , and most of the leading Chinese models are open-weight while US frontier models are closed. That combination — a months-long lag, released openly — is what turns a capability into a commodity on a predictable clock.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
foundation-models — Failure modes. The scissors close. Training costs compound at 2.4x a year while per-capability prices fall 10x . A lab must grow revenue faster than its own input costs, forever, on 33 percent gross margins . Blast radius: everything downstream that assumed cheap tokens.

The burn schedule slips. This is the layer's counterparty risk, and it lands on the cloud layer first: OpenAI is the largest single name in several other companies' backlogs.

Forecast, per OpenAI internal projections, via The Information: $121bn of compute spend and an $85bn loss in 2028 , with cash-flow positive not expected before 2030 . The originating reporting is paywalled and the accessible corroboration is secondary.

A strategy divergence resolves badly. Two companies selling into the same demand curve appear to disagree by a factor of four on the cost of staying at the frontier. One of them is wrong, and the answer is worth hundreds of billions.

Forecast, per secondary reporting on Anthropic's projections — single source, directional only: Anthropic's training costs are projected to peak near $30bn through 2028, roughly 4x below OpenAI's projected $121bn 2028 compute spend . Single secondary source. Treat the ratio as a direction, not a measurement.

An open-weight price shock. R1 cut the price of o1-class reasoning by more than an order of magnitude and its RL phase cost about $1m in hardware time . The next such event does not require a new frontier — only a good recipe and cheap GPU-hours.

Rival dependency. Renting 220,000 GPUs from a competitor's parent at a reported $1.25bn a month through 2029 is efficient until it is renegotiated — and the counterparty is the one company with a structural interest in the tenant's capacity being scarce.

Conditional capital. $35bn of a $50bn anchor commitment turns on an IPO or on reaching AGI . A funding round is only as good as its non-contingent tranche, and this one's contingency has no test attached.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: foundation-models — Open questions. - Does the overtake survive like-for-like accounting? $47bn against ~$33bn is roughly 1.4x on definitions that do not match, because the OpenAI figure excludes Microsoft licensing and one-time deals. No public dataset reconciles them, and until one does the ranking is an estimate, not a fact. - What does a seven-week run-rate mean? $30bn in April to $47bn in May is both endpoints company-stated and separately reported, so there is no source conflict — but annualizing a short window in which one large contract lands is not the same as a year of revenue. - Which binds first, power or data? Epoch names power as the first constraint on 2e29 FLOP runs and separately dates the text-data wall about five years from 2024 . Those two forecasts have not been reconciled against each other. - Is the 10-point open-weight gap stable? It is one reading on one index in one month. The entire commoditization timeline hangs on whether that gap is widening or closing. - What do frontier runs actually cost? The best-documented run in the corpus is DeepSeek's, and DeepSeek's own V3.2 paper discloses no training cost at all . Every US frontier figure is an estimate from the outside.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the grid layer: underbuilt. The US built 888 miles of high-voltage line in 2024 against a benchmark near 5,000 a year, and PJM's capacity auction has now cleared at its price cap twice. The queue is the product.

The counter, per Grid Strategies, and PJM's own realisation caveat: The queue numbers are nameplate, and Grid Strategies — the shop that documented the load surge — estimates utility forecasts overstate data-center load by about 25 GW. Only 24% of PJM's 2020 cohort ever signed an agreement.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
grid — Introduction. The bottleneck inverted. For twenty years the queue was full of generators waiting to sell power. Now it is full of buyers waiting to consume it.

That is the fact that reorganises this layer. ERCOT is tracking 438 GW of large-load interconnection requests, nearly 90% of them data centers — 5.1 times its all-time peak demand of 85,508 MW, set in August 2023 , both figures stated in the same ERCOT document. Its generation queue, by comparison, holds 432 GW . Two queues of almost identical size, pointing in opposite directions, and only one of them used to exist.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
grid — What this layer is. Between a power plant and a rack sit three things nobody photographs: a large power transformer, a high-voltage substation, and a position in a queue.

The first two are steel and copper with multi-year lead times. Large power transformer waits often exceed 24 months, with prices up roughly 77% since 2019 — and that is the weakest-sourced number on this page, a vendor blog relaying paywalled Wood Mackenzie research, so treat it as directional only.

The third is the actual product. A data center does not buy electricity from this layer. It buys the right to connect, and then a bill for the network upgrades its connection triggers. Everything else on this page follows from that.

The physical build is not keeping pace with the paperwork. The US built 888 miles of new transmission at 345 kV and above in 2024, against 322 miles in 2023 and roughly 5,000 miles per year indicated as necessary by the DOE's 2024 National Transmission Planning Study — and that DOE benchmark did not incorporate the load growth that has since been forecast, so it understates the need. NERC reports 41,000 miles above 100 kV under construction or in development over ten years, up from 28,275 miles a year earlier ; the increase is concentrated in planning phases, and miles actually under construction have not risen substantially.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
grid — Unit economics. PJM's capacity auction for the 2028–2029 delivery year cleared at its $325 per MW-day price cap on July 15 2026, totalling $16.4bn . Two things travel with that number. PJM states the $16.4bn total was unchanged from the prior auction — the cap is binding, but the auction total was flat year over year, not escalating. And PJM states it does not equate to a total cost to load, because load hedged through self-supply or bilateral contracts is not exposed to clearing prices. What the cap is hiding: PJM's uncapped simulation clears far higher, which is the more honest measure of scarcity.

The auction cleared 6.8 GW below its 20% installed reserve margin target and attracted 525 MW of new supply . Read those two figures together. At the maximum price the market is allowed to pay, half a gigawatt of new capacity showed up. Price is not the constraint. Delivery is.

Who pays. PJM's independent market monitor attributes $29.4bn of the $63.6bn in total capacity charges across the last four auctions to data centers, including $6.3bn of the $16.4bn in July 2026 — roughly 46% of the four-auction total, on the market monitor's own counterfactual attribution across the base residual auctions for delivery years 2025/26 through 2028/29. It is a model, and the monitor says so. It is also the most precise measurement of cost socialisation anywhere in this corpus, made by the entity paid to be adversarial to PJM.

Wholesale costs moved with it: PJM wholesale power costs rose 54% in one year per Monitoring Analytics in March 2026 . That is a headline-level capture on a specific window, and the monitor's later deck restates the increase on a different window — the window matters more than the number.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
grid — The players. PJM is the stress case, because it stopped taking applications. Its interconnection queue was effectively closed to new entrants from 2022 until April 2026 , on a pre-reform backlog it could not clear. It studied approximately 160 GW between the July 2023 reform launch and September 2025, with roughly 46 GW left to complete by end-2026 . Transition Cycle 1 closed in September 2025 with 130 requests totalling 17.4 GW — a rounding error against what arrived next.

Then the queue reopened, and the composition flipped. Cycle 1 drew 811 projects totalling 220 GW of nameplate capacity , led by gas at 106 GW — a reversal from the renewables-dominated queues of 2020 to 2024. PJM publishes the caveat that matters and it is usually dropped: the figures represent maximum potential output, and based on historical performance only a percentage of applicants will sign interconnection agreements. The corpus can put a number on that percentage. 24% of PJM's 2020 entry cohort reached an interconnection agreement or became operational — a generation cohort, but the only realisation prior anyone has. A 220 GW queue is not a 220 GW pipeline.

ERCOT is building the process the load queue exposed it as lacking. The PUCT approved its initial large-load batch-study process on June 18 2026, covering projects of 75 MW or larger . ERCOT attaches its own attrition caveat to the queue: Batch Zero developers face a commitment deadline to post financial security and prove site control before their requests survive. Its queue grew from 63 GW at end-2024 to 226 GW in November 2025 before reaching 438 GW.

MISO is the quieter version: 1,705 projects and 312 GW in the queue as of early 2025 , with a Definitive Planning Phase averaging three to four years against a stated goal of a one-year process by the 2028 cycle .

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
ERCOT is building the process the load queue exposed it as lacking. The PUCT approved its initial large-load batch-study process on June 18 2026, covering projects of 75 MW or larger . ERCOT attaches its own attrition caveat to the queue: Batch Zero developers face a commitment deadline to post financial security and prove site control before their requests survive. Its queue grew from 63 GW at end-2024 to 226 GW in November 2025 before reaching 438 GW.

MISO is the quieter version: 1,705 projects and 312 GW in the queue as of early 2025 , with a Definitive Planning Phase averaging three to four years against a stated goal of a one-year process by the 2028 cycle .

FERC is the referee, and it has started intervening on the load side rather than the generation side. In December 2025 it ordered PJM to create four transmission service options for co-located large loads, finding the existing tariff unjust and unreasonable . In June 2026 it issued show-cause orders to all six FERC-jurisdictional RTOs and ISOs, requiring them to justify or revise large-load interconnection rules within 60 days — its proposed elements include a standard large-load threshold, hourly forecast and telemetry requirements, and pro forma agreements making large-load customers bear network-upgrade costs. The regulator is trying to un-socialise the bill.

The hyperscalers are increasingly refusing to wait. Microsoft announced a 2 GW data center in Pecos, Texas in June 2026 with the company funding the energy infrastructure itself . FERC's earlier rejection of the amended Talen–Amazon interconnection agreement for a 480 MW behind-the-meter expansion at Susquehanna is the ruling that pushed co-location deals front-of-meter and made this the default shape.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
grid — Concentration & chokepoints. Load growth is not spread across the country. Six regions account for over 80% of forecast US five-year load growth: ERCOT 53 GW, PJM 30 GW, SPP 24 GW, MISO 16 GW, Georgia Power 8 GW, CAISO 7 GW . PJM's share is driven by Northern Virginia; ERCOT's by data centers, industry and oil and gas.

The chokepoint is therefore geographic and administrative at once. Two RTOs decide most of the outcome, one of them has just reopened a queue after four years , and the other is inventing its large-load process in public .

A second chokepoint is the load shape. The US power system operates at about a 60% load factor as of 2025, up from 58% three years earlier, and is forecast to reach 66% in 2030 . Data centers add energy faster than they add peak: they run flat, and utilities are now planning around load factors far above the system average. A flatter system is more efficient and also less forgiving — there is less slack to absorb the next large customer.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
grid — Lead times & capacity. Generation interconnection waits are the number everyone quotes, and the word "generation" has to stay attached to it. Average generation interconnection wait time in PJM was 40 months as of May 2026, against a federal target of 8 to 11 months . Active generation projects inside the data-center load-growth zones of PJM and ERCOT were waiting 36 to 48 months . These are not load-queue waits — the load queue is new enough that ERCOT is still designing the process that will produce its first timelines.

PJM still has roughly 46 GW of studies to finish by the end of 2026 before its reformed process is caught up . Against a data center shell that can be built in eighteen months, the study calendar is the schedule.

What happens if demand doubles is already partly on the record, as a forecast, from the reliability regulator.

Forecast, per NERC (2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment, published January 2026): US summer peak demand growth of approximately 224 GW over ten years, nearly 70% above the prior year's forecast . And 13 of 23 assessment areas face resource adequacy challenges over that period . The wording matters: NERC is explicit that Elevated-Risk areas meet resource adequacy criteria and fall short only under extreme conditions, and that only High-Risk areas exceed shortfall criteria. "Thirteen areas face shortfalls" overstates what the assessment says.

Forecast, per Ascend Analytics: A potential PJM capacity shortage reaching 15 GW by 2030 as load additions outpace new generation — consistent with an auction whose reserve-margin shortfall is already 6.8 GW while attracting 525 MW of new supply .

PJM's answer is procurement rather than construction: in April 2026 it proposed adding 14.9 GW through bilateral contracts and a central backstop matching large loads with generation sellers .

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
grid — 2019 → today. 2019. Interconnection is a specialist concern. Utility five-year peak load forecasts are essentially flat; the industry's planning problem is retirement, not growth.

2022. Aggregate US utility five-year summer peak load growth forecasts filed with FERC total 24 GW . PJM's queue closes to new entrants . Data centers are 4.4% of national electricity and nobody outside the sector is counting.

2026. Those same FERC filings total 166 GW by 2030 — a six-fold increase in three years , of which roughly 90 GW, about 55%, is linked to data centers . ERCOT's large-load queue goes from 63 GW to 438 GW inside eighteen months . FERC opens proceedings against all six RTOs . NERC issues its highest-tier alert on computational load .

The steelman, and its counter — both from the same report. Grid Strategies estimates the data center portion of utility load forecasts is overstated by roughly 25 GW of that ~90 GW, on the view that data center growth is unlikely to require much more than 65 GW through 2030 . The drivers it names are duplicate requests, unrealistically high assumed load factors, and timing optimism. That is the strongest available argument that this page is describing a paperwork bubble.
