But the same report notes that utility forecasts of 2022–2025 growth were revised up, not down, with actual load growth exceeding what had been forecast, and that PJM is evaluating forecast adjustments that would add to its 2030 load forecast. Utilities and RTOs continue to plan against the full 166 GW. Whoever quotes the overstatement finding without the revision finding is quoting half a paper.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
grid — Commoditization pressure. The opposite is happening here, and it is the most under-appreciated fact on this page.

Grid interconnection used to be a regulated, essentially free service with a queue that moved. It is becoming a priced, rationed, contractually complex asset — the exact reverse of commoditization. The evidence is structural, not rhetorical: a capacity auction clearing at its administrative cap , four distinct new transmission service classes for co-located load invented by regulatory order , a batch-study process with financial-security postings and site-control proof for anything at 75 MW or above , and six simultaneous FERC proceedings to define a threshold above which a customer becomes a different regulatory category entirely .

The historical analogue is not electricity. It is airport slots: a public good that became a tradeable, scarce, litigated asset the moment demand outran runway.

The one genuine commoditization pressure runs the other way, through flexibility. Google had signed 1 GW of data center demand response with five utilities as of March 2026 . If interruptible load becomes a standard product, the scarce asset is un-scarced by contract rather than by construction.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
grid — Failure modes. The reliability event. NERC issued a Level 3 Essential Actions alert — its highest tier — on May 4 2026 on computational load, after observing customer-initiated large load reductions and oscillations that occur within seconds; two data center load-reduction events exceeded 1,000 MW during 2025, the largest 1,800 MW . Four qualifiers travel with that, and the site prints all four. The reductions occur in seconds, not sub-second. There were two such events in 2025, not repeated ones — the largest caused by a transmission fault in the Eastern Interconnection. The alert is explicitly non-binding: it creates no mandatory obligation and carries no penalties. And NERC's "computational load" category includes cryptocurrency mining as well as AI data centers, so part of the event record is not AI at all. What survives all four qualifiers is still serious: the regulator's highest tier of alert, on a load type that can drop a gigawatt in seconds.

Cost socialisation becomes political. $29.4bn of $63.6bn in capacity charges attributed to data centers is a number that appears on retail bills. The market monitor has proposed separate capacity auctions for data centers. Blast radius: state legislatures, and the siting permission every layer above this one depends on.

Capacity shortfall in the largest market. Ascend Analytics' 15 GW PJM shortage by 2030 , against 525 MW of new supply attracted at the price cap , is a mechanism, not a scenario: prices cannot rise further, so the adjustment has to come through curtailment, backstop procurement or refused interconnections.

The queue turns out to be phantom. If the 24% realisation rate of PJM's 2020 cohort is anywhere near the right prior for today's 220 GW , every transmission investment sized against the queue is oversized — and the utilities making those investments recover them from ratepayers regardless.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: grid — Open questions. - What is the realisation rate on a load queue? The corpus has one for generation — 24% for PJM's 2020 cohort — and none for large load, because ERCOT's process is a month old . Every argument about the 438 GW rests on a number nobody has. - Overstated by 25 GW, or revised up again? Grid Strategies argues both in one report . The 2027 FERC 714 filings settle it. - Does the cap hold? The 2028/29 auction cleared at its $325/MW-day cap, as the prior auction cleared at its own . If the cap is raised, the total stops being flat; if it holds, the shortfall has to resolve physically rather than through price. - How much load is genuinely interruptible? Google's 1 GW comes with Google's own caveat that flexibility is limited and location-specific. Nobody has published a system-wide number. - How much of NERC's computational-load record is AI? The alert's category includes crypto mining , and the corpus cannot split the event record between the two. - What are transformer lead times, really? The best-sourced figure available is a vendor blog relaying paywalled research . For a component that gates every interconnection, that is not good enough, and the site says so rather than printing the more dramatic numbers circulating.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the inference layer: fairly-priced. Price per capability falls 50x a year, yet identical H100s still rent at a 1.8x spread across four first-party price lists. The margin case is thinner: two estimates, one analyst.

The counter, per Fireworks AI's own July 2026 statement: Fireworks says it passed $1bn of annualized run-rate in July 2026, most of it serving models its own customers had specialised. Commodities do not grow like that, and specialisation is the exit from parity pricing.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
inference — Introduction. This is the layer that is supposed to be a commodity and keeps refusing to behave like one.

The deflation is the fastest measured anywhere in the stack: across six benchmarks, the price of a fixed level of capability fell at a median 50x per year . And in July 2026 Anthropic scheduled a price increase — Sonnet 5 output goes from $10 to $15 per million tokens on 1 September 2026 . Both facts are true, which means the simple story about token prices is wrong.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
inference — What this layer is. Training produces a file. Inference is the business of turning that file into tokens on demand, profitably, for many users at once.

The physical anchor is memory, not arithmetic. Each in-flight conversation holds an attention cache on the accelerator; serving well means packing as many of those as possible into one pass of the same weights. Batching, KV-cache management, quantization and splitting prefill from decode are the whole craft, and they are what stands between a GPU-hour you rent and a token you sell.

Four kinds of company sell here. Model owners serve their own weights through their own APIs. Managed platforms — Fireworks, Together, Baseten — serve anyone's weights, mostly open ones, on rented or owned fleets. Routers sit above everything and sell placement. Silicon-backed servers build custom hardware and sell only its output.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
inference — Unit economics. Two units run this layer, and the spread between them is the business. Upstream you buy GPU-hours: Together's on-demand H100 was $3.99 per GPU-hour in July 2026 . Downstream you sell tokens.

And identical silicon does not rent at one price. Published H100 on-demand pricing across Modal, Baseten, Fireworks and Together spanned $3.95 to $7.00 per GPU-hour in July 2026, a spread of about 1.8 times — four first-party price lists, same hardware, fetched the same day. Hold that number. It is the cleanest evidence on this page that serving is not yet a commodity, and it is the only such evidence that does not depend on an analyst's estimate.

On the token side, open weights price at near-parity across independent providers, which is what commoditization looks like when it arrives. Groq serves gpt-oss-120B at $0.15 per million input and $0.60 per million output tokens at approximately 500 tokens per second . Frontier weights price roughly forty times higher: Claude Opus 5 at $5 input and $25 output per million , OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol at $5 and $30 . Cached-input and batch tiers cut both further; the discount structures are near-identical across the two vendors, which is itself a commoditization signal at the frontier tier.

Margins are the other half of the argument, and there the evidence is thin. Fireworks' gross margin was approximately 50 percent as of mid-2026, against a stated target of 60 percent . Sacra estimates Together's at approximately 45 percent . Read those two citations together: both legs of the "managed serving holds margin" case are the same analyst, and neither figure appears in a funding announcement, a company statement, or any independent coverage. The price dispersion above is T1 and first-party. The margins are one shop's estimates, and this page weights them accordingly.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
Margins are the other half of the argument, and there the evidence is thin. Fireworks' gross margin was approximately 50 percent as of mid-2026, against a stated target of 60 percent . Sacra estimates Together's at approximately 45 percent . Read those two citations together: both legs of the "managed serving holds margin" case are the same analyst, and neither figure appears in a funding announcement, a company statement, or any independent coverage. The price dispersion above is T1 and first-party. The margins are one shop's estimates, and this page weights them accordingly.

Forecast, per Fireworks AI, relayed by Sacra: Fireworks targets 60 percent gross margin , up from the ~50 percent estimated at mid-2026. A managed platform hitting that on rented accelerators would be the strongest single argument that serving is not a commodity — and it would also be the first such figure anyone had confirmed from outside the company.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
inference — The players. Fireworks surpassed $1bn in annualized revenue run-rate in July 2026 — company-stated, and a multiple of where it sat at the end of 2025. That supersedes the $800m Sacra estimated for May 2026 , which should now be read as a ten-week-old waypoint and never as a current figure; the difference resets the company's revenue multiple materially.

Together AI is estimated at $1.0bn annualized as of February 2026 . The independently corroborated figures for Together are its Series C and its bookings, and bookings are not revenue; the revenue estimate itself is single-source.

Baseten reached an estimated $600m annualized in March 2026, up from $200m in December 2025 . An apparent inconsistency between that step and the company's own year-over-year growth claim resolves as a misreading — they measure different intervals, not different numbers.

OpenRouter processed about 100 trillion tokens per month across more than 8 million developers as of May 2026 . Earlier volume figures still in circulation — including the one this corpus itself held until July 2026 — are more than an order of magnitude stale, and pair a 2026 date with a developer count from a year earlier. A router that sees a hundred trillion tokens a month knows more about real model demand than anyone selling models.

Groq is the cautionary tale. It signed a non-exclusive licensing agreement with Nvidia on 24 December 2025 worth $17bn in cash across three installments , distributed most of it to shareholders, and sent its CEO and president to Nvidia while promoting its CFO. It reads as a soft exit of the independent-accelerator thesis, even as the remaining company raised $650m in June 2026 to expand its inference cloud .

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
inference — Concentration & chokepoints. There are two chokepoints and they sit at opposite ends.

Below, the silicon is effectively one vendor, and the most credible independent challenger licensed its position to that vendor for $17bn . Serving-cost improvements therefore arrive on someone else's roadmap.

Above, demand discovery is concentrating into routers. At 100 trillion tokens a month , OpenRouter is a distribution chokepoint for every provider that does not own an end-user relationship — and it takes a percentage of routed spend for the service.

What is not concentrated is serving know-how. vLLM reported serving DeepSeek at 2,200 output tokens per second per H200 GPU using wide expert parallelism and async scheduling , published openly, alongside public work on FP8 KV-cache quantization and prefill-decode disaggregation. The efficiency frontier here diffuses through open-source blog posts within weeks. That is excellent for buyers and corrosive for anyone whose margin depends on a serving trick.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
inference — Lead times & capacity. This layer has no build queue of its own. It inherits one: GPU availability, power and shells, all upstream. What it controls is throughput per unit of rented capacity, and that is improving fast enough to be a substitute for capacity.

Demand-side efficiency moves too, and harder than most forecasts allow. Anthropic's code-execution-with-MCP example cut agent token consumption from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens, a 98.7 percent reduction . A single architectural change at the application layer can remove two orders of magnitude of demand from this one. Token-volume projections that extrapolate from current agent designs are extrapolating from a design that is actively being optimised away.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
inference — 2019 → today. 2019. Inference is an afterthought — a model runs on the machine that trained it, and serving cost is a footnote in a research budget.

2022–24. Serving becomes an industry with a price list. Frontier reasoning output sells at $60 per million tokens as late as January 2025 , and the deflation rate accelerates: restricted to data after January 2024, the median price decline rises to 200x per year .

2026. Three prices coexist that would have looked incoherent two years earlier. Open weights at $0.60 per million output tokens . Frontier weights at $25 to $30 . And a scheduled 50 percent list increase on a mid-tier model .

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
inference — Commoditization pressure. The case for commoditization is strong and quantitative. A median 50x annual price decline per unit of capability , rising to 200x when the data is restricted to after January 2024 . Near-parity pricing on identical open weights across independent providers . Serving optimizations published in public repositories . On the evidence a buyer sees, this looks like electricity.

The case against has four parts, of very unequal strength. The strongest is price dispersion: a 1.8x spread on identical H100s across four providers' own published rate cards . Commodities do not price 80 percent apart on the same day for the same hardware. Second, a hard fact — a vendor with pricing power raised list price 50 percent , ending introductory pricing rather than defending share. Third, and nearly invisible in price tables: a tokenizer that emits more tokens for the same text raises the effective price per request without changing a single number in the published rate card. Fourth and weakest, though the most quoted: gross margins of approximately 50 percent and approximately 45 percent at the two largest managed platforms — one analyst, twice.

So the honest reading is that the token is commoditizing and the platform is not, yet — and that the durable evidence for the second half is dispersion in first-party prices, not the margin estimates everyone cites. A single audited margin disclosure would settle the most important question on this page.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
inference — Failure modes. Margin inversion on agentic workloads. Replit's gross margin fluctuated between positive 36 percent and negative 14 percent during 2025 . That is the clearest public evidence that per-token COGS can invert a downstream business's economics — and it rests on a single unsourced sentence with no independent corroboration, which is itself the finding.

Router dependency. Providers that reach developers through a router do not own the demand. Placement and take rate are set by someone else.

Capacity mismatch. Reserved GPU commitments are long; token prices fall 50x a year per unit of capability . Contract the wrong duration at the wrong price and the deflation lands on your gross margin rather than your customer's bill.

Demand-side collapse. A 98.7 percent token reduction from one agent-architecture change shows how fast volume assumptions can break in the buyer's favour.

Estimate risk. Nearly every revenue and margin figure for the private companies in this layer is a Sacra estimate. If those estimates are systematically high, the layer's growth story and its margin story are both weaker than they appear, and nothing public would reveal it.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: inference — Open questions. - What are managed-serving gross margins really? Approximately 50 percent at Fireworks and approximately 45 percent at Together come from one analyst, and both are typed as estimates. Neither company has confirmed a margin. These remain the corpus's most load-bearing unverified numbers, and the layer's verdict leans on first-party price dispersion instead precisely because of that. - Is the Sonnet price increase an exception or a turn? One scheduled rise inside a 50x-a-year deflation could be the end of introductory pricing or the start of frontier pricing power. Nothing here distinguishes them. - Where does the deflation actually stop? 50x a year is a median across six benchmarks , and the per-benchmark rates spread widely around it — the corpus holds that range only in a source note. A median drawn from a wide spread is a description of the past, not a forecast. - Does specialisation survive open-weight parity? Fireworks attributes most of its volume to customer-specialised models. If specialisation is real differentiation, parity pricing on stock open weights is beside the point; if it is fine-tuning as a service, it is a feature, not a moat. - Who captures the router's economics at scale? OpenRouter sees 100 trillion tokens a month on a take rate the corpus records only in a source note. The margin structure of the layer's distribution chokepoint is not documented.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the memory-interconnect layer: underbuilt. A 72% operating margin on a product the industry still calls a commodity is the price of a shortage, and the scheduled 2027 supply response is 15-20% more bits. That does not clear it.

The counter, per TrendForce, July 2026 — the author of both forecasts: The deflation is inside the same forecasts: long-term agreements cap contract increases for some cloud buyers, and RDIMM bit supply grows 15-20% in 2027. Peak margins have never been structural in DRAM.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — Introduction. DRAM is the part of the stack everyone had filed under "commodity, cyclical, low margin."

In the first quarter of 2026, SK hynix reported a 72% operating margin . That is the layer's headline and it should be uncomfortable. It is also where the discourse around this number goes wrong, so the page will be pedantic about it once, up front: the comparison everyone reaches for is against NVIDIA's operating line, and NVIDIA's operating margin is not in this corpus. Setting 72% against a gross margin would be inventing the number that makes the point.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — What this layer is. Two things a rack cannot work without, both sold by the gigabyte-second and the bit-per-second rather than by the FLOP.

Memory is HBM stacked beside the accelerator die and DRAM in the host server. Google's Ironwood TPU carries 192 GB of HBM per chip at 7.37 TB/s — that per-accelerator content is the demand driver for the whole HBM squeeze. Interconnect is the fabric: NVLink inside the rack, Ethernet or InfiniBand between racks, optics between rows. NVLink 6 moves 260 TB/s of all-to-all bandwidth inside one Vera Rubin NVL72 rack .

The physical anchor: a stack of DRAM dies bonded vertically, sitting a few millimeters from the compute die on the same package, because the distance the electron travels is the thing being bought.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — Unit economics. SK hynix's Q1 2026 revenue was KRW 52,576.3bn, up 198% year over year and 60% quarter over quarter , at a 72% operating margin on operating profit of KRW 37,610.3bn . For the prior full year, revenue was KRW 97,146.7bn at a 49% operating margin . The margin went from very good to unprecedented in four quarters, and it was 58% as recently as the quarter before.

For scale on the other side of the package, NVIDIA's GAAP gross margin in the overlapping quarter was 74.9% . That is a different line of the income statement and the site will not score the two against each other — the like-for-like figure does not exist in the corpus. What survives without any comparison at all is the level: 72% of revenue converted to operating profit, in memory.

Interconnect earns less per dollar of revenue but is growing just as fast. NVIDIA networking revenue was $14.8bn in the April 2026 quarter, up 199% — larger, on its own, than AMD's entire data center segment at $5.775bn .

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — The players. SK hynix is the price-setter, and HBM is why: its HBM revenue more than doubled year over year in 2025 , though the absolute figure is not disclosed. It completed HBM4 mass production in September 2025 and moved to large-scale production in 2026 , and names custom HBM as the next differentiator — which is the tell: the "commodity" is being specified per customer.

NVIDIA is the interconnect incumbent, and it is now leading with Ethernet rather than InfiniBand. Spectrum-6, arriving in deployments in July 2026, is a 102.4 Tb/s Ethernet switch system, twice the previous generation's capacity, supporting pluggable and co-packaged optics .

Forecast, per Dell'Oro Group, July 2026: Dell'Oro forecasts the high-end router and aggregation switch market reaching $19bn by 2030, with cloud-provider spend growing at a 16% CAGR driven by AI infrastructure . Dell'Oro is the author of that forecast, not a relay of someone else's — but it is still a forecast, and the corpus has no direct Ethernet-versus-InfiniBand share split to sit beside it.

The thinness is worth stating: this layer has the fewest usable facts of any deep-adjacent layer on the site. Samsung and Micron pricing, HBM share by vendor, and optics unit economics are gaps, not conclusions.

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — Concentration & chokepoints. Memory bandwidth is now the legal chokepoint as well as the physical one. The BIS rule effective 15 January 2026 caps licensable China and Macau advanced-computing exports at total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s . Bandwidth, not FLOPS, is the gate that separates an H200-class part from a Blackwell-class one — regulators went where the binding constraint actually is.

The demand side is concentrated by construction: HBM content per accelerator is fixed by the accelerator's design , so every incremental GPU or TPU ships with a pre-committed memory order. There is no substitution and no downgrade path.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — Lead times & capacity. Forecast, per TrendForce, July 2026: Server DRAM contract prices are forecast to rise 13-18% quarter over quarter in Q3 2026 , with long-term agreements capping increases for some cloud buyers. Against that, total RDIMM bit supply is projected to grow 15-20% year over year in 2027 . Both are TrendForce's own forecasts.

Put those two side by side and the layer's condition is legible. Prices are rising by mid-teens percentages per quarter while the supply answer is mid-teens percentages per year. That is what an underbuilt layer looks like: the response is real, scheduled, and an order of magnitude slower than the signal.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text: memory-interconnect — 2019 → today. The corpus cannot write this section honestly and the page will not pretend otherwise. Its earliest memory anchor is full-year 2025 — a 49% operating margin — and HBM4 reaching mass production in September 2025 . The 2019 and 2022 DRAM troughs, which are the necessary comparison for judging whether 72% is a cycle or a regime , are not in the research. A Gate-3 pass on this layer should add them before anyone leans on the word "structural."

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — Commoditization pressure. This is the layer where the commoditization thesis is being tested in reverse. HBM began as a commodity product and is de-commoditizing: mass production of HBM4 , custom HBM as the stated next step, and margins that moved from 49% for 2025 to 72% in one quarter . When a part gets specified per customer, it stops being a spot good.

The counterweight is the historical base rate rather than any current datapoint. DRAM has run this cycle repeatedly, and every prior peak margin was followed by a supply response — which is precisely what the 2027 bit-supply forecast describes , and why long-term agreements exist at all . The honest reading is that HBM has partly escaped the cycle and server DRAM has not.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
memory-interconnect — Failure modes. Memory as the binding input. Because HBM content per accelerator is fixed , a memory shortfall does not slow the stack proportionally — it caps accelerator shipments outright. Blast radius: every layer above, immediately, with no workaround at the design level.

The stockpile running out. SemiAnalysis estimated China procured 13 million HBM stacks, enough for 1.6 million Ascend 910C packages, with Samsung supplying 11.4 million of them — purchases made before restrictions bit. That is a drawdown, not a domestic capability. What replaces it is the most consequential open number in this layer, and the corpus's only estimate for it sits behind a paywall and is therefore not on this site.

Price pass-through. Server DRAM rising 13-18% in a quarter lands on the bill of materials of everyone building racks. Where long-term agreements cap it, the cost moves to whoever lacks one — smaller buyers first.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: memory-interconnect — Open questions. - Is 72% a cycle or a regime? Without the 2019 and 2022 trough margins, the site cannot answer it, and neither can anyone quoting the number. - What does NVIDIA actually earn at the operating line? The comparison everyone wants to make against SK hynix needs a figure the corpus does not have; only the 74.9% gross margin is sourced . - Ethernet or InfiniBand, and in what proportion? NVIDIA is leading with a 102.4 Tb/s Ethernet switch , which is a signal about direction, not a share number. - How much of the 2027 supply response is HBM versus commodity DRAM? The 15-20% RDIMM bit-supply forecast says nothing about HBM specifically, and the two markets are now pricing differently. - Can domestic Chinese HBM replace the stockpile? The one available forecast is paywalled and single-source, so this page states the question and no number.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the primary-energy layer: underbuilt. Fuel is cheap and getting cheaper. The machines that burn it are sold out past 2029, priced at the top of guidance, with waits reaching 84 months. That is a shortage, not a bubble.

The counter, per Scott Strazik, GE Vernova's CEO, and Ed Crooks, Wood Mackenzie: The turbine makers say they are not the gating item. Strazik points at EPC, permitting and fuel availability; Crooks notes all three OEMs are expanding, and Wood Mackenzie expects orders to peak in 2026 — a cycle top, not a floor.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
primary-energy — Introduction. The cheapest input in the AI stack is the gas. The scarcest thing is the machine that burns it.

That inversion is the whole layer. EIA has Henry Hub averaging $3.67 per MMBtu in 2026 and just under $3.50 in 2027 — molecules are abundant, and getting cheaper. Meanwhile a heavy-duty gas turbine now carries an order book that runs past the end of the decade, and the queue for one is measured in years. Anyone arguing about whether AI has enough energy is arguing about the wrong noun.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
primary-energy — What this layer is. Everything above this page is downstream of three physical objects.

The heavy-duty gas turbine: a jet engine the size of a locomotive, bolted to a concrete pad, spinning a generator. Three companies on earth build them at scale — GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The nuclear plant: mostly not new, mostly being un-retired or contracted out of the existing fleet, occasionally a small modular reactor that does not exist yet. And solar plus storage: the only new supply that can be sited, built and energised inside three years, which is why it keeps winning on volume while losing the narrative.

The demand these three serve is real and measurable. US data centers consumed roughly 176 TWh in 2023, about 4.4% of national electricity, up from 58 TWh in 2014 . Where it goes from there is a forecast, and gets forecast treatment.

Forecast, per Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory: US data center electricity consumption of 325 to 580 TWh by 2028 — 6.7 to 12 percent of total US electricity . The range is the finding: the low case roughly doubles 2023, the high case more than triples it.

Forecast, per BloombergNEF: US data center power demand of 106 GW by 2035, from approximately 40 GW in 2026 .

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
primary-energy — Unit economics. Turbine pricing has a present-day level for the first time. BNP Paribas' Moses Sutton put heavy-duty gas turbines at about $790 per kW in July 2026, HA-class combined-cycle machines at about $950 per kW and aeroderivatives at about $1,800 per kW . Wood Mackenzie separately forecasts about $600 per kW by end-2027 . These are not two points on one line. The mid-2026 estimate already exceeds the end-2027 forecast, so they cannot be the same measure — most plausibly a global average across turbine classes against US order-book pricing by class. The site will not plot them as a series and neither should anyone else.

Whole-plant cost is a different animal again, and must never be set against turbine-only dollars per kW. BloombergNEF put US gas plant construction at $2,157 per kW in 2025, up from under $1,500 per kW in 2023 — a 66% increase in two years, with construction timelines 23% longer .

The direction of pricing power is not ambiguous. GE Vernova guided first-half 2026 gas equipment orders to 10 to 20 points above Q4 2025 on a dollar-per-kW basis, and reported in July 2026 that it landed at the higher end of that range .

Nuclear prices at roughly twice wholesale, and the discovery range is now visible. Microsoft's Three Mile Island restart PPA is estimated at $98 per MWh by Morgan Stanley and $115 per MWh by Jefferies — both estimates; the contract price is undisclosed. Meta's Clinton virtual PPA is estimated by Jefferies at $70 per MWh, about $20 per MWh above Illinois energy-plus-capacity compensation . Constellation itself guided 80 to 88 dollars per MWh for future front-of-the-meter nuclear offtake . A band is forming between roughly $70 and $115, and every number in it is an analyst estimate or a guide, not a printed contract.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
primary-energy — The players. GE Vernova is the layer's clearest instrument. Gas equipment backlog plus slot reservations reached 116 GW at the end of Q2 2026, up from 100 GW a quarter earlier . Total company backlog is $176bn , on $24.2bn of Q2 orders, up 88% organically .

The headline everyone repeats is that GE Vernova signed 20 GW of gas equipment contracts in Q2 2026 while shipping 3 GW . Roughly seven times what it ships, and it is the most generous of three available ratios. In the same presentation GE Vernova reports its own unit metric: 12.1 GW of gas turbine orders against 3.3 GW of sales, 3.7 times, not seven . The gap is composition: the 20 GW is firm orders plus a much larger block of non-binding slot reservation agreements, which the company reports separately from both orders and backlog . On new firm orders alone, the quarter's signings came in below its 3.3 GW of shipments . The scarcity is genuine. The multiple depends entirely on whether you count a reservation as a sale.

Data centers are the marginal driver, not the bulk of it. Data center load was 20% of GE Vernova's 100 GW under contract as of Q1 2026 — and because GE Vernova says that 20% explicitly supports data centers, excluding indirect service, it is a floor. Downstream, its Electrification segment booked over $5bn of data-center-linked orders in the first half of 2026, more than double its full-year 2025 total ; gas power orders are not in that number.

Siemens Energy carries a €154bn backlog with gas turbine delivery waits of up to four years , and holds 60 GW of firm gas turbine orders plus 27 GW of reserved future capacity . Data-center-related commitments were 24 GW of that 87 GW total, about 28% . Its North American arm booked 14 GW in the first three quarters of fiscal 2025 with 65% destined for data centers — the mix at the margin is far more AI-weighted than the stock.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
Siemens Energy carries a €154bn backlog with gas turbine delivery waits of up to four years , and holds 60 GW of firm gas turbine orders plus 27 GW of reserved future capacity . Data-center-related commitments were 24 GW of that 87 GW total, about 28% . Its North American arm booked 14 GW in the first three quarters of fiscal 2025 with 65% destined for data centers — the mix at the margin is far more AI-weighted than the stock.

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries planned as of September 2025 to double gas turbine manufacturing capacity over two years . EPRI's Bobby Noble supplies the deflating arithmetic: one manufacturer doubling raises overall industry output by a small fraction of that, and is likely not enough to drastically reduce wait times.

Nuclear, on this layer, is four hyperscalers buying from the existing fleet and funding the next one. Microsoft signed a 20-year, 835 MW PPA with Constellation to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 as the Crane Clean Energy Center , against roughly $1.6bn of recommissioning investment and a target pulled from 2028 to 2027 , helped by a $1bn DOE loan . AWS expanded its Susquehanna PPA with Talen to 1,920 MW . Meta signed 20-year agreements with Vistra for 2,100 MW from the existing Perry and Davis-Besse plants plus 433 MW of uprates in the early 2030s and a 20-year, 1,092 MW virtual PPA for Clinton starting June 2027 .

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
primary-energy — Concentration & chokepoints. Three manufacturers, one order book, and a global capacity number that has not moved fast enough.

Global gas turbine orders reached 110 GW in 2025 against global manufacturing capacity of 60 to 70 GW per year . That is the chokepoint stated in one line: the industry took roughly half again more orders than it can build in a year. GE Vernova had approximately 10 GW of combined 2029 and 2030 delivery capacity remaining after Q1 2026 — GE Vernova's slots, not the industry's. It is roughly a third of the heavy-duty market; Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi slots are not in that figure, and presenting a single vendor's remaining slots as an industry ceiling overstates the scarcity.

What one buyer can absorb: the SB Energy Portsmouth data center project is sized at 9.2 GW and requires 24 to 30 heavy-duty gas turbines . A single site can consume a meaningful share of a year of one vendor's output.

There is a second concentration on this layer that nobody prices, because it sits under the fabs rather than the racks. Taiwan imports about 97% of its energy and holds roughly two weeks of emergency supply without new imports . In any blockade scenario the grid fails before the cleanrooms do.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
primary-energy — Lead times & capacity. This is where the layer's two honest steelmen live, and both are named.

Waits for large gas turbines reached up to 84 months in 2025, from 30 to 36 months previously . GE Vernova's own directional lead time on new heavy-duty orders was approximately 36 months in Q1 2026 — a different scope from the industry maximum, and the gap between the two is the single most abused spread in this discourse.

Steelman one: the manufacturer says it is not the constraint. On that same call, GE Vernova CEO Scott Strazik said that in many of these projects "the gas turbines are really not the gating item," pointing instead at the EPC buildout, permitting and fuel availability over a three-year project cycle . The chief executive of the company whose slot scarcity anchors the shortage narrative does not hold the shortage narrative.

Steelman two: supply is already responding. Wood Mackenzie's Ed Crooks noted in February 2026 that GE Vernova, Siemens and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries have all announced significant gas-equipment capacity expansions since the start of 2025 , and says turbine makers are increasingly not the primary bottleneck for large loads seeking power.

The capacity plans behind that are concrete, and they are forecasts.

Forecast, per GE Vernova (Scott Strazik): Gas turbine production output of 20 GW per year by Q3 2026, 24 GW by 2028 and 30 GW by 2030 — with at least 125 GW of gas equipment under contract by end-2026 . Note the shape of it: the 2030 output target sits below 2025's industry order intake.

Forecast, per Wood Mackenzie: 63 GW of gas turbine manufacturing capacity additions between 2026 and 2030 , with orders expected to peak in 2026 . If both hold, the industry adds capacity into a falling order book — the overcapacity case, from the firm that documented the shortage.

Meanwhile the supply that does not queue for a turbine keeps growing fastest.

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
Forecast, per Wood Mackenzie: 63 GW of gas turbine manufacturing capacity additions between 2026 and 2030 , with orders expected to peak in 2026 . If both hold, the industry adds capacity into a falling order book — the overcapacity case, from the firm that documented the shortage.

Meanwhile the supply that does not queue for a turbine keeps growing fastest.

Forecast, per EIA (Short-Term Energy Outlook, July 2026): US solar capacity growing from 151 GW in 2025 to 183 GW in 2026 and 223 GW in 2027 ; natural gas generating capacity reaching 508 GW by end-2027 ; total generation rising from 4,502 to 4,636 billion kWh, roughly 3% growth .

Hold those two against each other. Total US generation grows roughly 3% to 2027 while the low end of LBNL's range has data center consumption roughly doubling off its 2023 base by 2028 . The system is not being asked for much more electricity in general. It is being asked for a great deal of electricity in a few places, on a schedule set by chip deliveries.

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text:
primary-energy — 2019 → today. 2019. The baseline year the whole price series is measured against. Gas is a mature, deflating business; turbine orders track utility retirements; nobody outside the industry can name the three manufacturers.

2022–23. Gas plant construction is still under $1,500 per kW . Turbine waits are 30 to 36 months . Nuclear plants are still closing — Palisades shuts in May 2022 .

2025–26. Orders hit 110 GW against 60 to 70 GW of annual capacity . Waits reach 84 months . Construction cost is $2,157 per kW . Wood Mackenzie's forecast has turbine prices reaching approximately 195% above 2019 levels by end-2027 . And the direction of the nuclear fleet reverses: the DOE closes a $1.52bn loan to restart the 800 MW Palisades plant, the first recommissioning of a retired US reactor .

The thing that changed is not the fuel. It is that a deflating capital-goods business discovered it was a bottleneck.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
primary-energy — Commoditization pressure. This layer is de-commoditizing, and it is doing so in exactly the places where a commodity story would predict the opposite.

Gas itself is the commodity, and it behaves like one: EIA has power-sector consumption reaching 38.1 Bcf per day in 2027, up 4% from about 37.5 Bcf per day in 2026, with a record monthly 50.6 Bcf per day in July 2027 — record volumes at falling prices. That is a commodity working correctly.

The turbine is going the other way. Prices at roughly 195% of 2019 levels on Wood Mackenzie's forecast , order pricing landing at the top of a 10-to-20-point guided increase , and slot reservation agreements — customers paying to hold a place in a queue — as a routine commercial instrument. Manufacturers are selling scarcity as a product.

Nuclear is pre-commodity: a price band being discovered deal by deal between roughly $70 and $115 per MWh , with the seller publishing a guide because there is no liquid market to reference.

Solar plus storage is the one genuinely commoditized segment, and it is the reason the layer's scarcity has a ceiling. EIA has US solar going 151 → 183 → 223 GW across 2025 to 2027 . If turbine slots stay sold out to 2030, that is where marginal load goes.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
primary-energy — Failure modes. The turbine order book turns out to be a cycle top. Wood Mackenzie forecasts 63 GW of manufacturing capacity additions to 2030 while expecting orders to peak in 2026 . Every slot reservation signed at today's pricing is a bet that does not clear. Blast radius: three manufacturers' margins, and the credibility of every AI power forecast that assumed the shortage was structural.

Nuclear slips, in the way nuclear slips. The clearest datapoint is not a forecast but a plant. Palisades had still not returned to power operations as of July 2, 2026 — 800 MW, a $1.52bn federal loan, and Holtec reporting the last major restart projects closed out with operational-readiness work still underway . Against that benchmark, read the SMR pipeline carefully. Google agreed to purchase up to 500 MW from Kairos Power reactors with the first targeted online in 2030 . Amazon and Energy Northwest announced four X-energy SMRs with a 320 MW first phase expandable to 960 MW in the early 2030s . Meta and Oklo announced support for development of up to 1,200 MW at Pike County, Ohio, first power possible as early as 2030 ; Meta and TerraPower announced funding for two Natrium units capable of up to 690 MW as early as 2032, plus rights to up to six further units producing 2.1 GW targeted for 2035 .

Read those two Meta agreements precisely, because the headlines do not. Both are "up to" ceilings on development and prepay frameworks, not contracted offtake. Oklo has no NRC-licensed operating unit. Nothing in either agreement obliges anyone to deliver a specific number of megawatt-hours on a specific date.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
Read those two Meta agreements precisely, because the headlines do not. Both are "up to" ceilings on development and prepay frameworks, not contracted offtake. Oklo has no NRC-licensed operating unit. Nothing in either agreement obliges anyone to deliver a specific number of megawatt-hours on a specific date.

Demand-side flexibility becomes the release valve, or does not. Google had signed 1 GW of data center demand response with five utilities as of March 2026 , with Google's own caveat attached: there are limits to how flexible a given data center can be, and the capability will only be available at certain locations. If flexibility scales, the turbine shortage matters less than anyone thinks. If it does not, every GW of load needs a firm GW behind it.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: primary-energy — Open questions. - Which turbine price is the real one? BNP Paribas at ~$790/kW in mid-2026 and Wood Mackenzie at ~$600/kW by end-2027 cannot both describe the same object. The corpus does not have the scope definitions to reconcile them, and until it does, no chart on this site joins them. - Do orders peak in 2026? Wood Mackenzie says yes ; GE Vernova is guiding to at least 125 GW under contract by year-end . This is the cleanest falsifiable test on the page and it resolves within twelve months. - Is the gating item the turbine or the project? Strazik says EPC, permitting and fuel ; Crooks says turbine makers are increasingly not the primary bottleneck . If they are right, the constraint lives one layer up — in the interconnection queue — and this page is the wrong place to look for it. - What do the SMR frameworks actually oblige? Every announced agreement is an "up to" volume with a first-power date in 2030 or later. The corpus has no disclosed prepay amounts, no penalty terms, and no NRC licence for the lead vendor on Meta's Oklo deal . - How much of the nuclear price band is real? Every figure in the $70–115/MWh range is an analyst estimate or a seller's guide . Not one contract price has been published.

chunks.heading: The verdict
chunks.text:
Verdict for the systems layer: fairly-priced. Integrators earned 1.8-3.6% operating margins in Q1 2026 while the thermal, power and connector content inside the same racks earned 17.8-25.4%. Capacity is fairly priced; the profit pool moved.

The counter, per Dell's own Q1 FY2027 filing, plus Hon Hai's Michael Chiang on raising the self-manufacturing ratio: Dell gave up 6.5 points of consolidated gross margin to AI mix and recognised $16.1bn of AI servers in a single quarter. At enough revenue velocity, scale beats ratio — falling margins and more dollars coexist.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
systems — Introduction. Assembling the rack is not a business. Supplying it is.

In the first quarter of 2026 the companies that bolt AI racks together reported operating margins of 1.8 to 3.6 percent, while the thermal, power and connector suppliers whose parts sit inside those same racks reported 17.8 to 25.4 percent . Same quarter, same demand, same physical object. What follows is mostly how that gap opened while revenue in this layer roughly doubled.

chunks.heading: What this layer is
chunks.text:
systems — What this layer is. The unit of sale changed. A GB300 NVL72 is 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs in one fully liquid-cooled rack with 37 terabytes of fast memory . Nobody buys a server any more; they buy the rack.

The physical anchor, from the generation NVIDIA has published numbers for: 120 kilowatts , 1.36 metric tonnes on the floor , more than two miles of copper in the NVLink spine , liquid coolant at two litres a second . Choosing copper over optics in that spine saves 20 kilowatts, a sixth of the rack's power budget, in Jensen Huang's framing . Every one of those specifications is a purchase order for somebody who is not the integrator.

Doing the work: the US OEMs (Dell, HPE, Supermicro), the Taiwanese ODMs (Hon Hai, Quanta, Wistron, Inventec, Wiwynn) and the western contract manufacturers (Flex, Celestica). NVIDIA says Vera Rubin NVL72 production is ramping across more than 350 factory sites in 30 countries — a company claim, and the best available proxy for how distributed this network already is.

chunks.heading: Unit economics
chunks.text:
systems — Unit economics. Nobody who sells a rack discloses its price. The one figure in the corpus is an estimate: Morgan Stanley put the Vera Rubin VR200 NVL72 at about $7.8m bought from an ODM, on the analyst's own assumption that NVIDIA resells procured content at a 70% gross margin . The primary note is not accessible and a competing figure circulates unreconciled, so it is an order of magnitude, not a price. At Quanta's filed Q1 2026 margins, a $3m rack leaves roughly $143k of gross profit and $86k of operating profit — this site's arithmetic over a company-level margin, not a rack-specific one.

One disclosure contaminates every margin on this page, including that one, and it belongs here rather than in a footnote. Hon Hai's CFO said consignment is now the main transaction model in its ASIC-server projects . Under consignment the customer owns the silicon, so the most expensive content in the rack never touches the integrator's revenue or its cost of sales — identical physical work reports a higher gross margin on a much smaller base. No integrator discloses its buy-and-sell versus consignment mix, so every comparison below is measured against a variable nobody outside these companies can size.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
systems — The players. Supermicro is the cleanest experiment, because it is only this business and nothing averages the dilution away. Gross margin ran 18.0% on $7.12bn of revenue in FY2023 and 11.1% on $21.97bn in FY2025, operating margin 10.7% to 5.7% . Then 6.3% on $12.68bn of net sales in the December 2025 quarter: its lowest gross margin ever, in its largest quarter ever .

Dell recognised $1,873m of AI-optimized server revenue in FY2024 and $24,683m in FY2026 , then $16,132m in a single quarter, up 757% . Infrastructure Solutions Group operating margin went the other way — 12.6%, 12.8%, 11.7% , then 10.5% on $29,009m of segment revenue in the May 2026 quarter — and consolidated gross margin fell from 24.3% to 17.8% over three years, which Dell's filing attributes without hedging to AI-server mix . The steelman is in the same document: Dell's stated reason the segment number held up is that its operating-expense rate declined faster than its gross-margin rate. That is a scale argument, not a pricing-power one, and it is fragile to volume falling. Dell also publishes the distinction this layer usually blurs — $24.4bn of AI orders booked against $16.1bn recognised in the same quarter .

Forecast, per Dell Technologies, Jeff Clarke, May 2026: Dell raised its fiscal 2027 AI server revenue expectation to $60bn — company guidance from the vice chairman, not a filed result.

HPE gave the clearest read of the pass-through and then removed the ability to track it. Server segment gross margin fell from 29.4% in FY2023 to 20.9% in FY2025 and segment operating margin from 12.7% to 7.6% while segment revenue grew 24% to $17,745m . Revenue up, segment profit down, and HPE attributes the growth to higher average unit prices — it is reselling accelerator content. The segment no longer exists.

chunks.heading: The players
chunks.text:
HPE gave the clearest read of the pass-through and then removed the ability to track it. Server segment gross margin fell from 29.4% in FY2023 to 20.9% in FY2025 and segment operating margin from 12.7% to 7.6% while segment revenue grew 24% to $17,745m . Revenue up, segment profit down, and HPE attributes the growth to higher average unit prices — it is reselling accelerator content. The segment no longer exists.

The ODMs say the same thing over a longer window. Hon Hai's gross margin was 6.15% in 2025 against 6.27% in 2018, while revenue rose from NT$5.29tn to NT$8.10tn ; operating margin improved from 2.57% to 3.20%, on leverage and in-sourcing rather than price . Quanta's AI margin bump is a completed round trip — 4.78% gross margin in FY2019, a 7.85% peak in 2024, 4.78% again in Q1 2026 — recorded in a half-year when its cumulative revenue rose 86.5% . Wistron doubled and got worse: revenue up 108% to NT$2,187bn in 2025, gross margin down from 8.01% to 6.13% . Selling direct helps and does not exempt: Wiwynn earned 6.72% against Quanta's 4.12%, on a fifth of the revenue .

Where the profit went. Asia Vital Components, which makes the cold plates liquid cooling created demand for, took its operating margin from 2.47% in 2018 to 19.73% in 2025 . Delta, in power shelves and busbars, went from 7.66% to 15.13% — diversified well beyond datacenter power with no AI segment broken out, so that attribution is inferential. Vertiv went from 4.9% in 2020 to 17.9% in 2025 . Amphenol earned 25.4% in 2025 on $23.09bn of revenue , with IT datacom sales rising about $4,593.7m in that year alone — roughly six times Quanta's operating margin on parts inside the same rack. The two contract manufacturers whose margins expanded did it by changing what they sell: Celestica from 4.0% to 8.4% on its own networking hardware, Flex from 1.7% to 4.9% .

chunks.heading: Concentration & chokepoints
chunks.text:
systems — Concentration & chokepoints. The concentration that bites is on the customer list. Four customers were 75.1% of Supermicro's accounts receivable at March 2026, the largest alone 32.2% .

Hon Hai is the largest single node: Cloud and Networking Products were 48% of its revenue in Q1 2026 , with AI servers above 50% of server revenue as a stated floor and no supporting table . Its spokesperson James Wu also claimed around 40% share of "the AI market" — no definition, no methodology, no corroboration, so this site records it as his opinion. Geography is moving slowly: Wistron opened a 324,000 square foot factory in Fort Worth in July 2026 under a roughly $700m commitment, building the first US GB300 compute baseboard , and Foxconn says it runs more than 40 facilities across 12 US states .

Forecast, per NVIDIA, July 2026: NVIDIA says it plans to produce up to $500bn of AI infrastructure in the United States with named partners . No time horizon, no contractual basis, no breakdown — and the facilities actually named in the same announcement total a few hundred thousand square feet .

chunks.heading: Lead times & capacity
chunks.text:
systems — Lead times & capacity. The corpus has no admissible figure for integration lead time, burn-in hours or test capacity, and this page will not invent one. The filings offer something better: the binding constraint is working capital, not floor space. Supermicro's cash fell from $5.2bn in June 2025 to $1.3bn in March 2026, and the filing names the causes — inventory build, customers asking for longer payment terms as system costs rise, longer lead times on key components . A company earning low single-digit operating margins cannot self-fund a doubling. Hon Hai's answer to the same arithmetic is consignment, which its CFO says cuts the working capital it carries .

Forecast, per Hon Hai, Michael Chiang, May 2026: Hon Hai guided 2026 AI rack shipments to more than double, with the condition stated explicitly and doing real work: only if supply-chain material availability can meet demand . Capex was around NT$174bn in 2025, up about 27%, guided to more than 30% growth in 2026 .

chunks.heading: 2019 → today
chunks.text: systems — 2019 → today. 2019 is boxes and airflow: Quanta's gross margin 4.78%, Asia Vital Components' operating margin 2.47% . 2022–24 is the bump everyone remembers — Supermicro peaking at an 18.0% gross margin, Quanta at 7.85%, Wistron at 8.01% — and rack-scale looks like a margin story. 2025–26 completes the round trip while revenue accelerates: Quanta back to 4.78% and Hon Hai's gross margin ending where it started , while Asia Vital Components reaches 19.73% and Amphenol 25.4% . Nothing about the demand disappointed. The ratios belong to someone else now.

chunks.heading: Commoditization pressure
chunks.text:
systems — Commoditization pressure. This layer was never un-commoditized, so the useful question is inverted: can any of it escape? The largest player says yes and names the route. Hon Hai is expanding into liquid cooling, mechanical components, high-speed transmission, power modules and system validation to raise its self-manufacturing ratio . Asia Vital Components and Delta are the proof it works ; Inventec is the proof it is not automatic, at a 1.48% operating margin in 2018 and 1.84% in 2025, straight through the whole cycle .

Absent that, the layer is a conduit and says so: Hon Hai's rotating CEO described many of its businesses as buy-and-sell models in which product prices are adjusted according to costs . That protects absolute profit against input inflation and means the layer cannot absorb a cost shock — it transmits it into the buyer's capital budget one layer up.

chunks.heading: Failure modes
chunks.text:
systems — Failure modes. Customer concentration at the integrator. Four customers at 75.1% of receivables , a 6.3% gross margin and $1.3bn of cash make one slipped large shipment a liquidity event rather than a bad quarter. Blast radius runs up into NVIDIA's revenue recognition and down into already-committed memory and PCB suppliers.

Falling margin is mix, not distress. Both Dell and Supermicro attribute the compression to AI mix in filed documents . If AI revenue keeps growing, reported ratios keep falling: the layer looks worse the better it does.

Trade policy lands here first. Supermicro's tariff expense rose $89.4m, up 608% year over year, in the March 2026 quarter alone .

Auditability is deteriorating as the layer grows. HPE dissolved the Server segment , the ODMs report no AI-server segment, and the consignment mix stays undisclosed . Several series on this page are now closed.

chunks.heading: Open questions
chunks.text: systems — Open questions. - What does a rack actually cost? The per-rack question rests on one second-hand analyst estimate with an unreconciled spread and one derivation from a company-level margin . No integrator or buyer discloses a rack price. - What is the buy-and-sell versus consignment mix? Until someone discloses it, every margin comparison here carries an error bar nobody outside the companies can size — including the ones this page just made. - Does self-manufacturing scale? It worked at component scale ; whether an NT$8.10tn revenue base can move its whole mix that way is unproven, and Inventec is the warning . - Does the US footprint change the margin or only the address? Nobody discloses AI-rack output by geography, so tariff exposure that is already a P&L line cannot be mapped onto it. The corpus also has no figure for how much rack content NVIDIA now specifies itself.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Accenture: It booked $5.9bn of generative AI in FY2025 inside a shrinking total book, then stopped disclosing the metric. The silence is the datapoint.

What to watch on Accenture: Whether the words 'generative AI' or 'GenAI' reappear with a number attached in any fiscal-2027 release. After three straight quarters of zero mentions, reinstatement is the disclosure event, not continuation. Whether fourth-quarter fiscal-2026 bookings return to growth after the third quarter's 2 percent decline. Two consecutive down quarters would separate a demand problem from a currency effect. Whether full-year fiscal-2026 revenue lands inside the cut 3-4 percent local-currency guidance or below it. The guidance was already reduced, so a miss against the reduced number is the meaningful signal. Whether Capgemini keeps publishing an AI share of bookings. If the last major integrator still disclosing one stops, AI demand through the services channel becomes unauditable from outside entirely. Whether Accenture ever quantifies AI-driven efficiency against its own headcount, approximately 799,000 in the third quarter of fiscal 2026. That number decides whether AI expands the billable base or eats it.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Accenture — Introduction. The most informative thing Accenture published about AI in fiscal 2026 is a word that does not appear.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Accenture — Role in the stack. The distribution layer's largest channel. Accenture does not build models or run inference; it sells the integration — the transformation programme, the change management, the systems work that moves a model into a Fortune 500 process. Roughly 799,000 employees are the product , and bookings are the demand signal the rest of the market reads.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Accenture — Exposure. Accenture recorded $5.9bn of generative-AI new bookings in fiscal 2025, including $1.8bn in the fourth quarter . That was approximately 7.3 percent of $80.62bn of total new bookings, in a year when total bookings declined 1 percent . A company-defined metric in an earnings release, so a company claim — but the standard proxy for systems-integration AI demand, which is why it mattered.

Read $5.9bn as a terminal value, not a point in a series. Accenture disclosed no generative-AI bookings or revenue figure in any of its three fiscal-2026 quarterly releases; the terms "generative AI" and "GenAI" appear zero times in each , verified by extracting all three releases and searching them. Nothing may present the $5.9bn as current or trending.

What replaced it is a turn in the total book. Third-quarter fiscal-2026 bookings were $19.32bn, down 2 percent in dollars and 3 percent in local currency, on revenue of $18.7bn, with full-year revenue growth guidance cut to 3 to 4 percent in local currency .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Accenture — The bull case. The steelman is Accenture's own, and it is not weak. Generative AI stops being separable once AI sits inside most transformation programmes. A metric with no clean boundary is worse than no metric, because every quarter becomes an argument about what counted; the mega-deal disclosures that replaced it may proxy the same demand more honestly.

There is also a bull reading of the fiscal-2025 numbers themselves. $5.9bn of generative-AI bookings arrived inside a year when the total book fell 1 percent — meaning AI was the only part growing, and the traditional book was the drag. And the category does appear to be still compounding at peers who still publish: Capgemini reported more than 8 percent of group bookings in 2025 and more than 10 percent in the fourth quarter, on €24,356m of bookings — stated as a floor, and above Accenture's terminal share. If a direct competitor's AI share is rising, Accenture's silence is more likely an accounting decision than a demand collapse.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Accenture — The bear case. Companies retire growth metrics when the metrics stop flattering them. The sequence is the argument: a disclosed $5.9bn in fiscal 2025 , then three quarters of nothing , then bookings down 2 percent in the quarter AI consulting was supposedly compounding . Suggestive rather than decisive — but a company confident in the number keeps printing it.

The structural version is worse than the disclosure question. Accenture sells hours applied to work that AI is meant to compress. A successful AI programme delivers fewer billable hours in the next contract, which means the more the technology works, the more the channel's own revenue base erodes. A declining book alongside a withdrawn AI metric is exactly what that would look like from outside, and the corpus cannot distinguish it from a measurement change.

The peer set makes the opacity structural rather than idiosyncratic. Infosys reported fiscal-2026 revenue of $20,158m with $14.9bn of large-deal contract value and no AI-specific figure anywhere in the release, while describing itself as AI-first . Cognizant reported trailing-twelve-month bookings of $29.6bn and headcount up 21,300, also with no AI figure . When the flagship metric is withdrawn and no competitor except one publishes a substitute, AI demand through the services channel becomes unauditable — and the blast radius of that is analytical, landing on everyone who cites integrator bookings as evidence.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Alphabet: Its backlog grew by more in one quarter than the whole figure was a year earlier — and it is not the cloud number people think it is.

What to watch on Alphabet: Whether Alphabet begins disclosing Google Cloud backlog separately from total-company remaining performance obligations. Everyone quoting $519.5bn treats it as a cloud metric; it is not. Until the split is filed, none of it can be attributed to AI demand with confidence. Whether the $175–185bn capex range is raised a second time. The top end has already moved toward $190bn once, and a further raise this late in the year would mean the constraint is cost inflation rather than ambition. Whether the six-year server and network life set in January 2023 survives the next 10-K. Alphabet took roughly $3.4bn of annual depreciation relief from that change and has not revisited it while Amazon moved the other way. Whether Alphabet's debt raising keeps compounding past the roughly $83bn taken between November 2025 and June 2026, and whether any of it arrives secured or through a special-purpose vehicle rather than as plain unsecured Alphabet paper. The structure tells you more than the size. Whether the multi-gigawatt next-generation TPU capacity announced with Broadcom starts arriving in 2027 as stated. That date is the test of whether Alphabet can sell accelerators at scale to labs it competes with.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Alphabet — Introduction. Alphabet's remaining performance obligations went from $108.2bn to $519.5bn in a year . The figure is filed, and it is enormous, and almost everyone quoting it is describing the wrong thing.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Alphabet — Role in the stack. Alphabet is the only vertically integrated player in the middle of the stack: it designs the accelerator, owns the datacenter, sells the cloud, trains the frontier model, and runs the distribution surface it all lands on. It is also the only company selling a rival frontier lab a genuine alternative to NVIDIA at gigawatt scale.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Alphabet — Exposure. The RPO number first, with its scope attached. $519.5bn at 30 June 2026, against $108.2bn a year earlier — and it is total-company remaining performance obligations from the filing, not the Google Cloud backlog management cites on calls . It also roughly doubled in a single quarter, which is a stranger fact than the annual comparison and gets less attention.

Capex is guided at $175–185bn for 2026, with the top end later pushed toward $190bn . The funding is the change in character: Alphabet raised approximately $83bn of debt between November 2025 and June 2026 — an aggregation across quarterly proceeds and shelf takedowns, by a company that spent two decades not needing any.

And the accounting is the same optimism as everyone else's. Alphabet extended server and network equipment life to six years effective January 2023, lowering depreciation by roughly $3.4bn .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Alphabet — The bull case. The TPU is the case, and it is a supply-side one. Ironwood delivers 4,614 TFLOPs per chip with 192 GB of HBM at 7.37 TB/s , scaling to 9,216-chip pods at 42.5 exaflops . Anthropic took access to up to 1,000,000 TPUs and more than 1 GW of capacity in October 2025 , then signed for multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU with Google and Broadcom from 2027 . Alphabet is selling its competitor the means of production, at a cost base no merchant-silicon buyer can match.

Efficiency compounds that. Alphabet reports 2025 fleet-wide PUE of 1.09 against a surveyed industry average of 1.54 — company-reported, but a structural cost advantage if it holds. And it is deflating the layers above it deliberately: Gemini File Search charges $0.15 per million tokens to index with nothing for storage , and Search grounding fell to $14 per 1,000 queries from $35 in one model generation .

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Alphabet — The bear case. RPO is obligations, not cash, and Alphabet publishes no cancellation or renegotiation terms — so the strongest number on the page cannot be stress-tested from outside. The scope problem makes it worse: a total-company figure cannot tell you how much of the buildout is contracted against.

The dependencies are also less controlled than the vertical-integration story suggests. Alphabet has signed 1 GW of datacenter demand response with five utilities, with its own caveat that flexibility has limits and will only be available at certain locations , and its order for up to 500 MW from Kairos small modular reactors does not target a first reactor online until 2030 . On data, a rival's cap table moved Alphabet's supply chain: it spent about $150m with Scale AI in 2024 and planned $200m for 2025, then moved to split after Meta's investment .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Amazon: The only hyperscaler that made its own machines worth less on purpose — while spending more on them than its operations produce.

What to watch on Amazon: Whether the FY2026 10-K extends the shortened five-year life to the rest of the fleet, or reverses it back to six. The 2025 disclosure named only a subset of servers and networking equipment; the scope of the next revision is the tell, because it says whether management thinks the problem is one generation of hardware or all of it. Whether trailing capex stays above 100% of operating cash flow in the next 10-Q. Q1 2026 was the first crossing since 2022. Two consecutive readings above parity make external funding structural rather than opportunistic. Whether the roughly $94.1bn of debt raised since November 2025 is revised upward when the next 10-Q lands. A June 2026 issuance is excluded from that total pending disclosure, so it is a floor, not a level. Whether the $35bn AGI-or-IPO tranche of Amazon's OpenAI commitment is ever funded, restructured, or redefined. No party to it has published a definition of the triggering event. Whether roughly 1 GW of Trainium2 and Trainium3 capacity is actually online for Anthropic by the end of 2026. That is the milestone that converts a $100bn ten-year commitment from an announcement into a delivery schedule.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Amazon — Introduction. In January 2025 Amazon did the one thing no other hyperscaler has done. It shortened the assumed life of its own machines, took the depreciation hit, and reported it — in the same year Meta extended in the opposite direction.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Amazon — Role in the stack. AWS is the largest cloud, the only hyperscaler whose in-house accelerator is deployed at frontier-lab volume, and — newly — one of the biggest corporate borrowers in the market. Those three facts are the same fact: Amazon is buying the whole vertical at once and is now doing it partly on credit.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Amazon — Exposure. Amazon guided approximately $200bn of 2026 capital expenditure, with Q1 2026 actual at $44.2bn . The number that matters is the ratio: trailing-twelve-month capex equalled 102% of operating cash flow at Q1 2026, the first reading above parity since 2022 . Amazon is now spending more on machines than its operations generate, and it is the only one of the four in that position.

So it borrowed. Roughly $94.1bn of long-term debt across three issuances between November 2025 and July 2026, including a $53.4bn multi-currency offering in March 2026 — an aggregation, and a floor, because a further issuance is excluded pending disclosure.

The accounting is the counterweight. Amazon extended server life from five years to six effective January 2024, lowering depreciation by about $3.2bn . Then it reversed on a subset, back to five years effective January 2025, adding $889m of depreciation and taking $677m off net income in nine months .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Amazon — The bull case. Amazon has the only credible answer to accelerator margin. Anthropic states it uses over 1,000,000 AWS Trainium2 chips to train and serve Claude and committed in April 2026 to spend more than $100bn on AWS over ten years , against up to 5 GW of new AWS capacity with roughly 1 GW of Trainium2 and Trainium3 online by end-2026 . No other cloud has a frontier lab running its silicon at that volume. Every chip served on Trainium rather than bought from NVIDIA is margin that stays inside AWS.

The reversal is also the bull case, not just the bear one. Management that shortens asset lives while its peers lengthen them is the management whose depreciation number you can lean on. The whole cloud-layer dispute is about whether the schedules are honest; Amazon volunteered the answer that hurt.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Amazon — The bear case. Amazon is now financing its customers as well as supplying them. It committed $50bn to OpenAI's March 2026 round, of which $35bn is contingent on an initial public offering or on reaching artificial general intelligence — a third of a commitment gated on an event with no agreed definition. It also sold the same counterparty a $38bn multi-year compute agreement . Vendor financing and vendor revenue, same name.

And the constraint is not on Amazon's side of the meter. It expanded its Susquehanna nuclear PPA to 1,920 MW , but FERC rejected the amended interconnection agreement for the 480 MW behind-the-meter expansion in November 2024 , and its X-energy SMR programme targets a 320 MW first phase in the early 2030s . Capex is annual; power is a decade.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
AMD: The credible second merchant supplier — which in October 2025 paid its largest prospective customer in equity to become one.

What to watch on AMD: Whether the first warrant tranche vests. It is contingent on the initial 1 GW of MI450 being deployed, targeted for the second half of 2026, and vesting shows up in AMD's share count and 8-K filings rather than in a press release. Whether non-GAAP gross margin moves off roughly 55%. A twenty-point structural gap to NVIDIA has not narrowed through the strongest demand environment either company will see; margin, not revenue, is the variable that would show AMD has priced up rather than in. Whether AMD's data center growth rate exceeds NVIDIA's in any single quarter. Both grew fast in Q1 2026 — 57% against 92% — so relative growth, not absolute revenue, is the share-shift test. Whether OpenAI is disclosed as a greater-than-10% customer in a subsequent AMD annual report. The warrant makes the customer a shareholder; the concentration disclosure is where that stops being a narrative and becomes an accounting fact. Whether any share-price tranche of the warrant is disclosed as vested. The final tranche is tied to $600 per share, so the schedule embeds AMD's own equity as the currency for the deal.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: AMD — Introduction. The most important document AMD filed in this cycle is not an earnings release. It is an 8-K describing a warrant that pays a customer to buy chips.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: AMD — Role in the stack. AMD is the second merchant accelerator supplier: EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs, a part with a price list, sold to anyone. That position is genuinely valuable — a rationed market needs a second source — and it is priced like a second source, which is the whole tension on this page.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
AMD — Exposure. Q1 2026 revenue was $10.253bn , with the data center segment at $5.775bn, up 57% , at a 55% non-GAAP gross margin — 53% GAAP . Q2 2026 was guided to approximately $11.2bn plus or minus $300m .

Two comparisons place it. AMD's entire data center segment is smaller than NVIDIA's networking line alone, which was $14.8bn in the quarter ended April 2026 , and is under a tenth of NVIDIA's $75.2bn of quarterly data center revenue .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
AMD — The bull case. Demand is contracted, at scale, by the buyer everyone wants. OpenAI agreed in October 2025 to deploy 6 GW of AMD GPUs over five years , with the first gigawatt of MI450 targeted for the second half of 2026 and a concurrent binding commitment to purchase it. A 57% data center growth rate is what the pre-MI450 base looks like; the deal is not in the numbers yet.

AMD is also differentiating by system rather than by die. It announced a disaggregated inference solution with Cerebras in July 2026 claiming up to 5x higher tokens per second per watt — a vendor claim on a vendor configuration, logged as one, and available through Cerebras Cloud rather than AMD's own channel.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
AMD — The bear case. Read the price AMD paid. It issued OpenAI a warrant on 5 October 2025 for up to 160 million shares at $0.01 each, vesting in tranches tied to Instinct deployments and to share-price targets escalating to $600 for the final tranche . Full vesting is contingent on the whole 6 GW . The structure is a supplier issuing equity to secure demand — the mirror image of NVIDIA investing in customers, and arguably the weaker side of it, because NVIDIA is buying upside in the buyer while AMD is handing upside to the buyer.

The economics behind that decision are the second half of the bear case. A 55% non-GAAP gross margin against NVIDIA's 74.9% GAAP is roughly twenty points of structural difference that has not narrowed in a market where advanced packaging is sold out and lead times run 52-78 weeks . If a second source cannot raise price when the first source cannot ship, the constraint on AMD is not capacity. It is software and system-level position — which is why the flagship differentiation claim of 2026 arrives through a partner's cloud rather than through AMD's own rack.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Anthropic: Passed OpenAI on revenue and rented GPUs from a rival's parent in the same month. Both are real, and both travelled wrong.

What to watch on Anthropic: Whether the confidential S-1 filed on 1 June 2026, once public, confirms or contradicts the run-rate path — specifically whether audited revenue supports annualizing the $30bn-to-$47bn seven-week window, and what share is pay-per-token API. Whether Claude Sonnet 5's scheduled 1 September 2026 list increase to $15 per million output tokens survives into invoices or is absorbed by enterprise discounting. It is the first testable claim of pricing power at this layer. Whether the SpaceX Colossus lease is renewed, repriced or dropped as Colossus 1 utilization recovers. The reported terms run to 2029, and the lessor's sibling company competes with the tenant. Whether the next AWS or Google disclosure converts 'up to 5 GW' into energized capacity with a date, or restates the same conditional language a year later. Whether any filing discloses the API-versus-subscription revenue split, which would settle Sacra's unsourced 70-75 percent and end the recurring conflation with the 80-percent-from-business-customers figure.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Anthropic — Introduction. Anthropic did two things in May 2026 that look contradictory. It passed OpenAI on revenue, and it rented 220,000 GPUs from a direct competitor's parent company. Both are true. Both are narrower and stranger than the versions that circulated.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Anthropic — Role in the stack. A frontier lab that sells tokens rather than a consumer habit. Sacra estimates 70 to 75 percent of revenue comes from pay-per-token API calls, with subscriptions at 10 to 15 percent . That makes Anthropic the most inference-exposed of the large labs — it lives on the per-token price curve, and it is also one of the three or four entities that sets it.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Anthropic — Exposure. Run-rate revenue crossed $47bn in May 2026 , up from the $30bn announced in April . Company-stated, unaudited, and annualized off a seven-week window in which a single large enterprise contract distorts the snapshot.
