The capital matched it: a $65bn Series H at a $965bn post-money valuation in May 2026 .

The overtake is real, and it is roughly 1.4x. Sacra estimates OpenAI at approximately $33bn in that same month . The wider figure everyone repeated — closer to 1.9x — comes from setting Anthropic's May against OpenAI's February number of $25bn , which Sacra states excludes Microsoft licensing revenue and large one-time deals. Anthropic's figure carries no such carve-out. Mismatched dates on mismatched definitions produce a lead that is real but smaller than advertised.

Customer exposure is enterprise and top-heavy: more than 500 companies each spending over $1m a year , and more than 300,000 business customers accounting for roughly 80 percent of revenue . That 80 percent is the business-customer cut, not the API cut, and conflating the two is how "80 percent from API" got into circulation. On share, Menlo Ventures puts Anthropic at 40 percent of enterprise LLM spend against 27 for OpenAI — Menlo is an Anthropic investor. The independent check points the same way but measures something else: 42.4 percent of AI-spending businesses on Ramp paid Anthropic in June 2026, versus 39.5 percent paying OpenAI , which counts payers, not dollars.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Anthropic — The bull case. The strongest version is about cost discipline, and it comes from Anthropic's own projections.

Forecast, per secondary reporting on Anthropic's own projections — single source, directional only: Training costs are projected to peak near $30bn through 2028, roughly 4x below OpenAI's projected $121bn of 2028 compute spend , with profitability projected for 2028-2029. One secondary source. Treat the ratio as a direction, not a measurement.

Pair that with the one thing nobody else at this layer has demonstrated: raising a list price. Claude Sonnet 5's output price rises from $10 to $15 per million tokens on 1 September 2026, ending introductory pricing . In a layer where per-capability prices fall about an order of magnitude a year, a scheduled 50 percent increase is the most interesting fact on this page.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Anthropic — The bear case. The obligations are enormous and mostly conditional. More than $100bn committed to AWS over ten years , $30bn of Azure capacity , access to up to 1,000,000 Google TPUs , and agreements for up to 5 GW of new Amazon capacity plus 5 GW of next-generation TPU capacity . Read the "up to" on all of it: these are announcements about future capacity, not energized load, and the queue that decides delivery sits three layers down.

Then the lease, which is the sharpest version of the bear case. Anthropic contracted with SpaceX — not xAI — for 220,000 GPUs and more than 300 MW across Colossus 1 and 2 , reported at $1.25bn a month through 2029, struck after Colossus 1 fell to about 11 percent GPU utilization when xAI moved training onto Colossus 2 . Those terms are press-attributed to SpaceX's IPO filing and typed as an estimate until someone checks the filing itself.

The utilization number is the mechanism, and it cuts both ways. An almost-idle cluster was worth more rented to a direct rival than held empty — which tells you the marginal price of frontier compute is softer than the commitment totals imply. It also tells you Anthropic's marginal capacity is leased from a landlord whose sibling company has a structural interest in that capacity being scarce at renewal.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
ASML: The whole leading edge runs through about sixty-five machines a year. ASML decides how many exist, and has committed to 2027 but not to 2028.

What to watch on ASML: Whether the 2028 expansion moves from 'investigating' to 'planning' in a subsequent ASML statement. CFO Roger Dassen distinguishes the two years sharply: 2027 is a plan, 2028 is only under investigation. Every 2028 accelerator-supply model implicitly assumes the upgrade happens. Whether China's share of net sales falls further after 10 November 2026, when the rare-earth export suspension ASML records in its own filings expires. The April 2025 licensing regime was never suspended, so the expiry adds a constraint rather than restoring one. Whether High-NA appears in more than one system in a quarter's net system sales. Q2 2026 included exactly one, so unit cadence — not the €380m list price — is the readable signal on adoption. Whether EUV net system sales growth stays above the 45% pace guided for 2026 once the tool count is capped near sixty-five. Revenue growth above unit growth means ASML, like TSMC, is being paid on price. Whether ASML's guidance is raised a third time. It went from EUR 36-40bn after Q1 to EUR 43-45bn in July; a company raising its own forecast twice in two quarters is telling you its order book moved faster than its planning.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: ASML — Introduction. ASML is the only company in the stack whose capacity can be stated as an integer. Roughly sixty-five extreme-ultraviolet lithography machines will ship in 2026, and nobody else makes one. Every argument about 2027 and 2028 accelerator supply is, underneath, an argument about that integer.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: ASML — Role in the stack. ASML sells the tool, not the wafer. It has a monopoly on EUV lithography and a strong position in the deep-ultraviolet immersion systems that do the rest of the patterning. Its customers are the four or five firms that can afford a leading-edge fab; its constraint is its own build rate, not demand.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
ASML — Exposure. Q2 2026 net sales were €9.3bn at a 54.0% gross margin , of which EUV was €3.8bn of €6.6bn in net system sales, including exactly one High-NA machine . Full-year guidance was raised in July to €43-45bn, from €36-40bn after Q1 . Customers in China were 29.1% of 2025 net sales, down from 36.1% in 2024 — still the single largest geographic exposure, and the one governed by export policy rather than by demand.

Unit economics are unusual for a supplier this critical: the High-NA EXE:5200-class system lists at approximately $380m , and fewer than a dozen exist anywhere.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
ASML — The bull case. Demand is running ahead of ASML's own planning. Guidance moved from €36-40bn to €43-45bn inside one quarter , and the company plans roughly 65 Low-NA EUV shipments in 2026 with EUV net system sales growing above 45% year over year — CFO Roger Dassen's figure, not the CEO's . Growth above 45% on a unit count that cannot expand much means ASML captures price the same way its customers do.

High-NA has also stopped being a science project. The first commercial logic product manufactured on High-NA EUV was announced in Q2 2026, produced by Intel — a milestone TSMC has deliberately not chased, holding Low-NA for N2 and A16. A second technology curve with one customer today is optionality; ASML owns both curves.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
ASML — The bear case. The relief everyone is modelling is not committed.

Forecast, per ASML (CFO Roger Dassen): ASML plans a 30% capacity increase for both Low-NA EUV and immersion systems in 2027, and is only investigating a further 30% increase for 2028 . Dassen's language separates the years: 2027 is an intention to increase, 2028 is an investigation. And the metric is capacity — what ASML could build — not output shipped.

That distinction is the bear case, because it cuts both ways. If 2028 does not arrive, the supply floor under every accelerator roadmap is lower than modelled. If it does arrive, ASML has added 30% twice into a demand curve funded by a handful of buyers whose own capital is being raised in private credit markets — and lithography is the longest-lead, least-cancellable item in that chain, which is exactly what makes it painful to hold when orders pause.

Policy is the second exposure, and it is bidirectional. ASML's own filings record that China suspended its rare-earth export restrictions for twelve months until 10 November 2026 , with existing risk-mitigation measures still in place. ASML does not control either end of that. Nor does it control the demand side of its China business, where BIS revoked Validated End-User authorisations for three foreign-owned fabs inside the country effective 31 December 2025 , removing blanket tool-import rights from ASML's largest non-Chinese customers there.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Broadcom: Custom silicon's share gains are real and, while packaging is rationed, additive — Broadcom has taken capacity that did not exist, not sockets from NVIDIA.

What to watch on Broadcom: Whether Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue growth and NVIDIA's data center growth decelerate together or in sequence. Simultaneous deceleration says both were supply-limited; Broadcom accelerating as NVIDIA slows is the first evidence of actual substitution. Whether the Apollo-led $35bn initial tranche is drawn, and against what — announced gigawatts and committed capital are different quantities and should never be added. Watch too for the residual value support on that vehicle being quantified in a Broadcom filing rather than reported: it is the largest contingent exposure attributed to the company anywhere in this corpus. Whether the multi-gigawatt Anthropic TPU capacity with Google lands in 2027 as announced. Broadcom's AI line is a claim on a small number of captive programmes; a slipped or resized programme is directly visible in guidance. Whether Broadcom's AI revenue growth survives the quarter after CoWoS lead times fall below a year. The additive read is conditional on scarcity, and the queue clearing tests it in both directions. Whether any captive customer moves design in-house or to a second ASIC vendor. Broadcom does not own the products it builds, so its position resolves on customer disclosures, not its own.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Broadcom — Introduction. Broadcom is the reason "can anyone catch NVIDIA" became the wrong question. Its AI business is now guided at $16.0bn a quarter , and NVIDIA accelerated anyway. Both things happened because the constraint is not in either company.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Broadcom — Role in the stack. Broadcom does custom silicon design, serialisation and packaging for buyers who own the resulting product — Google's TPU, Meta's and OpenAI's accelerators — plus the Ethernet switching those systems run on. It does not own the roadmap or the customer relationship at the end of it. That is the model's strength on margin and its weakness on durability.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Broadcom — Exposure. Q2 FY2026 revenue was $22.187bn, up 48% , following $19.311bn in Q1 . AI semiconductor revenue inside that was $10.8bn, up 143% — the best single datapoint anywhere on custom-ASIC share gains.

Customer exposure is concentrated in a handful of captive programmes. Anthropic disclosed agreements in May 2026 for up to 5 GW of new Amazon capacity plus 5 GW of next-generation TPU capacity with Google and Broadcom , and had announced in April 2026 that the Google-Broadcom partnership brings multiple gigawatts online starting 2027 . Both are "up to" commitments about future capacity, not energised load.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Broadcom — The bull case. Run the arithmetic that the additive-versus-substitutive argument turns on. NVIDIA's data center revenue grew 92% to $75.2bn in the April 2026 quarter , which is roughly $36bn of quarterly revenue added year over year . Broadcom's entire guided AI line, at $16.0bn , is under half of that single increment — and NVIDIA guided the next quarter up again to $91.0bn .

If ASICs were displacing merchant GPUs, those two series would move in opposite directions. They do not, because the market is rationed: CoWoS demand is rising toward about 1.0 million wafers in 2026 from roughly 670,000 in 2025 , against capacity that went from about 35,000 wafers a month at end-2024 to 72,500-80,000 at end-2025 , booked out with 52-78 week lead times . A TPU order does not cancel an NVIDIA order. It consumes capacity that did not exist a year ago. On that reading Broadcom's 143% growth costs NVIDIA nothing and is worth exactly what it prints.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Broadcom — The bear case. The strongest counter is that additive cuts against Broadcom too. Its growth is evidence that it won an allocation, not that it won a socket. Nothing in the numbers shows a buyer choosing an ASIC over a GPU on merit — only a buyer taking incremental packaging capacity while none was available at any price. When the queue clears, the comparison becomes real for the first time, and it will be made against a supplier holding a 74.9% gross margin and roughly 60% of 2026 CoWoS allocation on Morgan Stanley's projection .

The demand is also being funded rather than earned, and the Google–Anthropic programme shows how far that now goes. Broadcom agreed in April 2026 to buy 3.5 GW of TPU hardware from Google for deployment by Anthropic , and its filings disclose $128bn of purchase commitments — $55.2bn of deliveries scheduled for fiscal 2027 and $72.9bn for fiscal 2028 — relating almost entirely to that purchase . Against a company guiding $16.0bn of quarterly AI revenue , that is a purchase obligation several years of the AI line in size.

Then read what Broadcom did to make that hardware financeable. It guaranteed the two senior tranches of the vehicle that bought the chips through residual value support covering about $30bn of a $35bn financing, agreeing to cover any shortfall if Anthropic stopped paying and the hardware could not be resold for enough to make senior investors whole . So Broadcom buys the silicon from Google, sells it into a private-credit vehicle, and then stands behind the vehicle's senior debt. Its exposure is not the margin on a sale; it is the residual value of used accelerators in the scenario where the single tenant defaults — the one scenario in which used accelerators are worth least.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Then read what Broadcom did to make that hardware financeable. It guaranteed the two senior tranches of the vehicle that bought the chips through residual value support covering about $30bn of a $35bn financing, agreeing to cover any shortfall if Anthropic stopped paying and the hardware could not be resold for enough to make senior investors whole . So Broadcom buys the silicon from Google, sells it into a private-credit vehicle, and then stands behind the vehicle's senior debt. Its exposure is not the margin on a sale; it is the residual value of used accelerators in the scenario where the single tenant defaults — the one scenario in which used accelerators are worth least.

Forecast, per Broadcom, Apollo and Blackstone, June 2026: The platform announced in June 2026 targets more than 20 GW of global AI deployments through 2028 , on an initial tranche of $35bn led by Apollo . The gigawatts are an announced plan; the tranche is committed capital. When a chip vendor helps assemble the private credit that buys its chips, the order book and the credit cycle stop being independent.

A note on double counting, because it matters for reading the two paragraphs above together. The Apollo-led $35bn tranche and the $35bn Compute SPV that bought roughly 1 GW of TPU hardware agree on amount, month, sponsor and anchor investors. This site treats them as one vehicle described from two sides rather than two separate $35bn commitments. No filing in the corpus confirms that identity, so it is flagged here rather than asserted — but adding the two figures together would be the easiest way to overstate this programme by half.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
CoreWeave: The neocloud that runs the hyperscaler business model without the hyperscaler balance sheet — and shows what that costs.

What to watch on CoreWeave: Whether GAAP net loss narrows as revenue scales, or whether interest expense grows with it. Q1 2026 was a $740m loss against $536m of quarterly net interest — if the second number keeps pace with revenue, the first will not close. The 1.15x debt-service-coverage covenant on the March 2026 facility. It binds on cash flow, not on asset value, which makes it the first thing a demand pause would touch. Customer concentration in the next 10-Q. Microsoft was 62% of 2024 revenue; the Meta agreement diversifies the name at the top without changing the shape. Whether any GPU-secured facility is refinanced rather than repaid. The March 2026 loan put the GPUs themselves in the lien, so a refinancing tells you what the collateral is actually worth.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: CoreWeave — Introduction. CoreWeave is the cleanest natural experiment in the AI buildout. It does what Microsoft and Amazon do — buy accelerators, wrap them in power and networking, rent them out — with none of the software revenue that lets the hyperscalers absorb a bad year. Every cost the others can bury shows up on its income statement.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: CoreWeave — Role in the stack. A pure-play GPU cloud. It buys silicon on debt, sells capacity on multi-year contracts, and lives on the spread. That makes it the layer's price discovery mechanism: when reserved GPU pricing moves, CoreWeave's economics move with it, undisguised.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
CoreWeave — Exposure. Revenue was $2.078bn in Q1 2026, up 112% , on a backlog of $99.4bn . The company posted a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin and a $740m GAAP net loss in the same quarter . Both are true, and the bridge between them is $536m of quarterly net interest on $24.859bn of debt against $4.759bn of equity . Capex of $7.695bn ran against operating cash flow of $2.984bn .

Concentration is the other exposure. Microsoft was 62% of 2024 revenue ; NVIDIA holds equity, having bought 22,935,780 Class A shares at $87.20 for $2bn in January 2026 . Its supplier is also its shareholder, and its largest customers are the same firms building competing capacity.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
CoreWeave — The bull case. The contracts are signed. A $99.4bn backlog against $12–13bn of guided 2026 revenue is years of visibility, and the counterparties are OpenAI at up to $11.9bn and Meta at $21bn — not speculative demand. A 56% EBITDA margin says the operating business works; the losses are a financing structure, and financing structures can be refinanced.

The pricing environment supports it. One-year reserved H100 contracts bottomed at $1.70/GPU-hour in October 2025 and rebounded about 38% to $2.35 by March 2026 , because providers sold out and little Hopper capacity came off contract. The oversupply story is too simple.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
CoreWeave — The bear case. Michael Burry's depreciation argument lands here hardest , because CoreWeave has nowhere to hide it. And the financing has become explicit about what is really being lent against: the $8.5bn delayed-draw facility closed on 30 March 2026 sits in a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary, secured on substantially all of that subsidiary's assets and a pledge of its equity . It prices at SOFR plus 225 basis points with a 50 basis point undrawn fee, a 1.15x debt-service-coverage covenant and a 2032 maturity .

Read those terms together and they describe the risk precisely: a leveraged-credit spread, a fee that makes idle commitment expensive, a covenant that binds on cash flow rather than asset value, and a six-year tenor against hardware whose useful life the layer below cannot agree on — Amazon shortened server lives while Meta extended them in the same month .

There is also evidence the market will say no. Core Scientific's shareholders rejected CoreWeave's all-stock acquisition on 30 October 2025, with about 91% of votes cast against .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Fluidstack: Tenant of record in Google's TPU buildout: billions of secured debt sit behind leases it signed, and nobody has underwritten its balance sheet.

What to watch on Fluidstack: Whether Fluidstack ever files or publishes financials. Everything material in this page comes from its landlord's 10-Q, not from Fluidstack. Until that changes, its own revenue, debt and utilisation are unknown rather than merely unreported. Whether the reported $18bn valuation round closed, and on what terms. Bloomberg described talks in April 2026; a closed round with named investors and a disclosed structure would move this from rumour to fact. Whether Google converts the backstop into equity in Fluidstack itself. It already took warrants in the landlord, TeraWulf; taking a stake in the tenant would make the arrangement an operating subsidiary in all but name. Whether any Fluidstack lease commences without Google credit support. Every disclosed lease has it. The first one that does not is the moment the market prices Fluidstack's own credit. Whether Fluidstack becomes an owner rather than a tenant. A Fluidstack-led group agreed to buy a 168 MW campus outright in July 2026 — if that repeats, the asset-light operator thesis is over.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Fluidstack — Introduction. Fluidstack is the most structurally important company in this layer about which the least is verifiable. It appears in the middle of a chain that has raised billions of dollars of secured debt, and almost every hard fact on this page comes from someone else's filing.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text:
Fluidstack — Role in the stack. An AI cloud operator that runs clusters in buildings it does not own, on power it does not procure, for labs whose compute it does not manufacture. In the Google–Anthropic arrangement it is the operating layer: Google supplies TPUs and stands behind the rent, developers like TeraWulf supply the shells and the interconnects, Anthropic consumes the compute, and Fluidstack sits in between as the counterparty that signs the lease and operates the fleet.

That position exists for a reason. Google needed powered buildings faster than it could build them and did not want the leases on its own balance sheet — the programme ties together roughly $200bn of contracts to supply more than $150bn of chips to Anthropic . Fluidstack is the entity that makes those buildings leasable without Google being the tenant of record.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Fluidstack — Exposure. Start with what is filed. Fluidstack USA I Inc. is the named tenant on three leases signed in August 2025 covering 378 MW of critical IT load at TeraWulf's Lake Mariner campus, the majority of that campus's remaining contracted capacity; one had partially commenced by 30 June 2026 with the rest due in the second half of 2026 and early 2027 .

Then the term that defines the company. Under recognition agreements, Google backstops Fluidstack's payment and performance obligations: on a payment default or an insolvency event, Google may either pay the lease termination fee or pay all rent due and assume the lease as tenant itself . That second option is the load-bearing one. It means the bondholders behind these buildings are not underwriting Fluidstack — they are underwriting Google's willingness to take its place.

The evidence gets thinner from here, and this page will not pretend otherwise. Fluidstack is private and files nothing. Its revenue, debt, fleet size and utilisation are not publicly disclosed; for the shape of a neocloud's economics at scale, the closest disclosed proxies in this corpus are CoreWeave and Nebius, both of which publish quarterly. On valuation, Bloomberg reported in April 2026 that Fluidstack was seeking approximately $1bn at a valuation of about $18bn, led by Jane Street and Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness fund, after an earlier round reported near $7bn . That is reporting on talks, not a closed round, and it is carried here at low confidence because the counterparty's own capitalisation matters to leases it has already signed — not because the figure is solid.

One further datum, and it comes from the landlord again: a purchaser group led by Fluidstack agreed in July 2026 to acquire TeraWulf's entire 50.1% interest in a 168 MW Texas joint venture for approximately $530.0m in cash . Its tenant is becoming an owner.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Fluidstack — The bull case. Fluidstack has assembled the position every neocloud wants and almost none can finance: frontier capacity, at scale, on someone else's credit. It carries no chip purchase risk in this structure — Google supplies the TPUs — and its lease obligations are guaranteed by a company with one of the strongest balance sheets in the world . Compare that to the alternative: neocloud operators building around NVIDIA chips borrowed at a median 9.3% against 7.1% for Google-backed projects, which Jefferies analysts called a structural cost-of-capital disadvantage . Fluidstack is on the right side of a 220 basis point gap it did not have to earn.

The operating skill is real and it is the reason it was chosen. Google could have backstopped anyone; converting miners with secured power into AI-ready sites required an operator who could actually run frontier clusters in retrofitted buildings, and the FT identified five such projects totalling 1.4 GW raising $15bn of debt on the strength of that backstop . Being the operator of record across that programme is a position with genuine switching costs — the alternative to Fluidstack, mid-build, is Google operating the sites itself.

And the direction of travel is toward ownership. Buying a 168 MW campus outright converts a lease obligation into an asset and captures the development margin its landlord had been earning. If the reported $18bn valuation is anywhere near right , that is equity cheap enough to keep doing it.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Fluidstack — The bear case. The credit is borrowed, and borrowed credit can be withdrawn at the margin. Google's guarantees across ten developments carry exposure of as much as $44bn if every lease went bad, marked at $815m on its balance sheet — a judgment that these leases perform. The backstop also becomes effective only at each lease's commencement date , so Fluidstack's obligations during the construction window rest on Fluidstack. Nothing in this corpus establishes what that is worth, because nothing in this corpus discloses its balance sheet.

Its bargaining position is weaker than its footprint suggests. Fluidstack's tenancy is valuable to its landlord precisely because Google stands behind it, which means the guarantor holds the option and the operator holds the obligation. Google can pay a termination fee and assume the lease ; Fluidstack has no equivalent exit. An intermediary whose value comes from a third party's guarantee is disintermediable the moment that third party prefers to be the tenant.

The demand is one name deep. The chips, the buildings and the rent all terminate at Anthropic — $35bn of TPU hardware financed into a special-purpose vehicle and leased on to that single lab , inside a $200bn web of contracts pointed at the same place . Fluidstack has no disclosed revenue from anyone else at this scale.

And a valuation that reportedly moved from roughly $7bn to about $18bn inside a year is being set on contracted capacity, in a private round, for a business whose margins nobody outside it can check. The two comparable operators that do publish show what the disclosure would likely reveal: CoreWeave posted a $740m GAAP net loss against a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin in a single quarter , and Nebius guided 2026 capex of $20-25bn against revenue of $3.0-3.4bn . There is no reason to assume Fluidstack's version of that arithmetic is prettier. There is only no way to know.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
GE Vernova: The AI buildout's most-quoted scarcity story, told with the most-abused arithmetic. Its own reported ratio is 3.7x, not 7x.

What to watch on GE Vernova: Whether the 116 GW under contract shifts toward firm orders rather than slot reservations. The conversion rate from reservation to firm order is the number that decides whether this is a backlog or a waiting list, and GE Vernova reports the two separately in every deck. Whether GE Vernova reports at least 125 GW of gas equipment under contract at end-2026, as Scott Strazik has guided. It is the cleanest falsifiable test on the page and it resolves in one reporting cycle. Whether Wood Mackenzie's forecast that global orders peak in 2026 shows up in the 2027 order intake. If it does while 63 GW of manufacturing capacity is still being added to 2030, this becomes the overcapacity case rather than the shortage case. Whether H2 2026 gas orders hold the dollar-per-kW level already achieved. Pricing landed at the high end of a guided 10 to 20 point increase over Q4 2025; the next print tells you whether that was the ceiling or the new floor. Whether Electrification data-center orders grow off the $5bn booked in H1 2026. GE Vernova disclosed that figure under Q&A rather than in a table, so the disclosure itself may not survive — and its absence would be informative.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: GE Vernova — Introduction. GE Vernova is the instrument everyone reads the energy shortage on, which makes the arithmetic worth doing carefully. The circulating figure is that it signs seven times what it ships. Its own reported unit metric, in the same presentation, is 3.7 times.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: GE Vernova — Role in the stack. One of three companies on earth that build heavy-duty gas turbines at scale, alongside Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. It also sells the grid equipment behind the meter through its Electrification segment, which is where data centers show up most directly. Data center load was 20% of the 100 GW of gas capacity under contract as of the first quarter of 2026 — and because the company says that 20% explicitly supports data centers, excluding indirect service, it is a floor rather than a share.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
GE Vernova — Exposure. Gas equipment backlog plus slot reservation agreements reached 116 GW at the end of the second quarter of 2026, up from 100 GW a quarter earlier . Total company backlog is $176bn , on $24.2bn of second-quarter orders, up 88% organically . Electrification booked over $5bn of data-center-linked orders in the first half of 2026, more than double its full-year 2025 total ; gas power data-center orders are not in that number.

Now the ratio, because it is the most abused number in this discourse. GE Vernova signed 20 GW of gas equipment contracts in the quarter while shipping 3 GW — roughly seven times, and the most generous of three available readings. In the same presentation the company reports its own unit metric: 12.1 GW of gas turbine orders against 3.3 GW of gas turbine sales, 3.7 times . The gap is composition. The 20 GW is firm orders plus a much larger block of non-binding slot reservation agreements, which GE Vernova reports separately from both orders and backlog; on new firm orders alone, the quarter's signings came in below its 3.3 GW of shipments . The scarcity is real. The multiple depends entirely on whether a reservation counts as a sale.

The same care applies to the slot count. Approximately 10 GW of combined 2029 and 2030 delivery capacity remained after the first quarter of 2026 — GE Vernova's slots, not the industry's. Siemens Energy separately held 60 GW of firm orders plus 27 GW of reserved capacity , and none of that is in the 10 GW.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
GE Vernova — The bull case. Pricing is the evidence, not the backlog. GE Vernova guided first-half 2026 gas equipment orders to 10 to 20 points above the fourth quarter of 2025 on a dollar-per-kW basis, and reported in July 2026 that it landed at the higher end of that range . Sellers do not achieve the top of a guided price increase in a market with spare capacity. Behind it, global gas turbine orders reached 110 GW in 2025 against global manufacturing capacity of 60 to 70 GW a year , and industry wait times reached up to 84 months, from 30 to 36 months previously .

Forecast, per GE Vernova (Scott Strazik): Gas turbine output of 20 GW per year by Q3 2026, 24 GW by 2028 and 30 GW by 2030 , with at least 125 GW under contract by end-2026 . Note the shape: the 2030 output target sits below 2025's industry order intake .

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
GE Vernova — The bear case. The strongest version comes from the company's own chief executive. On the same call the corpus cites for lead times, Scott Strazik said that in many of these projects "the gas turbines are really not the gating item," pointing at EPC buildout, permitting and fuel availability across a three-year project cycle . The CEO whose slot scarcity anchors the shortage narrative does not hold the shortage narrative.

Supply is also already responding. Wood Mackenzie's Ed Crooks noted in February 2026 that all three manufacturers have announced significant gas-equipment capacity expansions since the start of 2025, and that turbine makers are increasingly not the primary bottleneck for large loads seeking power . Wood Mackenzie projects 63 GW of manufacturing capacity additions between 2026 and 2030 while expecting orders to peak in 2026 . If both hold, GE Vernova adds output into a falling order book, and every slot reservation signed at today's pricing is a bet that does not clear.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Harvey: Legal AI's capital winner. It publishes lawyer counts and nothing about revenue, so every multiple on it belongs to one research shop.

What to watch on Harvey: Whether Harvey publishes an ARR figure of its own. Until it does, every valuation multiple on the company rests on a Sacra estimate with no independent source, and the last well-sourced revenue number is from August 2025. Whether the next user disclosure grows lawyers faster than organizations. Seat depth inside large firms is what an $11bn valuation is priced on; adding small firms at the same seat count is not the same growth. Whether any Harvey round, secondary or tender prices below $11bn. With the denominator unobservable, the numerator is the only side of the multiple that can be resolved from outside. Whether a named Am Law 100 firm discloses replacing Harvey with Legora or with a lab's own product. There has been no measured churn event in legal AI, which is why the switching-cost claim is still an assumption. Whether Harvey ever discloses a gross margin. It buys tokens at prices set one layer down and sells fixed-price seats; the September 2026 Sonnet 5 list increase is the first visible squeeze on that spread.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Harvey — Introduction. Harvey publishes two kinds of number, and they are not the same kind. Its user counts are company disclosures. Its revenue figures are estimates from a single research shop, restated by aggregators that measure nothing. The $11bn valuation is priced on the second kind.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Harvey — Role in the stack. A vertical application sold to one profession. It buys tokens from the foundation-model layer at prices it does not set, wraps them in legal workflow, and sells seats to law firms and in-house teams on annual commitments. Nothing in the technology is proprietary to Harvey; the position it is defending is distribution inside a regulated profession.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Harvey — Exposure. Harvey served more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations in more than 60 countries as of March 2026 — its own disclosure . Sacra's higher count, 142,000 lawyers at 1,500 customers, post-dates Harvey's by two months, sits well above it and carries no source, so this page uses the company's figure and treats the other as unsupported.

Revenue is the inverse situation. The last well-sourced figure is the $100m ARR Harvey reached in August 2025, three years after founding . The $300m now attached to May 2026 is a Sacra estimate with no independent corroborator, and the aggregator figures near $190m that look like confirmation correspond to Sacra's own end-2025 estimate, not to $300m. Restatement is not corroboration.

Pricing is seat-based and enterprise-shaped: the base offering starts at about $1,200 per lawyer per month on twelve-month commitments . Sacra's wording is "starts at", so that is a floor, not a point price — and Harvey publishes no pricing at all.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Harvey — The bull case. The strongest version is that Harvey is buying the one thing at this layer that does not commoditize. Models get cheaper and capabilities get copied; a workflow embedded in a regulated profession, with conflict rules, privilege, and partner-level sign-off around it, does not get swapped on a benchmark result. On that reading, 100,000 lawyers at 1,300 organizations is a distribution asset, not a technology one, and it is the largest such asset in legal.

The capital reinforces it deliberately. Harvey raised at an $11bn valuation in March 2026 against Legora's $550m at $5.55bn . Two firms financed at that scale in one profession is a race to exhaust the market before a third entrant establishes itself — a distribution strategy, and one that works if the switching costs are as high as both companies are betting.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Harvey — The bear case. The valuation arithmetic rests on a number nobody outside the company has measured. $11bn against an estimated $300m is roughly 37 times forward revenue — arithmetic over the two facts cited in this sentence, with an unverified denominator. Run it on the last independently sourced figure instead, the $100m of August 2025 , and the same valuation is more than a hundred times trailing. A site that prints the flattering denominator without saying which one it used is doing marketing, not analysis.

The second problem is the spread. Harvey sells a fixed seat and buys variable tokens, and it controls neither end. Claude Sonnet 5's output list price rises from $10 to $15 per million tokens on 1 September 2026 , and the tokenizer change behind recent model generations raises effective per-request cost in ways a dollars-per-million table does not show. Harvey discloses no gross margin, so the effect on unit economics is unobservable from outside.

Third, the model layer can walk into the workflow. Claude Code reached an estimated $2.5bn annualized by February 2026 — a lab taking a vertical professional workflow directly, at a scale an order of magnitude above Harvey's estimated ARR. Legal is more defended than coding by regulation and procurement. It is not defended by anything Harvey owns.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn): The largest AI rack assembler on earth, and eight years of evidence that assembling racks confers no pricing power.

What to watch on Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn): Whether consolidated gross margin ever leaves the 6.1-6.3% band in the next TWSE quarterly filing. Q1 2026 printed 6.18%; eight consecutive years have stayed inside forty basis points of that, so a break in either direction is new information. Whether Hon Hai discloses its buy-and-sell versus consignment mix. A single percentage would revalue every margin comparison in this layer, including the ones on this page — right now the CFO has told us the denominator is moving without telling us how far. Whether the self-manufacturing push shows up in operating margin while gross margin stays flat. That is the specific signature of in-sourcing components rather than repricing assembly, and it is the only way to tell Chiang's strategy from operating leverage. Whether 2026 AI rack shipments actually more than double. The guidance carries an explicit condition on supply-chain material availability, and the monthly TWSE revenue filings resolve it before the annual report does. Whether Cloud and Networking crossing half of group revenue coincides with any margin movement at all. It was 48% in Q1 2026; if the mix keeps climbing and the ratio does not, the pass-through thesis is confirmed by the company's own reporting.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn) — Introduction. Hon Hai assembles more AI racks than anyone. It has not become more profitable per dollar in eight years — and the disclosure that would tell you whether that is even the right measurement does not exist.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn) — Role in the stack. The largest single node in systems integration, and increasingly the seller of a whole rack rather than a box. Cloud and Networking Products were 48% of group revenue in the first quarter of 2026 , with AI servers above half of server revenue as a stated floor and no supporting table . Spokesperson James Wu has claimed around 40% share of "the AI market" — no market definition, no methodology, no corroboration. This page records it as his opinion.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn) — Exposure. Gross margin was 6.15% in 2025 against 6.27% in 2018, while revenue rose from NT$5.29tn to NT$8.10tn . Revenue up by half; margin down twelve basis points. Operating margin did improve, 2.57% to 3.20% , and the first quarter of 2026 ran at 6.18% gross and 3.57% operating on NT$2.12tn of quarterly revenue . The company also runs more than forty facilities across twelve US states — its own claim, with no split of AI-rack output by geography.

One disclosure contaminates every margin comparison in this layer, including the three above, and it belongs here rather than in a footnote. Hon Hai's CFO said consignment is now the main transaction model in its ASIC-server projects . Under consignment the customer owns the silicon, so the most expensive content in the rack never enters revenue or cost of sales — and identical physical work reports a higher gross margin on a much smaller base. No integrator discloses its buy-and-sell versus consignment mix. Every ratio on this page is measured against a variable nobody outside these companies can size.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn) — The bull case. It belongs to rotating CEO Michael Chiang, and it is the strongest version available: pure assembly is a pass-through, so the escape route is owning the differentiated content. Hon Hai is expanding into liquid cooling, mechanical components, high-speed transmission, power modules and system validation to raise its self-manufacturing ratio . The operating-margin improvement is what that looks like early , and the proof the destination exists sits in the same supply chain: Asia Vital Components took operating margin from 2.47% to 19.73% making cold plates , Delta from 7.66% to 15.13% in power .

Forecast, per Hon Hai, Michael Chiang, May 2026: 2026 AI rack shipments guided to more than double, with the condition stated explicitly and doing real work — only if supply-chain material availability can meet demand . Capex was around NT$174bn in 2025, up about 27%, guided to more than 30% growth in 2026 .

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn) — The bear case. Eight years of flat gross margin on 53% more revenue is the cleanest evidence anywhere that scale confers no pricing power in rack assembly . Chiang describes many of these businesses as buy-and-sell models in which product prices are adjusted according to costs — which protects absolute profit against input inflation and means the layer cannot absorb a cost shock, only transmit it into the buyer's capital budget one layer up.

The read-across from peers is worse than Hon Hai's own flat line. Quanta's AI margin expansion is a completed round trip: 4.78% in 2019, a 7.85% peak in 2024, 4.78% again in the first quarter of 2026 . Wistron's revenue grew 108% in 2025 while gross margin fell from 8.01% to 6.13% . And in-sourcing is a strategy, not a mechanism: Inventec rode the same wave and moved operating margin from 1.48% to 1.84% across seven years .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Huawei: China's answer to NVIDIA, running at scale on a stockpile it cannot replace — the question is what happens when it runs out.

What to watch on Huawei: Whether Ascend shipments in 2026 exceed 2025's without a new source of leading-edge dies. The 2025 volume ran on a pre-controls TSMC stockpile that SemiAnalysis expected to deplete within about nine months of September 2025; if volume holds through 2026, the stockpile thesis is wrong and domestic capacity is larger than estimated. Whether the Ascend 950DT ships in Q4 2026 with self-developed HBM, as announced. Memory is the binding constraint, so shipping on domestic HBM would matter more than the FLOPS number attached to it. Whether any independent estimate converges with SemiAnalysis's 653,000 910C figure. It currently sits roughly 2x Bernstein's and 6.5x Huawei's own early-2025 plan — the total is far better established than the mix. Whether SMIC's disclosed capacity and utilisation move enough to supply Ascend at volume. SMIC does not break out advanced-node capacity, so this resolves only through inference on total capacity plus yield commentary.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Huawei — Introduction. Huawei is the test of whether export controls work, and the honest answer from the corpus is: not the way either side claims. The company shipped serious volume in 2025. It shipped it largely by drawing down chips bought before the rules landed. Both halves are true, and most commentary picks one.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Huawei — Role in the stack. Vertically integrated in a way no Western firm is: it designs the Ascend accelerator, builds the SuperPoD systems around it, sells the cloud, and courts the developers. That integration is a genuine advantage under sanctions — there is no supplier to cut off — and it is why Huawei, not SMIC, is the name that matters in China's AI silicon.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Huawei — Exposure. Huawei reported 2025 revenue of CNY 880.941 billion, about $126.0 billion, with R&D at 21.8 percent of revenue . On accelerators, SemiAnalysis estimated 805,000 Ascend units shipped in 2025, up from 507,000 in 2024 .

Treat the mix inside that total with more caution than the total itself. Independent estimates cluster at 700,000–805,000 for total Ascend shipments, but the 910C share is genuinely unsettled — SemiAnalysis puts it at 653,000, Bernstein at roughly 350,000, and Huawei's own early-2025 plan at 100,000. Nobody should present the 653,000 as settled, and this page does not.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Huawei — The bull case. The inputs were secured before the door closed. SemiAnalysis estimated Huawei had taken delivery of more than 2.9 million Ascend dies from TSMC , and that China had procured 13 million HBM stacks, enough for 1.6 million Ascend 910C packages, with Samsung supplying 11.4 million . That is years of headroom bought in advance.

Domestic supply is not zero either. SMIC's monthly capacity passed one million 8-inch-equivalent wafers at end-2025 at 93.5 percent utilisation , and SemiAnalysis's conservative estimate put advanced-node capacity at 45,000 wafers per month, of which at most 20,000 was needed for Ascend .

And demand is now policy. Chinese guidance issued in November 2025 requires state-funded data centre projects to use only domestically made AI chips . The clearest evidence that this bites is on the other side of the trade: NVIDIA booked $4,550 million from China-headquartered customers in the quarter ended April 2026, against $9,659 million a year earlier . Beijing did more to close that market than Washington did.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Huawei — The bear case. A stockpile is not a supply chain. The same estimate that credits Huawei with 2.9 million dies expected the bank to deplete within about nine months from September 2025 — and CSIS separately puts the figure at around 2 million chiplets for an earlier Ascend generation, a different unit measuring a different thing, so the real range is a bracket rather than a number. Either way, replacement has to come from SMIC at yields nobody publishes.

The roadmap concedes where the constraint is. Huawei announced the Ascend 950PR for Q1 2026 and the 950DT for Q4 2026 with self-developed HBM — memory is the thing it is trying to internalise, because that is what it cannot buy. Announcing it is not shipping it.

The ecosystem numbers are also company-reported with no published methodology: more than 4 million Ascend developers at end-2025 . Read them as a claim, not a measurement.

One gap worth stating plainly: the corpus has Huawei's total revenue but no citable figure for its AI cloud business specifically, so this page cannot test whether silicon volume is translating into compounding cloud revenue. That is the question that would settle the bull case, and it is currently unanswerable here.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Intel: The manufacturing revival is real; the customer list is not. 18A in volume, first High-NA logic product — and 95% of Foundry revenue is Intel selling itself.

What to watch on Intel: Whether Intel's next 10-Q still describes 14A external demand as uncommitted. The Q2 2026 filing did, three months after Reuters reported Tesla as the first external 14A customer on Elon Musk's word. One of those two statements has to move. Whether Intel Foundry external revenue clears $1bn in a quarter. It was $293m of $5,765m in Q2 2026. Until external revenue is a material fraction, 'foundry' describes an org chart, not a market position. Whether any named 14A customer appears in an Intel or customer filing rather than in a wire story citing comments. A filing-grade disclosure is the only version of this that is falsifiable. Whether 14A risk production actually starts in the second half of 2027, the milestone Intel committed to in Q2 2026 ahead of a 2028 high-volume ramp. Slipping risk production moves the ramp by definition. Whether the gross-to-net gap on 2026 capex is quantified. CFO David Zinsner guided gross capex above $20bn and attributed most of the bridge to grants and investment tax credits without sizing it, which leaves the real cash number undisclosed.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Intel — Introduction. There are two Intels in the corpus and they contradict each other. One is executing better than it has in fifteen years. The other still cannot name a leading-edge customer.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Intel — Role in the stack. Intel is the only US-owned company operating a leading-edge logic fab, which makes it the sole candidate for a second source at the top of the stack — and the reason the concentration question in fab-tooling has any answer other than "Taiwan." It is simultaneously a merchant chip designer competing with its own would-be foundry customers.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text: Intel — Exposure. Q2 2026 revenue was $16.1bn, up 25%, which Intel characterised as its strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years — the company's own framing, and deliberately vaguer than the "since 2011" that circulated. Intel Foundry revenue was $5.77bn against TSMC's $40.20bn in the same quarter , and only $293m of Foundry's $5,765m was external . Roughly 95% is intersegment. Capex guidance was raised to more than $20bn gross in July 2026 .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Intel — The bull case. The manufacturing claims are now filed rather than promised. Intel released its first 18A products in high-volume production at the start of 2026 — the start of the year, per Intel's own 10-Q, not the late-2025 date that reached the trade press. It also produced the first commercial logic product manufactured on High-NA EUV, announced in Q2 2026 , a curve TSMC chose not to ride for N2 or A16. Whatever else is true, Intel is ahead on one tool generation.

Demand signals exist below the customer line, too. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in May 2026 that four Taiwanese and two Japanese substrate suppliers were seeking upfront commitments to secure capacity for Intel's EMIB packaging . Suppliers do not ask for prepayment against capacity nobody expects to use. And NVIDIA put $5bn into Intel in September 2025 for roughly a 4% stake alongside x86 co-development .

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Intel — The bear case. The bear case is a single sentence in Intel's own filings. Intel committed in Q2 2026 to a 2028 high-volume ramp for 14A with risk production in the second half of 2027 — and the same quarter's 10-Q still describes external 14A demand as uncommitted. That is three months after Reuters, citing Elon Musk, reported Tesla as the first major external 14A customer for chips destined for Tesla's Austin Terafab complex . That report is sourced to comments rather than to any announcement or filing by either company, and every other outlet carrying it is syndicating the same wire.

So the $293m is not a starting point that grows mechanically . It is the measured size of Intel's merchant foundry business after a decade of trying, funded by capex above $20bn gross whose gross-to-net bridge Intel declined to quantify. A process node with no committed external volume is a cost centre with a roadmap.

Policy took something too: BIS revoked Validated End-User authorisation for Intel Semiconductor (Dalian) alongside two Korean fabs, effective 31 December 2025 .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Meta: $45.95bn of maximum exposure to loss carried at $1.83bn of equity — the clearest picture in the stack of AI capex moved off a balance sheet.

What to watch on Meta: Whether the Blue Owl venture ever consolidates. It is an unconsolidated variable interest entity under the equity method today; a change in the control analysis would move roughly $46bn of disclosed exposure onto Meta's balance sheet in one line, with no change in the underlying economics. Whether a residual value guarantee liability is ever recorded against that venture. None had been as of 31 December 2025. The quarter one appears is the quarter Meta's own accountants price the downside. Whether the 5.5-year server and network life set in January 2025 holds in the next 10-K. Depreciation rose to $18.0bn in 2025 despite the extension, which means the extension is losing to volume — and a reversal would land on top of that. Whether the $125–145bn capex range is raised a second time. The April 2026 raise was attributed to memory-chip prices and added data centre costs, both input costs Meta does not control. Whether Meta's neocloud commitments — roughly $27bn with Nebius and $21bn with CoreWeave — are reaffirmed in filings or quietly restructured. Both counterparties fund delivery with debt secured on the hardware, so Meta's capacity depends on someone else's credit window staying open.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Meta — Introduction. Meta's most important AI number is not its capex. It is a maximum exposure to loss of $45.95bn sitting against $1.83bn of carried equity , in a venture that does not consolidate.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Meta — Role in the stack. Meta is the pure buyer. It has no cloud business, so it cannot sell any of this capacity to anyone — every dollar is a cost recovered only through ads and ranking. That gives it the strongest incentive of the four hyperscalers to move the spend somewhere other than its own balance sheet, and it has built the most elaborate machinery for doing so.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Meta — Exposure. Meta raised 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $125–145bn in April 2026, from $115–135bn, attributing the increase to memory-chip prices and added data centre costs ; 2025 actual was $72.22bn .

Then the structure. The Blue Owl joint venture developing the Richland Parish campus commits the parties to fund pro rata shares of approximately $27bn in total estimated development costs — that is not the venture's size or its capitalisation . What was actually contributed at formation was $11.3bn: Meta $4.3bn and Blue Owl $7.0bn in cash, with Meta taking a one-time $2.6bn distribution back and holding a 20% interest . The gap between $11.3bn in and $27bn of eventual cost is the structure's entire point. Financing came through a joint-venture vehicle: roughly $27bn of A+ rated bonds plus about $2.5bn of equity, arranged by Morgan Stanley and anchored by PIMCO .

The filed exposure is the number to hold onto: maximum exposure to loss of $45.95bn against equity carried at $1.83bn as of 31 December 2025, as an unconsolidated variable interest entity under the equity method, with no residual value guarantee liability recorded .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Meta — The bull case. The market has repeatedly said yes at investment grade. Meta sold $30bn of its own investment-grade bonds in October 2025 against an order book of roughly $125bn — four times the deal — and the joint-venture paper priced at A+ . This is not exotic credit reaching for yield; it is the highest-quality end of the market funding datacentre shells.

Meta is also buying the scarce input early rather than late. A 20-year 1,092 MW virtual PPA for Clinton from June 2027 , 2,100 MW from Vistra's Perry and Davis-Besse plants plus 433 MW of uprates , and development frameworks for up to 1,200 MW with Oklo and up to 690 MW with TerraPower . And unlike a cloud provider, Meta needs no external customer to justify a GPU — improved ranking pays back inside a business it already owns.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Meta — The bear case. The useful-life extension is losing. Meta went to 5.5 years effective January 2025, worth about $2.9bn of depreciation relief — and depreciation on property and equipment still climbed from roughly $11.0bn in 2023 to $18.0bn in 2025 . The accounting lever is smaller than the volume it is fighting.

Its capital allocation record on AI assets is also mixed in a specific, documented way. Meta paid $14.3bn for a 49% non-voting stake in Scale AI at a $29bn valuation ; neutrality was the asset in data labelling, and Google — about $150m of 2024 spend with $200m planned for 2025 — moved to split afterwards . Meanwhile capacity increasingly comes from leveraged intermediaries: roughly $27bn with Nebius and $21bn with CoreWeave .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Microsoft: Its largest AI customer is also its largest AI investment, and the only quantity it will define precisely is the one it must file.

What to watch on Microsoft: Whether commercial RPO growth keeps decelerating. It was +110% at December 2025 and +99% at March 2026 — the level is enormous and the second derivative is already negative. Two more prints below 99% and the 'you do not sign that and then not need the machines' defence weakens. Whether Microsoft ever defines its AI revenue rather than quoting a run rate whose composition it does not disclose. A figure in the 10-K, or continued silence, tells you which kind of number it is. Whether the six-year server and network life set in fiscal 2023 survives the next 10-K. Microsoft has not touched it since; Amazon has already shortened a subset of its fleet back to five years. Whether the Microsoft 365 Copilot seat count moves from the earnings call into the press release or the filing. Today it exists only as a verbal CEO statement, and it is seats sold, not seats used. Whether the carrying value of the OpenAI stake changes in a filing. It is currently the largest single equity position underwriting a customer relationship anywhere in this stack, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal on that customer's compute in the same month it booked the commitment.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Microsoft — Introduction. Microsoft is the only company in this stack that is simultaneously its biggest AI customer's largest shareholder, its largest supplier, and its largest rival's landlord. That is not a metaphor. It is three disclosures from the same twelve months.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Microsoft — Role in the stack. Three businesses that reinforce each other. Azure sells the capacity. Microsoft Marketplace is the toll road other people's AI software travels to reach enterprise budgets. And Microsoft's balance sheet holds equity in the frontier labs on both sides of the model race — which means it books revenue from customers it partly owns.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Microsoft — Exposure. Two RPO numbers, two scopes, and they are not interchangeable. The 10-Q reports $633bn of total remaining performance obligations at 31 March 2026, up from $398bn six months earlier, alongside management's plain statement that demand continues to exceed supply . The earnings release from the same quarter reports $627bn of commercial RPO, up 99% . Do not average them. And the widely repeated "$80bn of backlog Microsoft cannot fulfil because of power" appears nowhere in the call — Amy Hood's position is qualitative, not quantified .

The AI figure is softer than it looks. Microsoft says its AI business passed a $37bn annual run rate, up 123% — a run rate, not recognised revenue, with no stated composition. Satya Nadella said on the same call that Microsoft 365 Copilot had passed 20 million paid enterprise seats, from 15 million a quarter earlier ; the release itself contains no seat count. At list price those seats imply roughly $7.2bn of annualised value — a ceiling, almost certainly above realised contract value, and about 19% of the $37bn .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Microsoft — The bull case. The strongest argument is the rail, not the run rate. Microsoft charges 3% on Marketplace transactions with no listing fee, on an agency model where it owns billing and collections . The mechanism that matters sits underneath: 100% of an eligible partner purchase made through Marketplace decrements the customer's Azure consumption commitment . A third-party AI purchase becomes a zero-marginal-cash decision for any enterprise already carrying a commitment, while buying direct requires new budget. That is distribution power the take rate does not capture.

On the asset question, Microsoft has the better historical record. It moved server life from four years to six in fiscal 2023 , and Azure retired V100 GPUs roughly 7.5 years after launch . Service life has exceeded book life.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Microsoft — The bear case. The counterparty is the exposure. Microsoft holds an OpenAI position valued near $135bn, about 27% as-converted , and OpenAI contracted an incremental $250bn of Azure — in the same transaction where Microsoft surrendered its right of first refusal as OpenAI's compute provider . Both sides of that relationship now move on one company's ability to pay. Anthropic's $30bn Azure commitment sits against a combined NVIDIA–Microsoft investment of up to $15bn in Anthropic — the same structure again, hedged onto the other lab.

Meanwhile the spend against it is not guided at all. Analysts track Microsoft toward roughly $190bn of calendar-2026 capital expenditure — an estimate, and marked as one, because Microsoft publishes no annual capex figure to check it against. The disclosure asymmetry runs through the whole page: Microsoft Cloud revenue of $51.5bn in the December quarter is filed and precise , while the AI business is a run rate it will not define and the Copilot seat count exists only as a sentence on a call.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Nebius: Contracted revenue measured in tens of billions, quarterly revenue in hundreds of millions, and capex guided at roughly seven times the revenue it funds.

What to watch on Nebius: Whether 2026 revenue tracks toward the $3.0-3.4bn guide. Q1's $399m annualises well below the low end, so the guide requires a steep intra-year ramp that either shows up in Q2 and Q3 or does not. Whether 2026 capex lands inside the $20-25bn guide, and how it is funded. Nebius raised about $2bn from NVIDIA in March 2026 via a pre-funded warrant; the size and structure of the next raise is the clearest read on the gap between contracted revenue and the capital needed to serve it. Whether the roughly $27bn Meta agreement appears in a Nebius filing with disclosed terms. Two press reports agree on the number and no company document in the corpus confirms it — the 6-K or annual report is what would. Whether Nebius reports a positive operating result in any quarter of 2026, not only positive adjusted EBITDA. The adjustment is where depreciation on a fleet being built at $20bn+ a year lives, and that gap widens before it narrows. Whether any Nebius facility is financed against the GPUs themselves. CoreWeave's March 2026 loan put the hardware in the lien inside a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary; if Nebius follows, the collateral question moves from theoretical to priced.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Nebius — Introduction. Nebius is CoreWeave's shape one lap earlier, and the interesting number is not the growth rate. It is the distance between what the company has contracted and what it must spend to deliver it.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Nebius — Role in the stack. A neocloud: it buys accelerators, wraps them in power and networking, and rents capacity on multi-year contracts, with no software business alongside to absorb a bad year. That makes it — like CoreWeave — a place where every cost the hyperscalers can bury inside a larger P&L is visible on the income statement.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Nebius — Exposure. Revenue was $399.0m in the first quarter of 2026, up 684% year over year, with adjusted EBITDA of $129.5m . Against that, two contracts: $17.4bn with Microsoft through 2031, scalable to $19.4bn, signed in September 2025 , and approximately $27bn with Meta over five years, announced alongside the Q1 2026 results . The Meta figure rests on two press reports that agree with each other; the corpus has no company filing confirming it, and this page flags that rather than smoothing it.

The capital structure is the exposure. Nebius guided full-year 2026 revenue of $3.0-3.4bn with capital expenditure of $20.0-25.0bn — the leverage-forward neocloud model in one ratio, roughly seven times capex to revenue. And its supplier is now a shareholder: on 11 March 2026 Nebius sold NVIDIA a pre-funded warrant for 21,065,936 Class A ordinary shares at $0.0001 each, raising approximately $2bn gross, with a six-month transfer lock-up .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Nebius — The bull case. The revenue is contracted, and by counterparties that do not fail. Microsoft at $17.4bn and Meta at roughly $27bn against a $3.0-3.4bn revenue year is more than a decade of visibility signed by two of the four largest capex payers on earth. NVIDIA putting $2bn into the equity is a supply-allocation signal as much as a financing one.

The pricing environment supports the unit economics too, and it argues against the simple oversupply story. One-year reserved H100 contracts bottomed at $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 and rebounded about 38% to $2.35 by March 2026 , because providers sold out and little Hopper capacity came off contract. Frontier-generation pricing is firmer still: B200 rentals ran $4.50-7.00 an hour in the second quarter of 2026 with marketplace rates rising month over month .

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Nebius — The bear case. Read the two guides together. Capex of $20.0-25.0bn against revenue of $3.0-3.4bn means the contracts run to 2031 while the spending happens now — and the first quarter's $399m annualises below the low end of the company's own revenue guide. Every dollar of that capex has to be financed before the contracted revenue arrives, and the gap is the business.

CoreWeave shows what the financing eventually looks like at scale: a $740m GAAP net loss alongside a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin in the same quarter , bridged by $536m of quarterly net interest on $24.9bn of debt , and an $8.5bn facility placed in a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary secured on substantially all of that subsidiary's assets . Nebius is earlier in that sequence, not exempt from it.

The competitive floor is softer than the contracts suggest. One estimate — a single source with unpublished methodology, from Value Add VC, so directional only — counts more than 300 new GPU cloud providers entering the market in 2025 . And the demand-side risk sits above: Nebius is a marginal seller of capacity to firms that are also building their own, so a pause in hyperscaler capex reaches the neoclouds first.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
NVIDIA: The stack's price-setter, now also its largest investor — and the one company whose biggest market was closed by the buyer's government, not the seller's.

What to watch on NVIDIA: Whether any subsequent filing reports non-zero revenue under the February 2026 H200 China licensing programme. As of May 2026 it was zero, and NVIDIA said it did not know whether imports would be allowed. This resolves on a revenue line, not on a policy announcement. Whether the Taiwan line in the geographic revenue table keeps growing while the China line falls. Revenue is booked by direct-customer headquarters, so the two moving together would suggest re-routing rather than lost demand. Whether the up-to-$100bn OpenAI letter of intent converts into a definitive agreement with recognised progress payments. NVIDIA's own forward-looking-statements section flags the $100bn as an intent; a signed contract with milestones would move it out of that section. Whether GAAP gross margin holds near 74.9% once CoWoS capacity reaches the 120,000-130,000 wafers-per-month target. The margin is currently supported by a rationed packaging line; the first quarter with slack is the test. Whether the 15% China revenue share ever appears in a published regulation. NVIDIA's 10-Q says the US government expressed the expectation but 'did not publish a regulation codifying such requirement.'

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: NVIDIA — Introduction. NVIDIA sets the price of AI compute, and in the last two years it also started paying for the demand. Both facts belong on the same page, because the company's revenue and its balance sheet now point at the same counterparties.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: NVIDIA — Role in the stack. Merchant accelerator silicon, sold increasingly as a rack rather than a chip — plus the networking that binds racks together, which is now a business in its own right. NVIDIA is also the layer's largest single equity investor, which means its customers' cost of capital and its own order book are not independent variables.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
NVIDIA — Exposure. Revenue was $81.6bn in the quarter ended April 2026, up 85% , with data center at $75.2bn, up 92% , at a 74.9% GAAP gross margin held straight through the Blackwell-to-Rubin transition . Networking alone was $14.8bn, up 199% .

China is the exposure that already resolved, and Beijing closed it. Revenue from customers headquartered in China including Hong Kong fell to $4,550m from $9,659m a year earlier — but the filing's own caveat is that geographic revenue is designated by the headquarters of direct customers, so this is not a China-destination measure. The destination facts are separate and starker: zero data center Hopper products shipped to China in the quarter, against $4.6bn a year earlier , and zero revenue under the February 2026 H200 licensing programme as of the May 2026 filing . Washington legalised the supply; Beijing had already barred the demand.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text: NVIDIA — The bull case. The margin is the argument. A 74.9% GAAP gross margin held through an architecture change is what pricing power looks like when a competitor is supposed to be taking share, and NVIDIA guided the following quarter to $91.0bn plus or minus 2% . Meanwhile the strongest architectural challenger left by licence rather than by benchmark: Groq signed a non-exclusive agreement with NVIDIA in December 2025 worth $17bn in cash .

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
NVIDIA — The bear case. NVIDIA is financing its own order book, and the list is now long enough to be structural: up to $100bn intended for OpenAI as each gigawatt deploys , a $6.3bn agreement to buy CoreWeave's unsold capacity through 2032 , $2bn of CoreWeave equity at $87.20 a share , a $2bn Nebius pre-funded warrant , up to $10bn of a combined $15bn into Anthropic with Microsoft , and $5bn into Intel . Vendor equity and vendor backstops make revenue quality harder to read, not easier.

The second bear point is that a single sovereign already demonstrated it can zero a segment. The cost of one reclassification was a $4.5bn charge for excess H20 inventory and purchase obligations . Twelve months after the AI Diffusion rule was rescinded, NVIDIA reported that the replacement's scope and timing remained uncertain , while US officials expressed an expectation of 15% or more of licensed China revenue with no regulation codifying it .

Forecast, per NVIDIA, July 2026: NVIDIA says it plans to produce up to $500bn of AI infrastructure in the United States with named partners . No time horizon, no contractual basis, no partner breakdown — a plan, not a booking.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
OpenAI: The stack's largest demand-side counterparty, whose most-quoted number is one executive's aggregate rather than a sum of contracts.

What to watch on OpenAI: Whether OpenAI itemises the portion of the $1.4tn that no public contract accounts for. The named agreements total $588bn. Until the remainder is disclosed, the figure is an attributed aggregate, not a verifiable commitment book — and no page on this site should treat it as one. Whether the NVIDIA arrangement converts from a letter of intent into a definitive agreement. NVIDIA's own filing says there is no assurance it completes, and the investment is structured to arrive progressively as each gigawatt is deployed — so the schedule, not the headline, is what to watch. Whether the $35bn AGI-or-IPO tranche of Amazon's commitment is funded, and against which trigger. No party has published a definition of artificial general intelligence for the purpose of the contract. Whether gross margin recovers above the 33% recorded for fiscal 2025. It fell from 40% the prior year against a 46% internal target, so the trend and the miss both point the same way; inference cost per dollar of revenue is the whole thesis. Whether the Ramp and Menlo readings of enterprise share converge or diverge further. Both currently put Anthropic ahead of OpenAI among enterprise buyers, and one of the two has a disclosed conflict of interest — a third independent measurement would settle it.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: OpenAI — Introduction. OpenAI's $1.4 trillion is not a sum of contracts. It is Sam Altman's own attributed figure, covering roughly 30 GW across about eight years , and treating it as an audited commitment book is the most common error in the entire discourse.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: OpenAI — Role in the stack. OpenAI occupies the model layer and the application layer at once — it trains the frontier system and sells the consumer product on top of it — and that makes it the largest single buyer in the capital layer. Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, AMD, NVIDIA and CoreWeave all have material forward exposure to one company's ability to pay.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
OpenAI — Exposure. Altman put total data centre commitments at about $1.4tn across roughly 30 GW and about eight years in November 2025 . The publicly named contracts are $300bn with Oracle , an incremental $250bn with Azure and $38bn with AWS — $588bn . The remainder is not itemised, and one widely circulated reconstruction of the total double-counted NVIDIA's inbound equity as an outbound purchase .

Pick the right denominator. Annualized revenue exited 2025 above $20bn; the roughly $13bn also in circulation is full-year 2025 recognised revenue, a different metric . The scale on the demand side is genuine: more than 900 million weekly ChatGPT users , over 50 million consumer subscribers and more than 9 million paying business users as of February 2026 . The 1 billion monthly active app users is a third-party estimate, not an OpenAI disclosure .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
OpenAI — The bull case. Nothing else in software has this shape. Run-rate revenue moved from about $20bn at end-2025 to roughly $25bn in February 2026 and about $33bn by May 2026 — estimates that explicitly exclude Microsoft licensing and large one-off deals, so they understate the total. Enterprise passed 40% of revenue and is tracking toward parity with consumer .

Capital has not been the binding constraint. OpenAI raised $122bn at an $852bn post-money valuation in March 2026 , after $500bn in an October 2025 secondary . And it converts capital into capability faster than the schedule implies: reasoning training compute scaled 10x from o1 to o3 in four months .

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
OpenAI — The bear case. The margin is going the wrong way. Gross margin fell to 33% in fiscal 2025 from 40% the prior year, against an internal 46% target . Inference cost was about $8.4bn in 2025 with $14.1bn projected for 2026 . Projected cash burn is roughly $27bn in 2026 and $63bn in 2027, with cash-flow positive not expected until 2030 , and internal projections put 2028 compute spend at $121bn against an $85bn loss .

The financing is softest where it is largest. NVIDIA's up-to-$100bn is a letter of intent, progressive on each gigawatt deployed, which NVIDIA's own release flags as forward-looking and yet to be finalised . $35bn of Amazon's $50bn is contingent on an IPO or on reaching AGI . AMD issued a warrant for up to 160 million shares at $0.01, vesting in tranches tied to Instinct deployments and to share-price targets escalating to $600 , against an agreement to deploy 6 GW of AMD GPUs over five years .

And it is not winning the enterprise. Menlo — an Anthropic investor, conflict noted — puts Anthropic at 40% of 2025 enterprise LLM spend against OpenAI's 27% ; Ramp's transaction data shows 42.4% of AI-spending businesses paying Anthropic versus 39.5% paying OpenAI . Meanwhile the price floor is set elsewhere: DeepSeek-R1 launched at $2.20 per million output tokens against $60 for o1 .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Oracle: A neocloud with an enterprise software business attached — and a forward book one customer could rewrite.

What to watch on Oracle: Whether Oracle discloses the as-of quarter and the customer composition of the $523bn RPO. The corpus cannot presently pin the quarter, and one contract plausibly accounts for more than half of it. A concentration disclosure would settle the single most important question on this page. Whether FY2027 capex guidance is set above the FY2026 actual of $55.7bn or below it. Above is a re-underwriting of the OpenAI build; below is a retreat, and the first credible sign that a hyperscale contract can be delivered more slowly than signed. Whether the contracted OpenAI capacity begins delivering in 2027 as reported. Delivery is the moment RPO starts converting into revenue, and Oracle has been spending against it for two years already.
