Whether the next funding tranche arrives as unsecured bonds like the $18bn September 2025 issue, or moves to secured and special-purpose structures. CoreWeave's March 2026 facility shows what the market charges when the collateral is named. Whether any part of the $300bn contract is re-scoped, re-priced, or re-phased. It is five years and 4.5 GW against a counterparty whose own commitments run about eight years, so a timing change on either side propagates straight into Oracle's book.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Oracle — Introduction. Oracle changed business model without changing its name. It now buys accelerators, wraps them in power and networking, and rents them on long contracts — the CoreWeave business, run from inside a database company.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Oracle — Role in the stack. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is a capacity landlord with an unusual advantage and an unusual dependency. The advantage is a database installed base that generates cash regardless of GPU pricing. The dependency is that the forward book is dominated by one counterparty.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Oracle — Exposure. Oracle spent $55.7bn of capital expenditure in fiscal 2026, against guidance of approximately $50bn — its own forecast missed high by about 11% in the first full year of the build.

The forward book grew faster than anything else in the layer. RPO was $455bn in Q1 FY2026, up 359% year over year , reaching $523bn — with the as-of quarter still unconfirmed from the filings, most likely the quarter ended November 2025. Inside it sits a single September 2025 contract with OpenAI for $300bn of computing power over five years, equal to 4.5 GW, with delivery reportedly starting 2027 . That one agreement is roughly 57% of the entire book .

Funding so far has been plain: $18bn of investment-grade bonds in September 2025, raised largely to serve that contract .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Oracle — The bull case. Oracle won the deal, and the deal is contracted. A book that went from $455bn to $523bn is not a pipeline or a letter of intent; it is signed revenue obligation, funded at investment grade rather than through the secured structures the neoclouds use .

The delivery model is also lighter than it looks. Oracle leases rather than owns the flagship Stargate site: the $7.1bn JPMorgan-led construction loan for the second phase at Abilene went to the Crusoe–Blue Owl joint venture developing the campus, not to Oracle and not to OpenAI . Someone else's balance sheet carries the shell.

And Oracle has the cover CoreWeave lacks. It runs the same buy-and-rent economics with a second, unrelated software business absorbing a bad quarter — which is precisely the structural difference the cloud layer identifies between hyperscalers and pure plays.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Oracle — The bear case. Concentration is worse than at any hyperscaler. Roughly 57% of the forward book rests on a counterparty whose annualized revenue run rate exited 2025 above $20bn , against a $300bn five-year obligation . Oracle does not need OpenAI to fail for this to hurt; it needs only a renegotiation.

The timing is adverse in both directions. Capex is being spent now and revenue begins in 2027 — and the first year of spending already overshot its own guidance by about 11% .

The surrounding paper is also thinner than the headlines. Stargate's founding equity split — SoftBank and OpenAI reported at $19bn each for 40%, with Oracle and MGX near $7bn each — was never confirmed by the parties and does not internally reconcile . Oracle's participation in the structure its largest contract depends on is, publicly, an unconfirmed report.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Scale AI: The labelling incumbent whose most valuable asset was not being aligned with any lab. In June 2025 it sold 49 percent of that.

What to watch on Scale AI: Whether Google's reported plan to split from Scale ever completes. The originating CNBC report describes intent, not an exit; resolution shows up in a disclosed vendor change or in Scale's next revenue figure, not in more reporting. Whether Scale discloses a 2026 revenue figure at all, and whether it grows off the estimated $2bn 2025 base — the only way to tell whether Meta became an anchor customer or a replacement for lost ones. Whether headcount recovers past the pre-July-2025 level. If it does not, the 200-person cut was a reset of the cost base rather than a reaction to one quarter. Whether Meta discloses in-housing of data operations it previously bought. The stake was reportedly about capability, and capability brought in-house is billings removed. Whether any per-task price or gross-margin figure is ever published by Scale or a customer. The corpus holds Scale's unit economics only in a source note, so the layer's oldest business model is currently unauditable.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Scale AI — Introduction. Scale AI is the only company in this stack whose most valuable asset was a negative: it was not aligned with any single frontier lab. In June 2025 it sold 49 percent of itself to one of them, and the layer got a natural experiment on what neutrality was worth.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Scale AI — Role in the stack. A data-supply vendor for the human-generated half of the layer — labels, preference rankings, demonstrations, graded answers. It priced per completed task at a markup and grew by managing the largest low-cost annotation workforce. That model built the autonomous-vehicle era of labelling and the RLHF era after it.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Scale AI — Exposure. Scale reported $870m of 2024 revenue against a $1.5bn annualized run-rate at end-2024, with an estimated $2bn in 2025 . The 2025 figure is an estimate; the 2024 one is reported. Meta then invested $14.3bn for a 49 percent non-voting stake at a $29bn valuation in June 2025 .

Customer exposure sat in exactly the accounts that stake threatened. Google spent about $150m with Scale in 2024 and had planned $200m for 2025 before moving to split after the Meta investment . The corpus holds Scale's per-task price points and gross-margin range in a source note rather than as citable facts, so this page will not print them — which means the most basic question about the business, what it keeps per dollar billed, has no admissible answer here.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Scale AI — The bull case. Start by correcting the story, because the widely told version overstates the damage. "OpenAI departed Scale" is false, and it is contradicted by the very CNBC report the claim is sourced to: OpenAI's chief financial officer said the company would keep working with Scale as one of several data vendors . Google's move is reported intent, not a completed exit. Microsoft was reported to be pulling back. Any account listing four clean departures has invented most of them.

What remains is a business with real reported revenue that roughly doubled from 2024 to an estimated 2025 , a $29bn arm's-length mark set by a sophisticated buyer with full diligence , and a shareholder that is also one of the three or four entities on earth that needs data at this scale. Meta did not buy 49 percent of a vendor it intended to stop using.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Scale AI — The bear case. The bear case does not need the departure list, and it is stronger without it. One month after the Meta stake, in July 2025, Scale laid off 200 full-time employees — about 14 percent of staff — and ended roughly 500 contractor relationships . That is a measured consequence rather than a reported intention, and it arrived inside a quarter. A labelling vendor's asset is that it is aligned with nobody; an investor can destroy that asset by buying in, and the payroll shows the damage before the revenue line does.

The second problem is that the growth in this layer moved to a different unit. Mercor reached $2bn of annualized gross revenue in June 2026, up from a $760m run-rate at end-2025 , buying credentialled expert hours at average rates above $85 with contractors keeping 60 to 70 percent of the top line . Those splits are Sacra estimates with no independent corroborator, so the netted number is soft. The direction is not: the reinforcement-learning era buys physicians and quantitative analysts by the hour, and Scale was built to buy annotation by the task.

Third, buyer concentration has no floor. Three or four labs need data at this scale, each is large enough to be a majority of a vendor's revenue, and each can build the capability internally. Meta's 49 percent stake is the most expensive in-housing attempt anyone has made, and it was aimed at this company.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
SK hynix: A 72% operating margin in a business the industry files under commodity. The level is the finding; the comparison everyone reaches for does not exist.

What to watch on SK hynix: Whether operating margin holds above 60% in the Q2 2026 release. The 2027 supply response is scheduled and modest, so a turn before it arrives would say the peak was demand-side, not capacity-side. Whether SK hynix ever discloses absolute HBM revenue instead of a growth multiple. It has said HBM revenue more than doubled in 2025 without publishing the number, and the HBM-versus-server-DRAM split is what decides whether 72% is de-commoditization or a DRAM cycle. Whether custom HBM turns into named per-customer programs in a filing or an earnings deck. SK hynix names it as the next differentiator; a disclosed design win is what would move it from positioning to a contracted, non-substitutable product. Whether the company quantifies the cost of losing Validated End-User authorisation at its China fab, effective 31 December 2025. A tooling or capex line attributed to it in the annual report is the first hard number on what the revocation actually did. Whether Q3 2026 server DRAM contract prices land inside TrendForce's 13-18% quarter-over-quarter forecast. Undershooting it while bit supply is still tight would be the earliest evidence the cycle has turned.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: SK hynix — Introduction. In the first quarter of 2026 SK hynix converted 72% of revenue into operating profit , in the part of the stack everyone had filed under "commodity, cyclical, low margin." That is the finding. The comparison the discourse immediately reaches for is against NVIDIA's operating line, and this page will not make it: the corpus has no NVIDIA operating margin, only a 74.9% gross margin . Scoring an operating margin against a gross margin would be inventing the number that makes the point.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: SK hynix — Role in the stack. The price-setter in high-bandwidth memory, and a major supplier of server DRAM alongside it. HBM is a stack of DRAM dies bonded vertically and sitting millimetres from the compute die, because the distance the electron travels is the thing being bought. Content per accelerator is fixed by the accelerator's design — Google's Ironwood TPU carries 192 GB of HBM per chip at 7.37 TB/s — so every incremental GPU or TPU ships with a pre-committed memory order, and there is no substitution and no downgrade path.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
SK hynix — Exposure. Revenue was KRW 52,576.3bn in the first quarter of 2026, up 198% year over year and 60% sequentially , at a 72% operating margin on operating profit of KRW 37,610.3bn . For the prior full year, revenue was KRW 97,146.7bn at a 49% operating margin . HBM revenue more than doubled year over year in 2025 , though the absolute figure is not disclosed — which means the mix behind the margin is not auditable from outside.

The policy exposure is the other half. BIS revoked Validated End-User authorisation for SK hynix's China fab, along with Intel's Dalian site and Samsung China Semiconductor, effective 31 December 2025 , removing blanket tool-import rights at the largest non-Chinese fabs operating inside China. Separately, the rule effective 15 January 2026 caps licensable China and Macau advanced-computing exports at total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s . Memory bandwidth is now the legal chokepoint as well as the physical one — regulators went where the binding constraint actually is.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
SK hynix — The bull case. HBM is de-commoditizing, and it is doing so in public. SK hynix completed HBM4 mass production in September 2025 and moved to large-scale production in 2026, naming custom HBM as the next differentiator . When a part gets specified per customer it stops being a spot good, and pricing is behaving accordingly.

Forecast, per TrendForce, July 2026: Server DRAM contract prices are forecast to rise 13 to 18% quarter over quarter in the third quarter of 2026 , while total RDIMM bit supply grows 15 to 20% year over year in 2027 . Both are TrendForce's own forecasts.

Put those side by side and the condition is legible: prices rising by mid-teens percentages per quarter against a supply answer of mid-teens percentages per year. The response is real, scheduled, and an order of magnitude slower than the signal.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
SK hynix — The bear case. The bear case is the base rate, and the corpus cannot rebut it. DRAM has run this cycle repeatedly and every prior peak margin was followed by a supply response — which is exactly what the 2027 bit-supply forecast describes , and why long-term agreements capping increases for some cloud buyers exist at all . TrendForce is the author of both the inflation and the deflation.

What makes this genuinely unresolved rather than rhetorical: the research has no 2019 or 2022 trough margin for SK hynix. Its earliest anchor is the 49% full-year 2025 figure . Without the troughs, nobody — including this site and including anyone quoting the 72% — can say whether it is a cycle or a regime.

There is also demand in the numbers that has already happened. SemiAnalysis estimated China procured 13 million HBM stacks, enough for 1.6 million Ascend 910C packages, with Samsung supplying 11.4 million of them — purchases made ahead of restrictions. That is a drawdown, not a durable order book, and it belongs on the demand side of any judgement about how much of the current squeeze is structural.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Super Micro Computer: The purest read on AI server integration, because it is only that business — and its record quarter carried its worst margin ever.

What to watch on Super Micro Computer: Whether gross margin recovers above the 11.1% full-year FY2025 level in the FY2026 10-K, or whether the 8.2% nine-month rate becomes the base. Supermicro's own MD&A attributes the decline to GPU servers, HPC systems and rack-scale solutions — a mix that is not going away. Whether cash rebuilds off $1.3bn in the next 10-Q. The filing named inventory build, customers asking for longer payment terms and longer component lead times; if cash falls again with receivables still concentrated, this stops being a margin story and becomes a liquidity one. Whether Customer A stays near 32.2% of accounts receivable, and whether a fifth ten-percent customer appears in the concentration footnote. A year before Q3 FY2026 only two customers cleared that threshold. Whether the tariff line keeps compounding. It rose $89.4m, or 608%, in the March 2026 quarter alone, against $1,019m of gross profit in the same quarter — the ratio, not the absolute, is what matters at a single-digit gross margin. Whether the March 2026 SDNY indictment stays with the named individuals or reaches the company. One defendant is a co-founder, board member and senior vice president of business development, and the allegations are unadjudicated.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Super Micro Computer — Introduction. Supermicro is the cleanest natural experiment in systems integration, because it is only this business and nothing averages the dilution away. Its largest quarter in company history carried the lowest gross margin in company history. Both facts describe the same racks.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Super Micro Computer — Role in the stack. A US OEM that builds and ships AI servers and full rack-scale systems. It sits between NVIDIA's silicon and the buyer's data hall, and unlike Dell or HPE it has no adjacent segment to average the economics against — which makes its income statement the layer's least flattering and most useful disclosure.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Super Micro Computer — Exposure. The series runs one way. Gross margin was 18.0% on $7.12bn of revenue in FY2023 and 11.1% on $21.97bn in FY2025 , with operating margin falling from 10.7% to 5.7% over the same span . Then 6.3% on $12.68bn of net sales in the quarter ended December 2025 , and 8.2% for the nine months to March 2026 against 11.6% a year earlier .

Three exposures compound underneath that. Four customers were 75.1% of accounts receivable at March 2026, the largest alone 32.2% . Cash fell from $5.2bn in June 2025 to $1.3bn in March 2026, with the filing naming inventory build, longer customer payment terms as system costs rise, and longer component lead times . Tariff expense rose $89.4m, up 608% year over year, in the March 2026 quarter alone .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Super Micro Computer — The bull case. Falling margin here is mix, not distress, and the company says so in a filed document: the nine-month decline is attributed to GPU servers, HPC systems and rack-scale solutions . Revenue tripled between FY2023 and FY2025 , which means the ratio deteriorated because the business won.

The strongest attributed version of that argument is not Supermicro's, it is Dell's. Dell's consolidated gross margin fell from 24.3% to 17.8% over three years on AI-server mix, by its own unhedged account , while consolidated operating margin rose in the same quarter because its operating-expense rate fell faster. At sufficient revenue velocity a low-gross-margin business out-earns a high-gross-margin one in dollars. Note precisely what that is: a scale argument, not a pricing-power argument, and it is fragile to volume falling.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Super Micro Computer — The bear case. A 6.3% gross margin , $1.3bn of cash and four customers at 75.1% of receivables is a combination in which one slipped large shipment is a liquidity event rather than a bad quarter. Working capital, not floor space, is the binding constraint on doubling output — a company earning single-digit operating margins cannot self-fund a doubling, and Supermicro's own filing describes customers pushing payment terms out precisely as the systems get more expensive.

The scale argument also has a governance problem attached. A March 2026 US indictment alleges that a Southeast Asian intermediary bought approximately $2.5bn of servers from a US manufacturer between 2024 and 2025 for unlicensed diversion to China , including at least approximately $510m between late April and mid-May 2025 . Two honesty notes travel with that. These are allegations, not adjudicated facts. And the corpus records the seller as "a US manufacturer" rather than by name — the identification rests on the defendants being officers of the filer, not on the charging language. What the allegation describes is a failure of end-use verification at the OEM, which is exactly where export control is designed to bind.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
TeraWulf: A bitcoin miner turned AI landlord that had to buy its own creditworthiness from Google — and disclosed what it cost.

What to watch on TeraWulf: Whether the 401 MW Anthropic lease in Kentucky gets a Google backstop. The Lake Mariner leases have one and the Kentucky lease does not; the financing terms TeraWulf gets for Hawesville are the cleanest test of what the guarantee is actually worth. Energized megawatts, not contracted megawatts. 102 MW were live in July 2026 against 378 MW plus 401 MW signed. This is the only number on the company that cannot be signed into existence, and it is the one to track quarter to quarter. Whether the warrant liability keeps compounding. It went from $844.7m to $1,816.7m in six months and flows straight through the income statement, so a strong equity year produces a larger reported loss. Whether Fluidstack's leases commence on schedule in the second half of 2026 and early 2027. One of three had only partially commenced by 30 June 2026, and the backstop on each lease only becomes effective at that lease's commencement date. What the Abernathy proceeds buy. TeraWulf sold a 50.1% JV stake to its own largest tenant for cash arriving in instalments through 2027 and says it will redeploy into wholly owned capacity — the next campus announcement tells you whether that happened.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: TeraWulf — Introduction. TeraWulf is where the Google financing machine touches dirt. It is also the only participant that has published, line by line, what standing behind someone else's lease is worth — because TeraWulf is the one who had to pay for it.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text:
TeraWulf — Role in the stack. A landlord, not a cloud. TeraWulf owns powered land and builds data centre shells on it, then leases critical IT load to operators who bring their own chips. That places it one rung below the neoclouds: it does not buy accelerators, does not carry GPU depreciation, and does not price compute. It converts secured grid interconnects into contracted rent.

It arrived here from bitcoin mining, which is the entire reason it matters. Miners hold the scarce input — energised, permitted power at scale — and Google has been systematically converting them. The Financial Times identified five such projects totalling 1.4 GW that raised $15bn of debt on the strength of a Google backstop . TeraWulf was the first.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
TeraWulf — Exposure. The operating business is small and just crossed over. Total revenue was $44.8m in the quarter to 30 June 2026, of which $31.9m — 71% — was HPC lease revenue and $12.8m was digital assets, against a net loss of $940.8m . Lease revenue passed mining revenue for the first time, while total revenue still fell year over year, because bitcoin declined faster than the leases ramped.

The contracts are large and mostly undelivered. Three leases signed with Fluidstack in August 2025 cover 378 MW of critical IT load at Lake Mariner in upstate New York; one had partially commenced by 30 June 2026, with the rest expected in the second half of 2026 and early 2027 . A second lease signed with Anthropic in July 2026 covers approximately 401 MW at the Justified Data Campus in Hawesville, Kentucky, on a 20-year initial term with two five-year extensions at Anthropic's election, first capacity expected in the second half of 2027 and full delivery in early 2028 . Against 779 MW contracted, 102 MW were energised as of July 2026 .

Now the part worth reading closely. Fluidstack is the named tenant on the Lake Mariner leases, and Google backstops its obligations: on a payment default or an insolvency, Google may either pay the lease termination fee or pay all rent due and assume the lease as tenant itself . That is what let TeraWulf raise $3,200.0m of 7.75% senior secured notes due 2030 through a subsidiary in October 2025 to fund the buildout .

The guarantee was not free. TeraWulf issued Google warrants over 73,580,000 shares at an exercise price of $0.01, expiring in August 2030, and Google pledged those warrants to the noteholders until the backstop became effective . TeraWulf booked the fair value at issuance as a $515.5m asset in deferred charges, amortised over the life of the leases — a company capitalising its own credit rating as an intangible and depreciating it alongside the transformers.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
TeraWulf — The bull case. The asset is the interconnect, and it is genuinely scarce. TeraWulf holds energised, permitted power that takes years and a queue position to replicate, and it monetises that without buying a single accelerator. No GPU depreciation, no obsolescence cycle, no exposure to whether Hopper or Blackwell holds its rental rate — the tenant absorbs all of it. The leases run 20 years with extension options at the tenant's election , which is utility duration on infrastructure that cost a fraction of the contracted rent.

The credit enhancement genuinely works, and the market prices it. Google-backed data centre projects borrowed at a median 7.1% against 9.3% for neocloud operators building around NVIDIA chips, a gap Jefferies analysts called a structural cost-of-capital disadvantage . TeraWulf's 7.75% coupon sits inside that spread. For a company with $44.8m of quarterly revenue to raise $3.2bn of secured debt at all is the backstop working exactly as designed.

And the counterparty risk is better than the tenant's own balance sheet suggests, because the guarantor can step into the lease . Google marks the aggregate liability across ten such developments at $815m while acknowledging exposure of as much as $44bn if every lease went bad — an accounting judgment that these leases do not default. TeraWulf's rent sits behind that judgment.

The Abernathy sale is evidence of underwriting, not just liquidity. TeraWulf put roughly $450m into a 168 MW Texas joint venture and agreed in July 2026 to sell its entire 50.1% for approximately $530.0m in cash at a premium to invested capital . A developer that can exit a stake at a premium mid-build has demonstrated the development margin is real.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
TeraWulf — The bear case. The reported loss is dominated by the guarantee, and it gets worse when things go well. TeraWulf recognised a $755.7m loss in the quarter and $972.0m across the half year on the change in fair value of the Google warrants, with the liability rising from $844.7m to $1,816.7m in six months . Those warrants strike at a cent, so their value tracks the share price: the better the equity story, the larger the loss booked on the instrument sold to buy the credit. It is non-cash, but it is not cosmetic — it is 73,580,000 shares of real dilution against 485.7m weighted average shares, and the $515.5m capitalised asset is the floor on what the arrangement cost, not the ceiling.

The Kentucky lease is the unhedged one. The Lake Mariner leases carry a Google backstop; no such support is disclosed for the 401 MW Anthropic lease , which is the larger of the two. Its reported $19bn of contracted revenue traces to the company's announcement and the press carrying it rather than to a filing — the 10-Q discloses the megawatts, the term and the options, but not the value . Financing Hawesville on Anthropic's credit alone is a materially different exercise from financing Lake Mariner on Google's, and TeraWulf has not yet shown it can.

Delivery is the actual risk, and the numbers are far apart. 102 MW energised against 779 MW contracted means most of the revenue depends on construction that has not happened, on a grid that has to deliver, to a schedule that runs into 2028. Each backstop only becomes effective at its own lease's commencement date — so during the build, the period of maximum capital at risk, the protection is not yet live.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Delivery is the actual risk, and the numbers are far apart. 102 MW energised against 779 MW contracted means most of the revenue depends on construction that has not happened, on a grid that has to deliver, to a schedule that runs into 2028. Each backstop only becomes effective at its own lease's commencement date — so during the build, the period of maximum capital at risk, the protection is not yet live.

And the concentration is nearly total. Two tenants, both routed to the same end user: Fluidstack leases capacity that serves Anthropic, and Anthropic leases the rest directly. The Abernathy buyer was a group led by Fluidstack itself , so TeraWulf's largest customer is also the acquirer of its assets. Every strand — the rent, the guarantee, the asset sale, the $35bn of TPU hardware financed to fill these buildings — terminates at one lab's ability to pay. TeraWulf is not diversified across the AI trade. It is a levered instrument on a single counterparty, wrapped in a guarantee from that counterparty's largest investor.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
TSMC: Revenue up 36% on units up 16.6%. TSMC is not selling more wafers to the AI boom — it is selling the same wafers for more, and rationing the packaging.

What to watch on TSMC: Whether Q3 2026 gross margin comes in below the 67.7% just reported. Management already guided it lower on N2 ramp dilution, so the reported number tests whether a new node's start-up cost outruns the price it commands. Whether unit growth converges with revenue growth in the next quarterly report. Today the gap is nineteen points, and pricing carries the story. When wafers shipped and revenue grow at similar rates, the pricing phase of this cycle is over. Whether C.C. Wei repeats on a subsequent call that advanced packaging capacity is limiting customers' growth. He is the highest-authority source in the corpus for packaging-as-bottleneck; the quarter he stops saying it is the quarter the queue clears. Whether top-ten customer concentration in the next 20-F exceeds 78%. It has gone 70%, 76%, 78% across three years while the largest customer's share fell from 22% to 19% — concentration is rising and broadening at the same time. Whether the gross margin absorbs the US fab mix. Construction at four to five times the Taiwan baseline has to show up somewhere; if it does not, customers are paying for it.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: TSMC — Introduction. Every argument about the AI buildout eventually arrives at one company's price list. TSMC's Q2 2026 says what that price list is doing, and it is not what a volume boom looks like.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: TSMC — Role in the stack. TSMC sells two things: a wafer start at a named process node, and a slot on an advanced packaging line. The second is now the scarcer good. Almost every accelerator on the site — NVIDIA's, AMD's, Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium — is a claim on the same two queues.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
TSMC — Exposure. Q2 2026 revenue was $40.20bn, up 36.0% , on 4.336 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers, up 16.6% . Nineteen points of that growth is price and mix. Gross margin was 67.7% against 59.9% for full-year 2025, 56.1% in 2024 and 54.4% in 2023 ; net profit was NT$706.56bn, up 77.4% . HPC reached 66% of revenue from 61% in Q1 , with N3 at 30% of wafer revenue and N2 booking its first-ever contribution at 3% .

Concentration is the counterweight: the ten largest customers were approximately 78% of 2025 net revenue, the largest at 19% and the second at 17% . TSMC names none of them.

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
TSMC — The bull case. Pricing power, demonstrated rather than asserted. N2 wafers are expected to run above $30,000 against roughly $20,000 at N3 — an estimate, because TSMC discloses no wafer prices — and the margin trajectory says customers are paying it. The company then raised 2026 capex to $60-64bn from $52-56bn , having spent $40.9bn in 2025 . Firms with pricing power and no demand problem behave exactly this way.

The strongest evidence for the scarcity is the CEO's. C.C. Wei said on the Q2 2026 call that TSMC's advanced packaging capacity was limiting its customers' growth . That is a named executive on the record describing his own line as the constraint on everyone above him — and it is a stronger citation than the widely circulated claim that the top three CoWoS customers hold more than 85% of 2026 capacity , which traces to an unattributed trade estimate with disputed wafer counts and is used here for nothing.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
TSMC — The bear case. The cost side is being rebuilt in the most expensive place available. US fab construction runs four to five times the Taiwan baseline, per CFO Wendell Huang in July 2026 , against $265bn of announced US investment after a further $100bn Arizona commitment . Depreciation from that arrives regardless of what pricing does.

The margin is already guided down. TSMC guided Q3 2026 revenue to $44.6-45.8bn and guided gross margin below the quarter just reported, attributing the step down to N2 ramp dilution. N2 is 3% of wafer revenue today ; the dilution scales with the ramp, and the pricing offset is an estimate rather than a disclosure .

Forecast, per TrendForce, relaying unnamed institutional investors via Taiwan's Economic Daily News: CoWoS capacity is reported to reach 120,000-140,000 wafers per month by end-2026, with the supply-demand gap narrowing from about 20% to about 10% . Third-hand provenance, and TSMC discloses no CoWoS capacity at all. But if the gap narrows, so does the reason customers accept the price.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Vertiv: The counterpoint to the integrators: power and thermal content earns roughly six times an ODM's margin inside the very same rack.

What to watch on Vertiv: Whether backlog grows again in the FY2026 10-K or flattens near $15.0bn. The 10-K already says customers may reduce or defer orders, usually with penalties, so the first flat print — not a decline — is the signal that ordering ahead has stopped. Whether adjusted operating margin lands inside the guided 22.8-23.8% band. Q1 2026 delivered 20.8% inclusive of tariff impacts; landing in the band would be a second consecutive year of expansion while absorbing trade costs, which is what pricing power looks like in a filing. Whether the 58% Americas revenue share moves. Vertiv's growth is concentrated in one region's build cycle, and a shift would show either diversification or that US permitting friction has started to bite. Whether any disclosure lets Vertiv's $15.0bn backlog be reconciled against Digital Realty's 1,402 MW under construction. The two may describe the same buildings from opposite sides, and nothing in either filing nets them. Whether direct-liquid-cooling orders keep converting at the rate the backlog implies. Uptime's Jacqueline Davis argues DLC stays confined to high-density AI and HPC for three years; if she is right, the retrofit demand behind part of that backlog arrives late.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Vertiv — Introduction. Vertiv is the answer to the question the systems layer keeps dodging. In the first quarter of 2026 the companies bolting AI racks together earned operating margins of 1.8 to 3.6 percent while the thermal, power and connector suppliers into those same racks earned 17.8 to 25.4 percent . Vertiv is on the profitable side of that line, selling into the identical demand.

chunks.heading: Role in the stack
chunks.text: Vertiv — Role in the stack. Coolant distribution units, sidecars, busway, switchgear and UPS — the power train and thermal loop that a 120 kW liquid-cooled rack cannot function without. Commercially it sits ahead of the data center layer rather than inside it: this equipment is ordered before the shell is finished, which makes Vertiv's order book the earliest hard read on how much capacity is actually being built.

chunks.heading: Exposure
chunks.text:
Vertiv — Exposure. FY2025 net sales were $10.2bn against $8.01bn in 2024, with 58% transacted in the Americas . Operating margin went from 4.9% in 2020 to 17.9% in 2025 on revenue up from $4.37bn to $10.23bn — against the 1.8 to 3.6 percent the rack integrators reported in the first quarter of 2026 . Estimated combined order backlog reached $15.0bn at the end of 2025, from $7.2bn a year earlier : about one and a half times annual revenue, with the 10-K stating that orders are being placed in advance of Vertiv's ability to fulfil them.

Q1 2026 net sales were $2,650m, up 30%, with 44% organic growth in the Americas and a 20.8% adjusted operating margin . The margin expanded inclusive of tariff impacts, which is the single most direct pricing-power evidence in the corpus for this part of the stack — compare Supermicro, where tariffs became an $89.4m line item against $1,019m of quarterly gross profit .

chunks.heading: The bull case
chunks.text:
Vertiv — The bull case. The rack-scale transition moved the profit pool and Vertiv is where part of it landed. A 120 kW rack carrying liquid coolant at two litres a second is a purchase order for cooling and power content that the integrator does not make, and the same shift shows up independently at Asia Vital Components, whose operating margin went from 2.47% to 19.73% , and Delta, 7.66% to 15.13% . Three companies, three countries, one direction.

Forecast, per Vertiv (company guidance, raised at Q1 2026): Full-year 2026 net sales of $13,500-14,000m with organic growth of 29 to 31% , on adjusted operating margin guided to 22.8-23.8%.

chunks.heading: The bear case
chunks.text:
Vertiv — The bear case. Backlog is not revenue, and Vertiv's own 10-K supplies the caveat: the majority is firm and expected to ship inside 12 to 18 months, and customers can reduce or defer, usually with penalties . It also says orders are arriving ahead of what Vertiv can build — which is a demand signal and a delivery risk in one sentence.

The deeper problem is that nobody can net this backlog against the buildings it serves. Digital Realty had 1,402 MW under construction, 54% pre-leased ; Vertiv has $15.0bn of equipment on order . Those may be the same demand counted from two sides, and no disclosure in either filing resolves it.

The named counterargument on the technology is Uptime Institute's Jacqueline Davis, who argued in April 2026 that direct liquid cooling will stay confined to high-density AI and HPC rather than reaching mainstream mission-critical adoption within three years , citing redundant CDU and manifold engineering, reduced ride-through time for generator start, and unresolved ownership of DLC components between facilities and IT teams. If she is right, the mainstream retrofit market is later than the order book implies. And the demand itself is borrowed from one layer down: 48% of surveyed data center experts named power availability as the most prominent obstacle to delivering projects on schedule . Vertiv sells the equipment; it does not sell the interconnection date.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: A compute buyer cannot pay. The question: What if one of the small number of counterparties underwriting the buildout cannot fund its commitments, and the sellers have to reprice a backlog built on one name?

Trigger: A round, an IPO or a contingent tranche that does not land — forcing a renegotiation, deferral or termination of contracted compute purchases by a counterparty that several sellers' backlogs depend on.

Tripwire: A contract modification, deferral or impairment disclosed against a named large customer by Oracle, Microsoft, CoreWeave or Nebius — or a fall in Oracle's remaining performance obligations not explained by delivery.. Likelihood: contested.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: A compute buyer cannot pay — Introduction. Start by throwing out the version of this argument you have already heard, because it is wrong in a way that discredits the real one.

chunks.heading: The bad version, and why it fails
chunks.text: A compute buyer cannot pay — The bad version, and why it fails. The popular framing sets Sam Altman's $1.4 trillion of data-center commitments against OpenAI's revenue and calls the gap a bubble. Do not. That figure is Altman's own attributed statement, covering roughly 30 GW over about eight years . It is not a sum of disclosed contracts, the balance is not publicly itemised, and setting an eight-year commitment against one year of revenue compares unlike things. This site's own corpus previously recorded it as an aggregation and had to delete the method: the addends did not reach the total, and the version in circulation counted NVIDIA's inbound equity as an outbound purchase.

chunks.heading: The honest version: concentration, not arithmetic
chunks.text:
A compute buyer cannot pay — The honest version: concentration, not arithmetic. What is disclosed is enough. OpenAI contracted about $300bn with Oracle over five years, equal to 4.5 GW ; an incremental $250bn of Azure services ; $38bn with AWS ; and up to $11.9bn with CoreWeave . Those four sum to roughly $600bn — and that is the number to argue with, because every addend is a disclosure rather than a paraphrase.

Against it: an annualized run rate above $20bn exiting 2025, on full-year 2025 revenue of roughly $13bn , reaching about $25bn annualized by February 2026 on an estimate that excludes Microsoft licensing . Gross margin was about 33% in FY2025, down from 40% the prior year , with projected cash burn near $27bn in 2026 and $63bn in 2027 and no cash-flow-positive year expected before 2030 .

The fragility is not the ratio. It is the financing terms. OpenAI raised $122bn at an $852bn post-money valuation in March 2026 — and of Amazon's $50bn commitment inside it, $35bn is contingent on an initial public offering or on reaching artificial general intelligence . Roughly a third of the largest private round ever raised is conditional on an event with no agreed definition. NVIDIA's much-quoted $100bn is a letter of intent, staged per gigawatt deployed, and NVIDIA's own filing says there is no assurance a transaction completes . AMD issued a warrant for up to 160 million shares at a cent, with full vesting contingent on 6 GW of deployment . Suppliers are paying equity for demand, which tells you how they price its certainty.

chunks.heading: The path the shock takes
chunks.text:
A compute buyer cannot pay — The path the shock takes. Capital to cloud. Oracle's remaining performance obligations of $523bn are dominated by one contract , and it spent $55.7bn of FY2026 capex against roughly $50bn of guidance to serve it. CoreWeave carries $24.9bn of debt on $4.8bn of equity , having been 62% Microsoft as recently as 2024 , and its March 2026 facility covenants on a 1.15x debt-service-coverage ratio — cash flow, not asset value . Nebius guided $20–25bn of 2026 capex on $3.0–3.4bn of revenue against contracts of $17.4bn with Microsoft and about $27bn with Meta . Each of these is a levered position on a handful of names.

Cloud to systems. Four customers were 75.1% of Super Micro's accounts receivable at March 2026, the largest at 32.2% , on a nine-month gross margin of 8.2% and cash down from $5.2bn to $1.3bn in nine months . Dell booked $24.4bn of AI orders against $16.1bn recognised in a single quarter . Thin margins plus concentrated receivables is how a customer's problem becomes an integrator's problem.

Systems to silicon. NVIDIA's data-center revenue was $75.2bn in the quarter ended April 2026, up 92% , and Broadcom guided Q3 FY2026 AI semiconductor revenue to $16bn, up 200% . Those growth rates are the last thing to break and the loudest when they do.

chunks.heading: Who says this will not happen
chunks.text:
A compute buyer cannot pay — Who says this will not happen. The filings, and they are not weak. Amy Hood reports $633bn of Microsoft remaining performance obligations while stating demand continues to exceed supply ; Alphabet's RPO reached $519.5bn from $108.2bn a year earlier . The buyer set is also broader than the discourse admits: Anthropic's run rate crossed $47bn in May 2026 and it raised $65bn in Series H funding the same month . A single failure would hurt; it would not empty the order book.

The macro steelman is the Federal Reserve's own: total US private nonfinancial credit stood at $42.2 trillion with the debt-to-GDP ratio at its lowest in two decades . This leverage is being layered onto an under-levered corporate sector. Bridgewater, forecasting about $650bn of 2026 big-four AI infrastructure investment , is on the cautious side of that same evidence — which is the point: the disagreement is about pace, not about whether the demand exists.

chunks.heading: What would falsify this
chunks.text: A compute buyer cannot pay — What would falsify this. - The OpenAI IPO completes and the $35bn contingent tranche converts . That single event removes the strangest term in the corpus and most of this page's force. - Oracle's RPO keeps rising while its capex is funded from operating cash flow. Concentration matters only if the seller is financing the buyer's growth. - A revenue year that covers a contract year. The commitments run about eight years; a run rate that makes the annualised obligation ordinary settles the argument on arithmetic. - Neocloud concentration falls with no customer above about a quarter of revenue, disclosed in a 10-Q rather than asserted on a call.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: The depreciation reset. The question: What happens to hyperscaler earnings if the assumed useful life of an AI server compresses back toward four years?

Trigger: One more large operator follows Amazon in shortening server lives — or an auditor forces the question — turning a private divergence of judgement into a sector-wide reset of the depreciation schedule.

Tripwire: A useful-life change disclosed in the accounting-policy note of a Microsoft, Alphabet or Meta 10-K or 10-Q, with the dollar effect on depreciation quantified in the same note.. Likelihood: already-happening.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: The depreciation reset — Introduction. This is the cheapest way for the buildout to disappoint. It needs no demand shock, no failed model, no bankruptcy — only an accounting estimate moving in the direction one of the four largest operators has already moved it.

chunks.heading: The mechanism
chunks.text:
The depreciation reset — The mechanism. Servers are capitalised and written off over an assumed useful life. Lengthen the assumption and reported operating income rises with no change in the business; shorten it and income falls the same way. The sensitivity is roughly $7bn of operating income per year, per year of change . Two qualifiers travel with that figure and this page will not print it without them: it was published as an illustrative example using approximate hyperscaler figures, and it is singular, not a big-four total.

What makes the estimate load-bearing now is the size of the pool it applies to. Combined big-four capital expenditure over the trailing four quarters to March 2026 ran at approximately 2.9 times the depreciation and finance-lease amortization behind it . Strip Amazon's bundled capitalised video content out of that denominator and the ratio goes above three. Every dollar of the gap becomes depreciation later, on a schedule nobody has agreed on.

chunks.heading: Why this is already happening, in part
chunks.text:
The depreciation reset — Why this is already happening, in part. January 2025 is the month the consensus broke, and it broke in filings rather than in commentary. Meta extended server and network useful life to 5.5 years, lowering depreciation by about $2.9bn . Amazon went the other way in the same month, shortening a subset of servers and networking equipment from six years to five, taking $889m of additional depreciation and $677m off net income in the nine months to September 2025 .

That comparison is the whole argument. Two companies buying similar machines for similar customers, in the same quarter, disagreed about how long the machines last. The reset is therefore not a hypothesis about the future — it is a disclosed accounting change at one operator, waiting to see whether the other three follow.

The direction of travel before that was uniformly the other way. Microsoft went from four years to six effective fiscal 2023 ; Alphabet to six, worth about $3.4bn of depreciation ; Amazon to six, worth about $3.2bn . Each was defensible alone. Together they lengthened the industry's assumed asset life exactly as the assets began changing fastest. And the extension does not stop the expense: Meta's depreciation on property and equipment still rose from about $11.0bn in 2023 to $18.0bn in 2025 despite the longer life .

chunks.heading: The path the shock takes
chunks.text:
The depreciation reset — The path the shock takes. Cloud first, because the charge lands on the income statement. A one-year compression is roughly $7bn a year of operating income per operator-year of change, against businesses where cash is already tight at the margin — Amazon's trailing-twelve-month capex equalled 102% of operating cash flow .

Then capital and policy, because the leveraged players have no software revenue to absorb it. CoreWeave posts a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin and a $740m GAAP quarterly net loss simultaneously ; depreciation and interest consume the middle of the P&L. Its $8.5bn March 2026 facility sits in a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary secured on substantially all of that subsidiary's assets — the GPUs are the lien — with a 1.15x debt-service-coverage covenant and a 2032 maturity . Shorter economic lives revalue that collateral against a six-year tenor. Nebius shows the reflex in the other direction: it extended server life from four to five years effective Q1 2026, in a quarter when depreciation and amortization rose to 40% of operating expenses .

Then compute silicon, where the sign flips. Shorter useful lives mean faster replacement cycles. The same event that cuts reported cloud earnings raises near-term accelerator demand. Anyone arguing this scenario as uniformly bearish has not followed it to the bottom of the stack.

chunks.heading: Who says this will not happen
chunks.text:
The depreciation reset — Who says this will not happen. Michael Burry makes the aggressive version — hyperscalers understating depreciation by about $176bn across 2026 to 2028 . He is a named short-seller with positions, and the counter-evidence is real.

Azure retired V100 GPUs roughly 7.5 years after launch , which is the single best datum against "GPUs are worthless in four years." Newer silicon is not following the deflation curve either: B200 rentals ran $4.50–7.00 an hour in Q2 2026 with marketplace rates rising month over month , and one-year reserved H100 pricing bottomed at $1.70 in October 2025 before rebounding about 38% to $2.35 by March 2026 . Demand is contracted, not hoped for: Microsoft reported $633bn of remaining performance obligations while stating that demand continues to exceed supply , and Alphabet's total RPO reached $519.5bn . Amy Hood's position is the strongest one available here — you do not sign that and then not need the machines.

chunks.heading: What would falsify this
chunks.text: The depreciation reset — What would falsify this. - Microsoft, Alphabet or Meta extends again rather than shortens in its next annual accounting-policy note. Three operators lengthening against one shortening makes Amazon the outlier, not the leading indicator. - Amazon reverses back to six years on the subset it shortened, and says why in the filing. - Reserved pricing on current-generation parts keeps rising through 2027 while Hopper capacity stays on contract past its seventh year. Residual value is the whole question, and the rental market prices it weekly. - The capex-to-depreciation ratio falls toward two without a capex cut — meaning depreciation caught up on the existing schedule and there is nothing left to reset.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: Power arrives late. The question: What if the machines are bought, the contracts are signed, and the electricity to run them is three years behind schedule?

Trigger: Load-queue studies, turbine deliveries and transmission builds slip past the in-service dates already written into contracted cloud capacity, so energisation rather than silicon sets the delivery date.

Tripwire: A hyperscaler or neocloud attributing a capacity or revenue shortfall to energisation delay on an earnings call or in a filing — or ERCOT's Batch Zero transmission plan, due fall 2027, pushing its cohort past 2030.. Likelihood: material.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Power arrives late — Introduction. The queues are not forecasts. They are filings, and they are the least speculative evidence on this site.

chunks.heading: The mechanism: the bottleneck inverted
chunks.text:
Power arrives late — The mechanism: the bottleneck inverted. Until about 2024 the interconnection problem was about getting generation onto the grid. It is now about getting load off it. ERCOT was tracking 438 GW of large-load interconnection requests, nearly 90% of it data centers , against an all-time peak demand of 85,508 MW — roughly five times the largest hour the system has ever served. The queue got there fast: 63 GW at the end of 2024, 226 GW by November 2025 .

PJM reopened its queue in April 2026 and drew 811 projects totalling 220 GW of nameplate capacity , gas-fired generation leading at 106 GW . Nameplate is the word that matters, and PJM says so itself. Only 24% of its 2020 entry cohort ever reached an interconnection agreement or became operational . Generation interconnection in PJM averaged 40 months against a federal target of eight to eleven , and in the data-center load-growth zones of PJM and ERCOT, active projects were waiting 36 to 48 months .

chunks.heading: Equipment and wires, separately
chunks.text:
Power arrives late — Equipment and wires, separately. Turbines. GE Vernova had roughly 10 GW of combined 2029 and 2030 delivery capacity left after Q1 2026 — one vendor, roughly a third of the global heavy-duty market, not an industry ceiling. Directional lead times on new heavy-duty orders were about 36 months , with industry waits reported as high as 84 months . Global orders hit 110 GW in 2025 against manufacturing capacity of 60 to 70 GW a year , and BNP Paribas put heavy-duty pricing near $790 per kW by July 2026 . Scarcity is showing up in price, which is the honest test of a shortage claim.

Wires are worse, and nobody is expanding them. The US built 888 miles of new 345 kV and above transmission in 2024 against roughly 5,000 miles a year indicated as necessary by the DOE's own planning study . Capacity markets are already pricing the gap: PJM's 2028–2029 auction cleared at its $325 per MW-day cap , 6.8 GW below the installed reserve margin target, attracting just 525 MW of new supply . A price cap and a shortfall in the same auction means the market cleared on administrative fiat, not on supply.

chunks.heading: The path the shock takes
chunks.text:
Power arrives late — The path the shock takes. Primary energy to grid is where the delay originates and where it compounds — turbine slots and interconnection studies are sequential, not parallel.

Grid to datacenter is already observable. Power availability was named the most prominent obstacle to on-schedule delivery by 48% of more than 280 surveyed industry experts . Local politics adds to it: Data Center Watch counted 75 US projects worth about $130bn blocked or delayed in Q1 2026 , a count from an advocacy-adjacent tracker with no published method, which is why it is an estimate here.

Datacenter to cloud is where it becomes financial. Contracted backlog carries delivery dates. Microsoft holds $633bn of remaining performance obligations and says demand exceeds supply ; Alphabet's RPO is $519.5bn ; CoreWeave's backlog is $99.4bn . Late energisation does not cancel that revenue, it defers it — while the machines bought to serve it depreciate on schedule. Nebius guided $20–25bn of 2026 capex against $3.0–3.4bn of revenue ; that ratio only works if the capacity energises roughly when planned.

chunks.heading: Who says this will not happen
chunks.text:
Power arrives late — Who says this will not happen. The steelman here is stronger than for any other scenario on this site, and it comes from inside the industry.

Scott Strazik, GE Vernova's CEO, says the turbines are "really not the gating item," pointing instead at EPC buildout, permitting and fuel availability — said on the same call that produced the 36-month lead time . Ed Crooks of Wood Mackenzie says GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries have all announced significant gas-equipment capacity expansions since the start of 2025 . Wood Mackenzie projects 63 GW of turbine manufacturing capacity additions between 2026 and 2030 and expects orders to peak in 2026 ; GE Vernova targets 30 GW of annual output by 2030 .

Grid Strategies supplies the demand-side counter: the data-center portion of utility load forecasts is likely overstated by roughly 25 GW . The same report's other half must travel with it — 2022–2025 load forecasts were revised up, not down. Meanwhile faster supply exists: EIA projects US solar capacity rising from 151 GW in 2025 to 223 GW in 2027 , fuel is cheap at a forecast $3.67 per MMBtu Henry Hub , and buyers are simply paying to bypass the queue — Microsoft's 2 GW Pecos site is being built with the company funding the energy infrastructure .

chunks.heading: What would falsify this
chunks.text: Power arrives late — What would falsify this. - PJM's Cycle 1 realisation rate runs well above the 24% precedent . If most of the 220 GW nameplate reaches an interconnection agreement, the queue is a pipeline rather than a waiting room. - GE Vernova hits its output ramp on schedule and 2029 slots reopen. Published slot availability moving out rather than in kills the equipment leg. - 345 kV-plus mileage climbs toward the DOE benchmark. This is annual, published, and currently off by roughly a factor of five. - A PJM capacity auction clears below its cap with meaningful new supply. Two consecutive uncapped clears with new entry would say the market solved it.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: Taiwan interdiction. The question: What breaks, in what order, if the island holding most of the world's advanced-process capacity stops shipping — and what can this corpus honestly say about the cost?

Trigger: A blockade, quarantine or shipping interdiction halting Taiwan's export flow. This page argues the transmission mechanism only; the corpus holds nothing that would support a probability.

Tripwire: TSMC moving a Taiwan shipment interruption from a risk factor to a current-period disclosure in a 20-F or 6-K. Absent that, the only published proxy is Taiwan's advanced-capacity share failing to fall on its projected 2027 path.. Likelihood: low.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Taiwan interdiction — Introduction. Every other scenario on this site is argued from disclosures. This one cannot be, and the useful thing it can do is say exactly where the evidence stops.

chunks.heading: The exposure, which is measurable
chunks.text:
Taiwan interdiction — The exposure, which is measurable. Taiwan held 66% of global advanced-process foundry capacity — 16/14nm and below — in 2024, against Korea at 11%, the United States at 10% and China at 9% . That is a 2024 baseline on a 2026 page. The same analysis projects the Taiwanese share falling toward the mid-fifties by 2027 as US share roughly doubles, but that projection sits in the corpus's annotations rather than in a citable fact, so this page treats it as directional and does not print it. Rhodium separately put Taiwan's share of sub-10nm logic at 92% , an estimate dated 2022.

The tighter chokepoint is above the wafer. C.C. Wei said on TSMC's Q2 2026 call that the company's advanced packaging capacity was limiting its customers' growth — a named CEO stating that his own packaging line caps demand. CoWoS lead times ran 52 to 78 weeks with capacity booked through end-2026 , and NVIDIA's 2026 allocation is estimated at about 595,000 wafers, roughly 60% of the total .

Two structural facts make substitution slow. ASML plans to ship around 65 Low-NA EUV systems in 2026, with about 30% more capacity planned for 2027 — an annual flow, not an installed base, and the hard ceiling on how fast anyone builds a replacement. And Taiwan itself is fragile before the fabs are: it imports about 97% of its energy and holds roughly two weeks of emergency supply . The grid fails before the cleanrooms do.

chunks.heading: What this corpus cannot support
chunks.text:
Taiwan interdiction — What this corpus cannot support. There is no AI-era model of this event in the research corpus, and this page will not manufacture one.

What exists is two estimates that measure different things. Rhodium Group estimated that a Chinese blockade halting all Taiwan trade would put well over $2 trillion of global economic activity at risk — activity at risk, which Rhodium itself calls a conservative and partial estimate excluding second-order effects, escalation and sanctions. Bloomberg Economics models something else entirely: a first-year GDP loss. Its figures are paywalled at source, carried in the corpus as a dispute flag, and not printed here. Averaging the two would be a category error, and neither uses AI-era trade weights — both predate the buildout that makes the question urgent. The honest output is therefore a mechanism, not a magnitude. Anyone quoting a dollar cost for an AI-era interdiction is extrapolating, and should say so.

chunks.heading: The path the shock takes
chunks.text:
Taiwan interdiction — The path the shock takes. Fab and tooling to compute silicon. NVIDIA's data-center revenue was $75.2bn in the quarter ended April 2026 at a 74.9% gross margin , and essentially all of it passes through Taiwanese wafers and Taiwanese packaging. Below that sit substrates, where four Taiwanese and two Japanese suppliers were seeking upfront commitments for Intel's EMIB capacity , and ABF build-up film, whose maker reported a segment business profit margin above 50% with its next plant not operating until 2032 . The deepest layer has the longest replacement time.

Silicon to systems. Rack integration is Taiwanese too. Hon Hai turned NT$8.10tn of 2025 revenue at a 6.15% gross margin , with Cloud and Networking Products at 48% of Q1 2026 revenue . Foxconn says it runs more than 40 US facilities across 12 states , but discloses no split of AI-rack output by geography — so that footprint cannot be scored as substitution capacity.

Systems to cloud. The buyers have signed for capacity with no alternate supply: $633bn of Microsoft remaining performance obligations against volume GPU lead times of 36 to 52 weeks on an industry backlog of roughly 3.6 million units . In this scenario the depreciation argument inverts — installed hardware becomes more valuable, not less.

chunks.heading: Who says this matters less than it looks
chunks.text:
Taiwan interdiction — Who says this matters less than it looks. Diversification is real and partly funded. TSMC's announced US investment reached $265bn . Intel put 18A into high-volume production at the start of 2026 and produced the first commercial logic product on High-NA EUV .

The counter to the counter is cost and time. US fab construction runs four to five times the Taiwan baseline , and N2 contributed just 3% of TSMC wafer revenue in Q2 2026, its first quarter of contribution — leading-edge share moves slowly even when the money is committed. China's alternative is further back still: SMIC's entire 2025 revenue was $9.33bn at a 21.0% gross margin , on advanced-node capacity conservatively estimated at 45,000 wafers a month .

No named expert in this corpus argues the probability of this event in either direction. The site's expert prediction ledger failed its attribution audit and is quarantined, so it cannot be cited. That absence is why the standing here is low rather than contested — not because the risk is small, but because nothing licenses a stronger claim.

chunks.heading: What would falsify this
chunks.text: Taiwan interdiction — What would falsify this. - Taiwan's advanced-process capacity share falls faster than the projected 2027 path, in the next annual TrendForce update, with US share ahead of schedule. Concentration is the whole scenario. - The CoWoS supply-demand gap closes and lead times fall inside a year. A packaging chokepoint that stops being a chokepoint removes the sharpest link. - A non-Taiwan advanced-packaging line qualifies at volume for a top-three accelerator customer. Announced capacity is not qualified capacity; a shipping product is. - Intel 14A lands committed external customers. Its own 10-Q still describes 14A external demand as uncommitted; that changing would give the West a second leading-edge source rather than a second fab.
